Interproximal reduction (Option C) and fixed orthodontics (Option D) are premature and unnecessary because physiological tongue pressure naturally relocates the permanent incisor once the physical barrier is removed.

oral-pathology-medicine-110.question: A 55-year-old male chronic smoker presents for management of a persistent, irregular white plaque on the lateral border of the tongue that cannot be wiped off with gauze. An incisional biopsy confirms epithelial dysplasia with hyperkeratosis. What is the MOST appropriate definitive management for this potentially malignant lesion according to US oral pathology standards?
options: Complete surgical excision with histologically negative margins and long-term clinical surveillance
Prescription of systemic antifungal therapy with fluconazole for 14 days
Application of high-potency topical corticosteroid ointment for two weeks
Immediate prophylactic extraction of adjacent mandibular molars
oral-pathology-medicine-110.explanation: Option A is correct because according to Neville's oral and maxillofacial pathology standards and ADA clinical guidelines, oral leukoplakia exhibiting epithelial dysplasia on a high-risk anatomic site (lateral tongue) carries a significant risk of malignant transformation and requires complete surgical excision with histologically clear margins combined with lifelong surveillance. Systemic antifungal therapy (Option B) is ineffective because the lesion has been histopathologically confirmed as epithelial dysplasia rather than hyperplastic candidiasis. Topical corticosteroids (Option C) are indicated for immune-mediated chronic ulcerative diseases such as lichen planus and do not reverse or treat dysplastic epithelial alterations. Prophylactic tooth extraction (Option D) is completely non-therapeutic, mutilating, and unrelated to the management of mucosal epithelial dysplasia.

oral-pathology-medicine-328.question: A 35-year-old female presents with multiple radiolucent lesions of the jaws diagnosed as odontogenic keratocysts. Physical examination reveals multiple cutaneous basal cell carcinomas, palmar and plantar pits, calcification of the falx cerebri, and bifid ribs. Which genetic syndrome should this patient be evaluated for?
options: Gardner syndrome
Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin-Goltz syndrome)
Cleidocranial dysplasia
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
oral-pathology-medicine-328.explanation: Option B is correct because nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin-Goltz syndrome) is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by multiple odontogenic keratocysts of the jaws, cutaneous basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, bifid ribs, and calcification of the falx cerebri due to mutations in the PTCH1 gene. Gardner syndrome presents with gastrointestinal polyps, osteomas, and supernumerary teeth rather than keratocysts and basal cell carcinomas. Cleidocranial dysplasia manifests with aplastic or hypoplastic clavicles and delayed exfoliation of teeth, while Peutz-Jeghers syndrome features intestinal hamartomatous polyps and perioral melanotic macules.

oral-pathology-medicine-394.question: Which of the following malignant salivary gland neoplasms classically exhibits marked neurotropism with perineural invasion, frequently causing localized facial pain, paresthesia, or cranial nerve palsy?
options: Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Pleomorphic adenoma
Warthin tumor
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
oral-pathology-medicine-394.explanation: Option A is correct because adenoid cystic carcinoma classically demonstrates a high predilection for perineural invasion (neurotropism), which frequently results in localized pain, paresthesia, and facial nerve paralysis. Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign mixed tumor that can undergo malignant transformation but does not invade perineural spaces when benign. Warthin tumor is a benign cystic parotid neoplasm associated with smoking, and while mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common salivary gland malignancy, it does not demonstrate perineural spread as classically or aggressively as adenoid cystic carcinoma.

oral-pathology-medicine-376.question: A 28-year-old female presents with multiple well-defined radiolucencies in the posterior mandible and maxilla associated with unerupted teeth. Physical examination reveals prominent frontal bossing, ocular hypertelorism, palmar pitting, and bifid ribs on chest radiography. What is the most likely diagnosis of these jaw lesions?
options: Cherubism
Central giant cell granuloma
Odontogenic keratocyst
Ameloblastoma
oral-pathology-medicine-376.explanation: Option C is correct because the patient exhibits classic signs of nevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin-Goltz) syndrome—including frontal bossing, hypertelorism, palmar pitting, and bifid ribs—in which the multiple jaw radiolucencies are odontogenic keratocysts (OKCs). Cherubism is a benign childhood condition characterized by bilateral symmetrical painless jaw expansion with giant cells that typically regresses after puberty and lacks frontal bossing or palmar pits. Central giant cell granuloma and ameloblastoma typically occur as isolated, non-syndromic, solitary jaw lesions rather than multiple syndromic cysts.

oral-pathology-medicine-362.question: A 35-year-old female presents for a routine dental examination. A periapical radiograph reveals a well-defined, uniformly radiopaque area at the apex of a vital, asymptomatic mandibular first molar (#19). The periodontal ligament space and lamina dura around the root apex remain intact, and no radiolucent halo is present. Histological examination of this area reveals dense, avascular lamellar bone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Condensing osteitis
Periapical cemento-osseous dysplasia
Cementoblastoma
Idiopathic osteosclerosis
oral-pathology-medicine-362.explanation: Option D is correct because idiopathic osteosclerosis (dense bone island) is an asymptomatic, radiopaque focus of dense lamellar bone that occurs adjacent to vital teeth without an inflammatory cause, characteristically lacking any surrounding radiolucent rim or capsule. Condensing osteitis occurs in response to chronic pulpal inflammation or necrosis in non-vital or irreversibly inflamed teeth. Periapical cemento-osseous dysplasia and cementoblastoma both typically exhibit a peripheral radiolucent halo, and cementoblastoma is fused directly to the tooth root with obliteration of the periodontal ligament space.

oral-pathology-medicine-371.question: Which of the following odontogenic tumors is characterized histologically by duct-like structures (pseudoducts) lined by cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells and whorled masses of polyhedral cells surrounded by a well-developed fibrous capsule?
options: Calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor
Ameloblastic fibroma
Ameloblastoma
Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor
oral-pathology-medicine-371.explanation: Option D is correct because adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) histologically exhibits duct-like tubular structures (pseudoducts) lined by cuboidal or columnar epithelial cells, rosette-like cellular arrays, and whorled polyhedral odontogenic epithelium enclosed within a thick fibrous capsule. Calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor (Pindborg tumor) is characterized by sheets of polyhedral cells with amyloid-like material and concentric Liesegang ring calcifications. Ameloblastic fibroma consists of cords of odontogenic epithelium in a cell-rich primitive dental papilla-like ectomesenchyme, whereas ameloblastoma features nests with peripheral ameloblast-like columnar palisading and central stellate reticulum.

oral-pathology-medicine-461.question: A 40-year-old female presents with loose maxillary anterior teeth. Clinical examination reveals severe generalized periodontitis, deep probing depths (>9 mm), and Class III mobility of teeth #7, #8, #9, and #10. Periapical radiographs show horizontal and vertical bone loss extending beyond 75% of the root length, resulting in a hopeless prognosis for these teeth. What is the MOST appropriate treatment plan for teeth #7, #8, #9, and #10?
options: Scaling and root planing with adjunctive systemic antibiotics
Extraction and consideration for prosthetic replacement
Periodontal splinting followed by routine supportive periodontal therapy
Open flap debridement with guided tissue regeneration bone grafting
oral-pathology-medicine-461.explanation: Option B is correct because teeth with a hopeless periodontal prognosis—characterized by Class III mobility, loss of functional stability, and attachment loss extending beyond 75% of the root length into the apical third—cannot be maintained and require extraction to halt ongoing alveolar bone resorption and prepare for prosthetic replacement. Scaling and root planing with systemic antibiotics cannot restore bone or achieve reattachment on hopeless teeth. Periodontal splinting is contraindicated for hopeless teeth with severe active attachment loss, and regenerative bone grafting requires self-contained osseous defects rather than generalized terminal bone loss.

oral-pathology-medicine-464.question: A 45-year-old female presents with a persistent dull ache in her maxillary left posterior quadrant. She underwent root canal treatment on tooth #14 (maxillary left first molar) six months ago. Clinical examination reveals localized buccal vestibule tenderness and mild swelling adjacent to tooth #14. Radiographs demonstrate an enlarging periapical radiolucency around the mesiobuccal root, suggesting an untreated second mesiobuccal canal (MB2). What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-surgical endodontic retreatment
Periodontal scaling and root planing
Analgesic prescription and annual radiographic monitoring
Systemic antibiotic therapy alone
oral-pathology-medicine-464.explanation: Option A is correct because post-treatment apical periodontitis with an enlarging periapical radiolucency and symptoms indicates persistent intraradicular infection, most commonly caused by an untreated second mesiobuccal (MB2) canal in maxillary first molars, for which non-surgical endodontic retreatment is the primary treatment of choice per AAE guidelines. Periodontal scaling and root planing treats marginal periodontitis and does not address endodontic root canal infections. Analgesic monitoring or antibiotic therapy alone without mechanical cleaning and disinfection fails to remove the bacterial biofilm within the canal system.

oral-pathology-medicine-425.question: A 40-year-old male presents with mild tenderness to percussion on tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor). The tooth does not respond to cold or electric pulp testing. A periapical radiograph reveals loss of the apical lamina dura and a well-circumscribed radiolucency approximately 1.5 cm in diameter at the apex of tooth #8. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate extraction of tooth #8
Immediate periapical surgical apicoectomy with biopsy
Clinical and radiographic observation without treatment
Non-surgical root canal treatment, followed by surgical intervention only if the lesion fails to resolve
oral-pathology-medicine-425.explanation: Option D is correct because AAE standards dictate that non-vital teeth with extensive periapical radiolucencies (periapical cysts or granulomas) should initially undergo conservative non-surgical root canal treatment, as many large lesions heal completely without surgical intervention, reserving surgery or biopsy for non-healing cases. Immediate extraction is unnecessarily destructive for a structurally restorable tooth with intact coronal and radicular tooth structure. Immediate apicoectomy without prior root canal disinfection violates fundamental biological principles of endodontic therapy, and observation alone will result in advancing infection and bone destruction.

oral-pathology-medicine-441.question: A patient presents with a deep Class II carious lesion on tooth #19. Following complete caries excavation, the remaining dentin thickness over the pulp is less than 1 mm. The dentist applies a thin layer of calcium hydroxide liner followed by a zinc oxide-eugenol (ZOE) base prior to placing a dental amalgam restoration. What is the primary clinical rationale for placing the ZOE base in this scenario?
options: To provide chemical adhesion between the cavity walls and the amalgam restoration
To provide thermal and mechanical insulation to protect the pulp from condensation forces
To stimulate reparative dentin bridge formation through direct contact with pulp tissue
To acid-etch the dentinal tubules and create a micromechanical hybrid layer
oral-pathology-medicine-441.explanation: Option B is correct because under an amalgam restoration where remaining dentin thickness is less than 1 mm, an intermediate cement base such as ZOE provides thermal insulation against temperature fluctuations and mechanical strength to resist amalgam condensation forces. Amalgam does not chemically bond to tooth structure or to ZOE. Reparative dentin bridge formation is stimulated by calcium hydroxide (or bioceramics) rather than ZOE, and acid etching/hybridization is an adhesive resin protocol inapplicable to amalgam restorations.

oral-pathology-medicine-473.question: A 28-year-old female patient (non-smoker, systemically healthy) presents for a periodontal evaluation. Clinical examination reveals localized 8 mm probing depths, clinical attachment loss ≥5 mm, and radiographic bone loss extending to the middle third of the root on teeth #3, #14, and #19, with otherwise healthy gingival tissues and minimal plaque accumulation. Her medical history is unremarkable, but she reports that her mother lost multiple teeth at an early age. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Stage I, Grade A periodontitis
Stage III, Grade C periodontitis
Necrotizing periodontitis
Dental biofilm-induced gingivitis
oral-pathology-medicine-473.explanation: Option B is correct because under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, severe attachment loss with probing depths ≥6 mm and bone loss extending into the middle third of the root qualifies as Stage III periodontitis, while rapid progression disproportionate to local biofilm deposits in a young patient with a family history indicates Grade C. Stage I, Grade A represents initial, mild periodontitis with minimal bone loss (<15%) and slow progression. Necrotizing periodontitis presents with painful punched-out necrotic papillae, pseudomembranes, and fetid odor, while gingivitis is confined to the gingiva without clinical attachment loss or radiographic bone loss.

oral-pathology-medicine-501.question: A 14-year-old male presents with acute pain and swelling in the maxillary right quadrant 3 days following the extraction of tooth #3 (maxillary right first molar). Clinical examination reveals a localized, fluctuant, tender swelling at the extraction site, purulent exudate discharging from the socket, and ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Prescribe oral antibiotics alone and schedule follow-up in one week
Debride and irrigate the socket, establish drainage, and prescribe systemic antibiotics and analgesics
Place an eugenol-impregnated sedative dressing in the socket and observe
Recommend warm saline mouth rinses and over-the-counter analgesics only
oral-pathology-medicine-501.explanation: Option B is correct because the presence of purulent discharge, localized swelling, and regional lymphadenopathy indicates an acute post-extraction surgical site infection requiring mechanical debridement, copious saline irrigation to evacuate purulent exudate, and systemic antibiotics combined with analgesics. Prescribing antibiotics alone without mechanical debridement or establishing drainage fails to remove the underlying necrotic nidus. Placing an eugenol-containing sedative dressing is indicated for alveolar osteitis (dry socket), which lacks purulence and lymphadenopathy, and is contraindicated in acute purulent infections. Warm saline rinses and analgesics alone are insufficient to manage an active infection exhibiting regional lymphatic involvement.

oral-pathology-medicine-503.question: A 55-year-old female with a known history of stable angina develops retrosternal chest pain radiating to her left arm, diaphoresis, and shortness of breath during dental hygiene treatment. The procedure is immediately halted. Her blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg, and her pulse is 90 bpm. What is the MOST appropriate immediate step in the management of this patient?
options: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) and provide supplemental oxygen
Place the patient in a fully supine position and administer nitrous oxide
Initiate chest compressions and deploy an automated external defibrillator (AED)
Administer sublingual aspirin and immediately discharge the patient home
oral-pathology-medicine-503.explanation: Option A is correct because the immediate first-line management for a conscious patient experiencing an acute episode of known stable angina is to position the patient comfortably (upright or semi-reclined), administer supplemental oxygen, and provide sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) while monitoring vital signs. Placing the patient supine increases venous return and cardiac preload, thereby increasing myocardial oxygen demand and exacerbating anginal pain. CPR and AED deployment are indicated only for cardiac arrest in an unresponsive, pulseless patient. Aspirin must be chewed and swallowed—not given sublingually—and activating EMS is indicated if chest pain fails to resolve after nitroglycerin therapy or if myocardial infarction is suspected.

oral-pathology-medicine-508.question: A 10-year-old male patient presents with his parents, who are concerned about the eruption pattern of his maxillary teeth. Clinical and radiographic examinations reveal that tooth #11 (permanent maxillary left canine) is erupting palatally and significantly displaced from its normal arch position, impinging on the root of tooth #10. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Monitor the eruption of tooth #11 for 6 months to allow potential self-correction
Extract primary tooth H immediately and observe without orthodontic evaluation
Refer the patient for an orthodontic consultation and comprehensive treatment planning
Surgically expose tooth #11 and initiate immediate fixed appliance traction
oral-pathology-medicine-508.explanation: Option C is correct because an ectopic, palatally erupting permanent canine (#11) actively impinging on adjacent root structures (#10) requires comprehensive orthodontic evaluation and 3D imaging (such as CBCT) to plan interceptive traction or space creation and prevent lateral incisor root resorption. Option A is incorrect because watchful waiting allows progressive, irreversible root resorption of the lateral incisor and further canine impaction. Option B is incorrect because while extracting primary tooth H can aid eruption in early non-impinging cases, active root impingement demands orthodontic diagnostic planning first. Option D is incorrect because surgical exposure and traction require careful preparatory anchorage and biomechanical planning rather than immediate unilateral intervention.

oral-pathology-medicine-513.question: A 7-year-old female patient is brought to the dental office 30 minutes after sustaining trauma to her anterior teeth. Clinical examination reveals an uncomplicated crown fracture of tooth #8 involving enamel and dentin without pulpal exposure. The tooth is mildly tender to percussion with slight mobility, but no displacement is noted. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management for tooth #8?
options: Pulpectomy and placement of a stainless steel crown
Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide or mineral trioxide aggregate
Dentin sealing and composite resin restoration
Observation and periodic vitality testing without restorative treatment
oral-pathology-medicine-513.explanation: Option C is correct because an uncomplicated crown fracture involving enamel and dentin without pulpal exposure requires prompt sealing of exposed dentinal tubules and composite resin restoration to protect the vital pulp of an immature permanent tooth (#8) from bacterial invasion and thermal irritation. Option A is incorrect because pulpectomy is an invasive, non-vital procedure contraindicated in a restorable, vital tooth without pulpal exposure. Option B is incorrect because direct pulp capping is indicated only when there is a mechanical or carious pinpoint pulpal exposure. Option D is incorrect because leaving dentinal tubules unsealed risks bacterial contamination, pulp inflammation, and eventual necrosis.

oral-pathology-medicine-514.question: According to the 2021 AHA/ADA guidelines, which of the following oral antibiotics is the recommended first-line regimen for infective endocarditis prophylaxis in an adult patient with a history of a non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy?
options: Amoxicillin
Cephalexin
Clindamycin
Azithromycin
oral-pathology-medicine-514.explanation: Option B is correct because the 2021 AHA/ADA guidelines designate oral cephalexin (2 g) as the preferred first-line alternative for infective endocarditis prophylaxis in patients with a history of a non-anaphylactic (non-IgE-mediated) penicillin allergy. Option A is incorrect because amoxicillin is a penicillin derivative and is strictly contraindicated in patients with a confirmed penicillin allergy. Option C is incorrect because clindamycin is no longer recommended by the AHA/ADA due to high rates of adverse events and Clostridioides difficile colitis. Option D is incorrect because macrolides like azithromycin are reserved for patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria to penicillins or cephalosporins.

oral-pathology-medicine-517.question: A 48-year-old female presents with severe, spontaneous, throbbing pain in the maxillary left posterior region that wakes her from sleep. She reports that thermal stimuli provoke severe pain that lingers for several minutes. Clinical examination reveals tooth #14 has a deep composite restoration approaching the pulp. The tooth is non-tender to percussion and palpation, but cold testing produces severe pain that lingers for 45 seconds. Periapical radiography shows normal periodontal ligament space and no periapical radiolucency. According to the American Association of Endodontists (AAE), what is the pulpal diagnosis for tooth #14?
options: Normal pulp
Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Pulpal necrosis
oral-pathology-medicine-517.explanation: Option C is correct because spontaneous, nocturnal throbbing pain and thermal responses that linger significantly after stimulus removal are the classic diagnostic hallmarks of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis under AAE terminology. Option A is incorrect because a normal pulp produces only a mild, transient response that resolves immediately after stimulus removal. Option B is incorrect because reversible pulpitis is characterized by quick, non-lingering discomfort upon stimulation and lacks spontaneous nocturnal episodes. Option D is incorrect because pulpal necrosis produces complete unresponsiveness to thermal and electric sensibility testing.

oral-pathology-medicine-520.question: A 72-year-old male presents with loose maxillary and mandibular complete dentures fabricated 10 years ago. Clinical examination demonstrates severely worn denture teeth, a markedly decreased occlusal vertical dimension (OVD), and poor retention and stability due to advanced alveolar ridge resorption. What is the MOST appropriate definitive prosthodontic management?
options: Fabrication of new complete dentures
Chairside hard reline of the existing dentures
Laboratory rebase of the existing dentures
Application of a temporary soft tissue conditioner
oral-pathology-medicine-520.explanation: Option A is correct because fabricating new complete dentures is the definitive treatment indicated when existing 10-year-old prostheses exhibit severely abraded denture teeth, inadequate retention, and loss of occlusal vertical dimension (OVD), which cannot be corrected by relining alone. Options B and C are incorrect because hard relining and rebasing merely adapt the denture base to resorbed ridges but fail to restore severely worn artificial teeth or collapsed vertical dimensions, inadvertently locking in occlusal errors. Option D is incorrect because soft tissue conditioners are short-term diagnostic or therapeutic liners used to condition inflamed mucosal tissues rather than a definitive solution for worn, unstable prostheses.

oral-pathology-medicine-522.question: According to ANSI/ADA Specification No. 19 for elastomeric dental impression materials, which physical property is specifically evaluated by the material's capacity to reproduce a continuous scribed line 20 micrometers in width into a gypsum die?
options: Elastic recovery
Detail reproduction
Dimensional stability
Tear strength
oral-pathology-medicine-522.explanation: Option B is correct because detail reproduction is defined under ANSI/ADA Specification No. 19 as the ability of an elastomeric impression material to cleanly record and transfer a continuous line 20 micrometers in width to a gypsum cast. Option A is incorrect because elastic recovery reflects the percentage of recovery from elastic deformation following removal from oral undercuts. Option C is incorrect because dimensional stability measures the resistance to dimensional shrinkage or expansion over time due to polymerization contraction or volatile byproduct release. Option D is incorrect because tear strength measures the resistance of a material to fracturing in thin sulcular or interproximal margins during impression removal.

oral-pathology-medicine-525.question: A 52-year-old male with a history of generalized severe periodontitis successfully completed active surgical and non-surgical therapy 6 months ago. At his evaluation, he presents with no bleeding on probing, probing depths of 2–3 mm with isolated 4 mm sites, and no progressive attachment loss. According to American Academy of Periodontology (AAP) standards, what is the MOST appropriate recall interval for periodontal maintenance in this patient?
options: Every 3 months
Every 6 months
Every 9 months
Every 12 months
oral-pathology-medicine-525.explanation: Option A is correct because the American Academy of Periodontology (AAP) recommends a 3-month periodontal maintenance interval for patients treated for severe periodontitis, as subgingival pathogenic microflora typically repopulate treated periodontal pockets within 9 to 12 weeks. Option B is incorrect because a 6-month interval permits mature pathogenic biofilm establishment and increases the risk of recurrent disease in patients with a history of severe periodontitis. Options C and D are incorrect because recall intervals of 9 to 12 months are clinically inappropriate for periodontal maintenance and allow unchecked subgingival calculus formation and progressive attachment loss.

oral-pathology-medicine-569.question: According to the American Dental Association (ADA) Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct, the dentist's obligation to safeguard patient confidentiality and medical records is derived primarily from which core ethical principle?
options: Beneficence
Nonmaleficence
Justice
Patient autonomy
oral-pathology-medicine-569.explanation: Option D is correct because Section 1 of the ADA Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct places patient confidentiality under Patient Autonomy ('self-governance'), affirming the patient's right to control their own healthcare information. Option A is incorrect because Beneficence ('do good') mandates promoting patient welfare and providing competent, timely care. Option B is incorrect because Nonmaleficence ('do no harm') dictates avoiding harm and keeping clinical skills and knowledge up to date. Option C is incorrect because Justice ('fairness') involves delivering care without bias and ensuring fair distribution of dental resources.

oral-pathology-medicine-570.question: A 35-year-old female presents for a routine dental examination. A periapical radiograph of the maxillary right first molar (#3) reveals a well-circumscribed, uniform radiopacity adjacent to the apex of the mesial root. Tooth #3 is asymptomatic, non-carious, non-tender to percussion or palpation, and responds normally to thermal pulp testing. What is the MOST appropriate management for this radiopacity?
options: Initiate endodontic therapy on tooth #3
Perform surgical enucleation and biopsy of the apical lesion
Prescribe systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics
Periodic observation and radiographic monitoring
oral-pathology-medicine-570.explanation: Option D is correct because an asymptomatic periapical radiopacity associated with a vital, non-carious tooth is classic for idiopathic osteosclerosis (dense bone island), a benign developmental variation of trabecular bone requiring no intervention beyond periodic radiographic monitoring. Option A is incorrect because endodontic therapy is contraindicated on a vital, asymptomatic tooth without pulpal disease. Option B is incorrect because idiopathic osteosclerosis is non-neoplastic, does not expand cortices, and requires no surgical exploration or biopsy. Option C is incorrect because this lesion is a non-infectious bony variation that does not respond to antibiotic therapy.

oral-pathology-medicine-546.question: A 28-year-old female presents with a crown fracture of her maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8) extending subgingivally 2 mm apical to the cementoenamel junction on the facial aspect. Clinical and radiographic examinations demonstrate that the tooth is vital and has adequate root length, but an adequate restorative ferrule cannot be obtained without exposing sound tooth structure. What is the MOST appropriate treatment sequence to restore tooth #8?
options: Surgical crown lengthening followed by full-coverage crown restoration
Placement of a subgingival direct composite resin restoration
Preparation and bonding of a porcelain laminate veneer
Immediate extraction and implant placement
oral-pathology-medicine-546.explanation: Option A is correct because surgical crown lengthening re-establishes the supracrestal attached tissues (biological width) and exposes 1.5 to 2 mm of sound supragingival tooth structure needed for a mechanical ferrule, enabling predictable full-coverage crown restoration on tooth #8. Option B is incorrect because placing a direct composite 2 mm subgingival impinges on biological width, promoting chronic periodontal inflammation, bleeding, and crestal bone loss. Option C is incorrect because porcelain veneers require sound peripheral enamel margins and cannot restore extensive subgingival structural fractures. Option D is incorrect because extraction is unnecessarily aggressive when the tooth has sufficient root length and periodontal support to be saved.

oral-pathology-medicine-548.question: A 38-year-old male presents with persistent cold sensitivity and spontaneous discomfort on tooth #30 two weeks after placement of a deep composite restoration. Clinical examination shows no occlusal prematurities, but cold testing elicits sharp pain that lingers for 30 seconds after the stimulus is removed. The tooth is also mildly sensitive to percussion. According to the American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic criteria, what is the pulpal diagnosis for tooth #30?
options: Normal pulp
Reversible pulpitis
Pulpal necrosis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
oral-pathology-medicine-548.explanation: Option D is correct because exaggerated pain to cold that lingers significantly after stimulus removal, combined with spontaneous pain, meets the AAE diagnostic criteria for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis. Option A is incorrect because a normal pulp responds mildly to thermal testing and the sensation dissipates immediately. Option B is incorrect because reversible pulpitis is characterized by quick, sharp discomfort that subsides within seconds once the stimulus is withdrawn. Option C is incorrect because pulpal necrosis manifests as a complete lack of response to thermal or electric pulp sensibility testing.

oral-pathology-medicine-571.question: A 58-year-old male presents with severe mobility and pain associated with his remaining mandibular central incisors (teeth #24 and #25), which serve as abutments for an existing removable partial denture. Clinical examination reveals Class III mobility, deep periodontal probing depths of 8 mm with bleeding on probing and suppuration, and radiographic examination reveals horizontal bone loss extending into the apical third (>75% attachment loss). What is the MOST appropriate management for teeth #24 and #25?
options: Extraction of teeth #24 and #25 with modification of the prosthesis
Periodontal flap surgery with regenerative bone grafting
Subgingival debridement and composite splinting to adjacent teeth
Endodontic therapy followed by surgical crown lengthening
oral-pathology-medicine-571.explanation: Option A is correct because teeth #24 and #25 have a hopeless periodontal prognosis due to Class III mobility, suppuration, and severe horizontal bone loss extending to the apical third, necessitating extraction and prosthodontic modification. Option B is incorrect because advanced horizontal bone loss in the apical third lacks the 3-wall osseous architecture required for successful periodontal bone regeneration. Option C is incorrect because splinting periodontally hopeless teeth cannot arrest deep microbial suppuration or severe attachment loss and compromises overall oral hygiene. Option D is incorrect because endodontic therapy and crown lengthening address pulpal or ferrule deficits and would further reduce alveolar bone support in teeth already lacking periodontal stability.

oral-pathology-medicine-618.question: A 10-year-old male presents with his parents, who are concerned about the spacing of his front teeth. Clinical examination reveals delayed eruption of the maxillary permanent incisors and a wide diastema between teeth #8 and #9. An anterior occlusal radiograph demonstrates an impacted conical supernumerary tooth (mesiodens) situated between the roots of teeth #8 and #9, impeding normal incisor alignment. What is the MOST appropriate initial management strategy?
options: Surgical extraction of the mesiodens
Immediate orthodontic mechanics to close the diastema
Periodic radiographic monitoring until permanent canines erupt
Placement of a removable Hawley appliance to align incisors
oral-pathology-medicine-618.explanation: Option A is correct because surgical extraction of an impacted mesiodens causing diastema or delayed eruption is the standard of care to eliminate physical obstruction and facilitate spontaneous or guided eruption of adjacent permanent incisors. Orthodontic space closure (Option B and Option D) without prior surgical removal of the supernumerary tooth is contraindicated and will result in treatment failure or root resorption. Periodic observation (Option C) allows continued displacement, root resorption, or dentigerous cyst formation to develop.

oral-pathology-medicine-623.question: A 9-year-old female presents for a routine recall examination. She resides in a non-fluoridated municipal area and has no significant medical history. Clinical examination confirms that her first permanent molars (teeth #3, #14, #19, and #30) are fully erupted, caries-free, and possess deep, anatomically complex pits and fissures. What is the MOST appropriate preventive intervention for these teeth?
options: Application of resin-based pit and fissure sealants
Topical application of 5% sodium fluoride varnish alone
Prescription of systemic dietary fluoride supplements
Radiographic monitoring with bitewing examinations every 6 months
oral-pathology-medicine-623.explanation: Option A is correct because the American Dental Association (ADA) recommends pit and fissure sealants as the primary evidence-based preventive measure for newly erupted permanent molars with deep, caries-susceptible occlusal fissures. Topical fluoride varnish alone (Option B) is primarily effective at remineralizing smooth enamel surfaces but does not provide physical protection against fissure caries. Systemic fluoride supplements (Option C) and biannual radiographic monitoring (Option D) do not mechanically occlude high-risk pits and fissures from cariogenic biofilm.

oral-pathology-medicine-625.question: A 50-year-old male presents with a persistent dull ache in his maxillary right posterior quadrant that sharpens noticeably when chewing. He has an extensive multisurface amalgam restoration on tooth #2 placed five years ago. Clinical examination reveals normal periodontal probing depths without caries. Thermal and electric pulp tests are normal, but biting pressure on a Tooth Slooth elicits sharp pain upon release on the mesiobuccal cusp, and transillumination reveals an incomplete fracture line extending across the mesial marginal ridge. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis; perform nonsurgical root canal therapy
Cracked tooth syndrome; fabricate a full-coverage crown
Reversible pulpitis; place a sedative temporary restoration
Periodontal abscess; perform incision, drainage, and curettage
oral-pathology-medicine-625.explanation: Option B is correct because sharp pain on release of masticatory pressure on a heavily restored vital tooth with transillumination confirming an incomplete fracture across a marginal ridge is diagnostic of cracked tooth syndrome, which requires full-coverage crown placement to splint the cusps. Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (Option A) presents with lingering thermal pain rather than normal pulp vitality responses. Reversible pulpitis (Option C) does not exhibit localized rebound pain on cusp loading, and periodontal abscess (Option D) presents with deep probing defects, swelling, and purulent exudate.

oral-pathology-medicine-676.question: A 28-year-old female presents with a persistent, localized dull ache and unilateral nasal congestion in the maxillary left posterior region that worsens upon bending forward. Clinical examination shows that tooth #14 is non-responsive to cold and electric pulp testing but is tender to percussion. A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography scan reveal periapical bone loss at the palatal apex of tooth #14 with contiguous mucosal thickening of the left maxillary sinus floor. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Acute reversible pulpitis of tooth #14
Generalized chronic periodontitis
Myofascial pain dysfunction syndrome
Maxillary sinusitis of dental origin
oral-pathology-medicine-676.explanation: Option D is correct because an odontogenic infection from a necrotic, non-vital tooth (#14) exhibiting periapical bone resorption in close proximity to the sinus floor resulting in secondary sinus mucosal thickening is diagnostic for maxillary sinusitis of dental origin. Reversible pulpitis (Option A) requires a vital pulp responsive to thermal testing and does not cause sinus mucosal thickening or periapical bone loss. Periodontitis (Option B) exhibits marginal bone loss and periodontal pocketing rather than an isolated periapical lesion, while myofascial pain (Option C) involves masticatory muscle trigger points without radiographic mucosal or periapical changes.

oral-pathology-medicine-678.question: A 55-year-old male presents with sudden, unilateral, severe electric shock-like shooting pain in the maxillary right quadrant. The paroxysms last for several seconds, occur multiple times a day, and are triggered by light tactile stimulation such as shaving or a light breeze touching his right upper lip and nasolabial fold. Clinical and radiographic examinations of teeth #3 and #4 are unremarkable, and thermal and electric pulp vitality tests on both teeth are normal. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Trigeminal neuralgia
Reversible pulpitis
Cracked tooth syndrome
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
oral-pathology-medicine-678.explanation: Option A is correct because paroxysmal, unilateral, lancinating electric shock-like pain triggered by light, non-noxious stimulation within dermatomal trigger zones, accompanied by completely normal dental and pulpal testing of teeth #3 and #4, is classic for trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux). Reversible pulpitis (Option B) produces brief thermal discomfort rather than dermatomal electric pain triggered by light cutaneous touch. Cracked tooth syndrome (Option C) and symptomatic apical periodontitis (Option D) demonstrate sharp masticatory rebound pain or marked vertical percussion tenderness, both of which are absent here.

oral-pathology-medicine-686.question: A 45-year-old female presents for a periodontal recall examination. Medical history is notable for well-controlled hypertension. Clinical evaluation reveals generalized marginal inflammation with bleeding on probing at 80% of sites, interdental probing depths ranging from 4 to 5 mm across multiple quadrants, and interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm. Full-mouth periapical radiographs demonstrate horizontal bone loss affecting 20% to 25% (coronal third) of root length with no tooth loss due to periodontal disease. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Dental biofilm-induced gingivitis
Necrotizing periodontitis
Generalized periodontitis, Stage II
Generalized periodontitis, Stage IV
oral-pathology-medicine-686.explanation: Option C is correct because interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm, probing depths up to 5 mm, and horizontal radiographic bone loss confined to the coronal third (15% to 33%) involving greater than 30% of teeth fulfill the 2017 AAP/EFP criteria for Generalized Periodontitis, Stage II. Biofilm-induced gingivitis (Option A) features gingival inflammation without clinical attachment loss or alveolar bone destruction. Necrotizing periodontitis (Option B) requires interdental necrosis, ulceration, pseudomembrane formation, and pain, while Stage IV periodontitis (Option D) is characterized by severe attachment loss (≥5 mm), bone loss extending to the mid-root or apical third, and significant tooth loss.

oral-pathology-medicine-688.question: A 50-year-old female presents with mild, transient sensitivity to cold on her maxillary right first molar. Clinical examination reveals an intact dentition with a deep occlusal carious lesion on tooth #3. Radiographically, the carious lesion extends into the inner third of dentin approximating the pulp chamber, with no widening of the periodontal ligament or periapical radiolucency. The tooth tests vital to cold with immediate cessation of sensation upon stimulus removal, and percussion is negative. What is the MOST appropriate restorative management strategy?
options: Indirect pulp capping using a biocompatible liner and coronal restoration
Immediate nonsurgical root canal therapy followed by full-coverage crown
Direct pulp capping followed by immediate pin-retained amalgam core
Extraction of tooth #3 and replacement with an endosseous dental implant
oral-pathology-medicine-688.explanation: Option A is correct because indirect pulp capping (selective caries removal) with a biocompatible liner (e.g., calcium silicate or resin-modified glass ionomer) followed by an immediate hermetic seal is the established standard of care for vital teeth with deep dentinal caries approximating the pulp without signs of irreversible pulpitis. Immediate root canal therapy (Option B) is overly invasive and contraindicated when the pulp is vital and asymptomatic or reversibly inflamed. Direct pulp capping (Option C) is indicated only when a pinpoint pulpal exposure has already occurred, and extraction (Option D) is inappropriate for a structurally restorable tooth.

oral-pathology-medicine-671.question: A 16-year-old female presents with severe pain, swelling in the right mandibular angle, marked trismus, and dysphagia. Clinical examination reveals an erythematous, fluctuant operculum partially covering the crown of erupting tooth #32, with purulent exudate expressed upon gentle palpation. Radiographs confirm that tooth #32 is partially impacted with no periapical pathosis. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Subopercular debridement with irrigation, analgesics, and systemic antibiotics
Immediate surgical extraction of tooth #32 under local anesthesia
Application of topical anesthetic gel and close clinical observation
Prescription of anti-inflammatory analgesics and warm saline rinses alone
oral-pathology-medicine-671.explanation: Option A is correct because acute pericoronitis presenting with systemic and fascial space involvement (trismus, dysphagia, purulence) represents a spreading infection requiring immediate mechanical debridement, antimicrobial irrigation under the operculum, and systemic antibiotic therapy prior to definitive surgical management. Immediate surgical extraction (Option B) during acute severe pericoronitis with trismus is contraindicated due to compromised tissue pH hindering local anesthesia and the high risk of disseminating infection into the submandibular and lateral pharyngeal spaces. Topical anesthetics (Option C) or analgesics alone (Option D) fail to eradicate the bacterial infection and leave the patient at risk for life-threatening airway compromise.

oral-pathology-medicine-674.question: A 7-year-old male presents with his parents, who are concerned about discolored patches on his newly erupted teeth. Clinical examination demonstrates well-demarcated, creamy-yellow to brownish enamel opacities on the occlusal surfaces of all four permanent first molars (teeth #3, #14, #19, and #30) and the incisal thirds of the maxillary central incisors (teeth #8 and #9). Several molar cusps exhibit post-eruptive enamel breakdown and heightened sensitivity to cold air. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Amelogenesis imperfecta
Dental fluorosis
Molar incisor hypomineralization
Dentinogenesis imperfecta
oral-pathology-medicine-674.explanation: Option C is correct because well-demarcated, qualitative enamel hypomineralization affecting one to four permanent first molars with frequent involvement of the permanent incisors, presenting with post-eruptive enamel breakdown and cold sensitivity, is pathognomonic for molar incisor hypomineralization (MIH). Amelogenesis imperfecta (Option A) is a generalized inherited condition that affects all teeth in both the primary and permanent dentitions. Dental fluorosis (Option B) presents symmetrically as diffuse, ill-defined horizontal white striations that are caries-resistant without post-eruptive fracturing, while dentinogenesis imperfecta (Option D) causes hereditary amber-brown opalescent dentin and bulbous crowns with obliterated pulp chambers.

oral-pathology-medicine-695.question: A 55-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of a continuous burning sensation involving her anterior tongue, palate, and labial mucosa for the past 6 months. Her medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, for which she was started on lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) 7 months ago. Clinical examination reveals normal, intact oral mucosa with no signs of erythema, ulceration, candidiasis, or xerostomia. Laboratory evaluations, including fasting blood glucose, serum ferritin, iron, folate, and vitamin B12 levels, are all within normal limits. What is the MOST likely etiology of her symptoms?
options: Medication-induced adverse reaction
Erythematous oral candidiasis
Primary (idiopathic) burning mouth syndrome
Nutritional deficiency stomatitis
oral-pathology-medicine-695.explanation: Option A is correct because angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors such as lisinopril are established causes of secondary oral burning sensations (oral dysesthesia) and dysgeusia due to local mucosal accumulation of bradykinin and substance P. Erythematous oral candidiasis (Option B) is ruled out by the absence of mucosal erythema, depapillation, or positive fungal cytology. Primary (idiopathic) burning mouth syndrome (Option C) is strictly a diagnosis of exclusion that cannot be assigned while an active pharmacological culprit is present, and nutritional deficiency (Option D) is excluded by normal serum ferritin, iron, folate, and vitamin B12 levels.

oral-pathology-medicine-631.question: A 38-year-old male presents with a chief complaint of sharp, localized pain in his maxillary right quadrant when chewing firm foods, which resolves instantly when chewing stops. Clinical examination reveals an extensive occlusal amalgam restoration on tooth #2 with a visible crack line extending across the distal marginal ridge. The tooth exhibits normal responses to thermal testing, and periodontal probing and periapical radiographs are normal. Application of a bite stick to the distobuccal cusp reproduces the sharp pain specifically upon release of biting pressure. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Cracked tooth syndrome
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
oral-pathology-medicine-631.explanation: Option C is correct because sharp, momentary pain elicited upon the release of masticatory pressure (rebound pain) on a vital, heavily restored tooth with an identifiable marginal ridge fracture line is pathognomonic for cracked tooth syndrome. Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (Option A) is characterized by prolonged, lingering thermal pain rather than immediate cessation upon release of biting pressure. Reversible pulpitis (Option B) presents with transient cold sensitivity without localized mechanical bite-release pain, and symptomatic apical periodontitis (Option D) is characterized by persistent pain on vertical percussion and apical tenderness.

oral-pathology-medicine-635.question: A 5-year-old male presents to the dental clinic with his parents 1 hour after sustaining a fall on a concrete sidewalk. Clinical examination reveals that primary tooth E is severely intruded, with only a small portion of the incisal edge visible, and there is bleeding from the gingival sulcus. Periapical radiography reveals that the root apex of tooth E is displaced palatally into the developing follicle of permanent successor tooth #8. What is the MOST appropriate clinical management?
options: Immediate surgical extraction of tooth E
Surgical repositioning and semi-rigid splinting of tooth E
Passive observation to allow spontaneous re-eruption of tooth E
Pulpectomy of tooth E and obturation with zinc oxide-eugenol
oral-pathology-medicine-635.explanation: Option A is correct because American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) trauma guidelines mandate immediate extraction of an intruded primary incisor when the root apex is displaced palatally toward or into the developing permanent tooth germ to prevent severe developmental disturbances (e.g., enamel hypoplasia or crown dilaceration) to tooth #8. Surgical repositioning and splinting (Option B) are contraindicated in the primary dentition due to further iatrogenic injury to the underlying permanent follicle. Spontaneous re-eruption (Option C) is only indicated when the root apex is displaced labially away from the permanent successor, and pulpectomy (Option D) cannot relieve mechanical follicular compression.

oral-pathology-medicine-574.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of sharp, localized pain in her maxillary right quadrant that is elicited by cold beverages and sweets, which subsides within 2 to 3 seconds after the stimulus is removed. Clinical examination reveals a deep carious lesion on the occlusal surface of tooth #3. Thermal testing elicits a sharp response that dissipates immediately upon stimulus removal. Percussion and palpation tests are negative. Radiographs confirm deep caries approaching the pulp with normal periapical tissues. What is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis?
options: Pulp necrosis
Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
oral-pathology-medicine-574.explanation: Option C is correct because reversible pulpitis is characterized by sharp pain provoked by thermal stimuli or sweets that subsides rapidly within a few seconds after stimulus removal, accompanied by a vital pulp without percussion tenderness or periapical changes. Option A is incorrect because necrotic pulps do not respond to thermal vitality testing. Option B and Option D are incorrect because apical periodontitis produces periapical tenderness or radiographic lesions, while symptomatic irreversible pulpitis features spontaneous episodes or prolonged, lingering pain lasting over 30 seconds.

oral-pathology-medicine-581.question: A 20-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of discoloration of her maxillary left central incisor (tooth #9) following a traumatic injury five years ago. Clinical examination reveals an intact coronal restoration and a dark, grayish hue of the clinical crown of tooth #9. The tooth is completely asymptomatic, with negative responses to percussion and palpation. A periapical radiograph confirms an adequate, well-sealed root canal filling and normal periapical tissues. What is the MOST appropriate initial treatment for the discoloration?
options: Full-coverage ceramic crown
Internal bleaching (walking bleach technique)
External vital home bleaching
Porcelain laminate veneer
oral-pathology-medicine-581.explanation: Option B is correct because internal bleaching (the walking bleach technique) using sodium perborate is the most conservative and effective initial treatment for intrinsic discoloration in an asymptomatic, adequately obturated endodontically treated incisor. Options A and D are incorrect because full-coverage crowns and porcelain veneers are significantly more invasive and should be reserved for teeth with substantial loss of coronal structure. Option C is incorrect because external vital bleaching is largely ineffective against intrinsic discoloration caused by pulpal degradation products sealed within the pulp chamber.

oral-pathology-medicine-582.question: A 40-year-old male patient presents five days after the surgical extraction of his mandibular left third molar (tooth #17) with severe increasing pain, firm swelling, and difficulty opening his mouth. He reports a foul taste and a slight fever. Clinical examination reveals marked facial swelling in the left submandibular space, severe trismus, and purulent exudate draining from the extraction socket. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Temporomandibular joint disorder
Alveolar osteitis (dry socket)
Postoperative hematoma
Post-extraction fascial space infection
oral-pathology-medicine-582.explanation: Option D is correct because postoperative fascial space infection (such as submandibular space involvement) presents days after extraction with progressive swelling, trismus, purulent drainage, and systemic signs like fever. Option A is incorrect because temporomandibular joint disorders do not cause purulent drainage, facial swelling, or fever. Options B and C are incorrect because alveolar osteitis presents with severe throbbing pain and a denuded socket without swelling, fever, or pus, while an uncomplicated hematoma exhibits firm swelling and ecchymosis without purulence or systemic infection.

oral-pathology-medicine-532.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with a persistent dull ache in her mandibular left first molar (tooth #19), which had root canal therapy completed five years ago. Clinical examination reveals that tooth #19 is tender to percussion and mastication, with no swelling or sinus tract present. Radiographic examination reveals a well-defined periapical radiolucency associated with the mesial root apex of tooth #19. What is the MOST likely periapical diagnosis?
options: Acute apical abscess
Condensing osteitis
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
oral-pathology-medicine-532.explanation: Option C is correct because symptomatic apical periodontitis is defined by AAE diagnostic standards as inflammation of the apical periodontium producing clinical symptoms, including tenderness to percussion or mastication, and may be accompanied by a radiographic periapical radiolucency. Option A is incorrect because an acute apical abscess is characterized by rapid onset, intense spontaneous pain, and active purulent swelling. Options B and D are incorrect because condensing osteitis appears radiographically as a localized radiopacity, whereas asymptomatic apical periodontitis manifests as a radiolucency that is clinically asymptomatic and painless on percussion.

oral-pathology-medicine-535.question: A 6-year-old male patient presents with his parents, who are concerned about the future alignment of his anterior teeth. Radiographic examination confirms congenitally missing permanent maxillary lateral incisors (teeth #7 and #10). The primary maxillary lateral incisors (teeth D and G) have already exfoliated, and the primary maxillary canines (teeth C and H) are clinically present and intact. What is the MOST appropriate management strategy?
options: Immediate placement of endosseous dental implants
Composite resin bonding on primary canines to simulate lateral incisors
Observation without intervention until all permanent teeth erupt
Referral for orthodontic consultation to plan for long-term space management
oral-pathology-medicine-535.explanation: Option D is correct because early referral for orthodontic evaluation allows for long-term space analysis and planning (space maintenance for future implants versus space closure with canine substitution) as the mixed dentition transitions. Option A is incorrect because endosseous implants are strictly contraindicated in growing pediatric patients due to inevitable infraocclusion and alveolar growth inhibition. Options B and C are incorrect because bonding primary canines at age 6 is premature and ineffective for definitive arch coordination, while passive observation risks arch collapse and loss of restorative space.

oral-pathology-medicine-593.question: A 12-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic 1 hour after a bicycle accident resulting in a complicated crown fracture of his permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). Clinical examination reveals a pinpoint pulp exposure (less than 0.5 mm in diameter) that is vital and bleeding normally. Radiographic examination confirms an immature root with an open apex and no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management to preserve pulp vitality and promote apexogenesis?
options: Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide
Indirect pulp capping with glass ionomer cement
Partial pulpotomy (Cvek pulpotomy) with mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA)
Complete pulpectomy and root canal obturation
oral-pathology-medicine-593.explanation: Option C is correct because a partial (Cvek) pulpotomy with MTA or bioceramic material preserves healthy coronal and radicular pulp tissue, promoting apexogenesis and continued physiologic root wall thickening in an immature permanent tooth. Option A is incorrect because direct pulp capping has a significantly lower success rate in traumatic exposures due to superficial bacterial contamination and microleakage risk. Options B and D are incorrect because indirect pulp capping is indicated only for deep non-exposed caries, whereas a full pulpectomy halts root development and leaves fragile dentinal walls vulnerable to cervical root fracture.

oral-pathology-medicine-652.question: A 50-year-old female patient presents to your dental office with a chief complaint of dull, throbbing pain in her maxillary left posterior region that started gradually several weeks ago and is now persistent, especially at night. She reports a history of root canal treatment on her maxillary left first molar (tooth #14) five years ago. Clinical examination reveals mild tenderness to percussion on tooth #14, but no swelling or sinus tract. A periapical radiograph reveals an underfilled mesiobuccal root canal and a diffuse periapical radiolucency associated with the mesiobuccal root apex. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
Acute apical abscess
Chronic apical abscess
Symptomatic apical periodontitis of endodontic origin
oral-pathology-medicine-652.explanation: Option D is correct because symptomatic apical periodontitis of endodontic origin is characterized by persistent, throbbing pain or percussion discomfort associated with an endodontically treated tooth displaying an apical radiolucency. Option A is incorrect because asymptomatic apical periodontitis presents with a periapical radiolucency but is completely devoid of clinical pain or symptoms. Options B and C are incorrect because an acute apical abscess requires active, fluctuating purulent swelling, whereas a chronic apical abscess presents with an actively draining sinus tract rather than persistent throbbing pain.

oral-pathology-medicine-654.question: A 6-year-old male patient presents to the dental office following the premature extraction of his mandibular left primary first molar (tooth L) due to severe caries. Clinical and radiographic examination reveals that the mandibular left primary second molar (tooth K) and the permanent first molar (tooth #19) are present, but the permanent mandibular incisors have not fully erupted. What is the MOST appropriate appliance to maintain space in this quadrant?
options: Distal shoe space maintainer
Mandibular lingual holding arch
Observation without space maintenance
Band-and-loop space maintainer
oral-pathology-medicine-654.explanation: Option D is correct because a band-and-loop space maintainer is the standard appliance for the premature unilateral loss of a primary first molar when the primary second molar is present. Option A is incorrect because a distal shoe is indicated exclusively for the premature loss of a primary second molar before the emergence of the permanent first molar. Options B and C are incorrect because a mandibular lingual holding arch is contraindicated before the permanent mandibular incisors have fully erupted, while unmonitored neglect leads to mesial drifting of posterior teeth and permanent tooth impaction.

oral-pathology-medicine-656.question: A 28-year-old female patient presents for a routine check-up, expressing concern about the appearance of a discolored maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). She reports a traumatic injury during childhood, after which root canal therapy was completed five years ago. The tooth is asymptomatic, and radiographs show an intact, well-obturated root canal with no periapical pathology. Clinical examination reveals a dark grey intrinsic discoloration of the clinical crown with sound marginal ridges. What is the MOST appropriate conservative treatment to improve esthetics?
options: Direct composite veneer
Internal bleaching (walking bleach technique)
Full-coverage ceramic crown
External vital bleaching
oral-pathology-medicine-656.explanation: Option B is correct because internal bleaching (walking bleach technique) with sodium perborate is the most conservative and esthetically effective initial intervention for intrinsic discoloration in an asymptomatic, endodontically treated anterior tooth with sound structure. Options A and C are incorrect because composite veneers and full ceramic crowns require irreversible reduction of healthy dental tissue and are reserved for severely broken-down crowns. Option D is incorrect because external vital bleaching cannot resolve intrinsic staining originating from pulpal breakdown products and endodontic materials within the pulp chamber.

oral-pathology-medicine-602.question: A 40-year-old male patient presents with a persistent, dull ache in his right maxillary posterior region, accompanied by unilateral nasal congestion and a feeling of pressure below his right eye. He reports a history of root canal treatment on his maxillary right second molar (tooth #2) several years ago, which has recently become tender to percussion and mastication. A periapical radiograph reveals a periapical radiolucency associated with the apices of tooth #2 and localized mucosal thickening of the right maxillary sinus floor. What is the MOST likely initial diagnosis?
options: Odontogenic maxillary sinusitis
Allergic maxillary sinusitis
Trigeminal neuralgia
Chronic periodontitis
oral-pathology-medicine-602.explanation: Option A is correct because odontogenic maxillary sinusitis is characterized by unilateral maxillary sinus symptoms (dull ache, facial pressure, congestion) secondary to adjacent periapical pathology, confirmed by percussion tenderness and periapical radiolucency on tooth #2 with sinus floor mucosal thickening. Option B is incorrect because allergic rhinosinusitis presents with bilateral nasal symptoms, clear rhinorrhea, and sneezing without isolated odontogenic periapical radiolucencies. Options C and D are incorrect because trigeminal neuralgia manifests as sudden, unilateral electric-shock paroxysms without sinus thickening, and chronic periodontitis causes marginal alveolar bone loss rather than periapical pathosis.

oral-pathology-medicine-605.question: A 20-year-old male patient presents with severe pain, localized swelling, and difficulty opening his mouth (trismus) in the area of his partially erupted mandibular right third molar (tooth #32). Clinical examination reveals inflamed, erythematous, and edematous opercular tissue overlying the distal aspect of the crown, with purulent exudate upon gentle palpation. What is the MOST appropriate initial management step?
options: Immediate surgical extraction of tooth #32
Local debridement, irrigation, analgesics, and systemic antibiotics if indicated
Immediate surgical operculectomy
Initiation of root canal therapy
oral-pathology-medicine-605.explanation: Option B is correct because initial management of acute pericoronitis focuses on gentle local debridement, antimicrobial irrigation, analgesics, and systemic antibiotics when trismus or purulence indicates spreading infection. Option A is incorrect because immediate surgical extraction during acute inflammation risks disseminating infection into fascial spaces and is complicated by inadequate local anesthesia. Options C and D are incorrect because an immediate operculectomy during active infection induces severe hemorrhage and high recurrence, while pulpectomy is inappropriate since the pathology involves pericoronal soft tissues rather than the dental pulp.

oral-pathology-medicine-606.question: A 28-year-old female patient presents for a routine dental check-up. Radiographic examination reveals a deep carious lesion extending into the inner third of dentin approximating the pulp chamber of her mandibular left first molar (tooth #19). The patient reports no spontaneous pain, only transient mild sensitivity to cold that dissipates immediately upon stimulus removal. Clinical examination confirms a large carious lesion without pulp exposure. What is the MOST appropriate management strategy to preserve pulp vitality?
options: Complete pulpectomy and root canal treatment
Complete caries excavation to hard dentin regardless of pulp exposure risk
Selective caries removal followed by a protective liner and a definitive coronal seal
Full coronal pulpotomy and intermediate restorative placement
oral-pathology-medicine-606.explanation: Option C is correct because ADA caries management guidelines recommend selective caries removal (indirect pulp therapy) leaving affected dentin over the pulp followed by a protective liner and a well-sealed restoration to preserve pulp vitality and avoid mechanical exposure. Option A is incorrect because pulpectomy is overly aggressive and unnecessary for a vital pulp showing only transient, reversible sensitivity. Options B and D are incorrect because complete excavation to hard dentin significantly increases the incidence of unnecessary pulp exposure, while full coronal pulpotomy is unnecessarily destructive when the pulp remains unexposed.

oral-pathology-medicine-636.question: A 72-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of severe instability and dislodgement of her 15-year-old maxillary complete denture during mastication and speech. Clinical examination reveals advanced alveolar ridge resorption, particularly in the anterior maxilla, making conventional retention challenging. Her medical history is unremarkable. What is the MOST appropriate long-term management strategy for her denture instability?
options: Routine daily application of an over-the-counter denture adhesive
Laboratory hard reline of the existing complete denture
Fabrication of a new conventional complete denture without surgical intervention
Placement of dental implants to support a maxillary overdenture
oral-pathology-medicine-636.explanation: Option D is correct because dental implants provide the necessary mechanical retention and stability required to overcome severe alveolar ridge resorption, which cannot be adequately managed by mucosal support alone. Options A and B are incorrect because denture adhesives and relining provide only temporary, palliative retention and cannot overcome advanced anatomical ridge deficiency or correct a worn 15-year-old prosthesis. Option C is incorrect because fabricating another conventional mucosally-borne complete denture will still lack retention and stability due to the severe loss of alveolar ridge height and surface area.

oral-pathology-medicine-637.question: A 30-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of sharp, brief pain in her mandibular left posterior region only when consuming cold beverages. The pain disappears almost immediately after the cold stimulus is removed. Her medical history is non-contributory. Clinical examination reveals that tooth #19 has a moderate carious lesion with no pulp exposure. Pulp vitality testing elicits a sharp, transient response to cold that quickly subsides. Percussion and palpation tests are negative. What is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis?
options: Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
oral-pathology-medicine-637.explanation: Option A is correct because reversible pulpitis is characterized by sharp, transient pain elicited by thermal stimuli (such as cold) that resolves immediately upon removal of the stimulus, along with negative percussion and palpation findings. Option B is incorrect because symptomatic irreversible pulpitis produces lingering thermal pain that persists well after stimulus removal or spontaneous throbbing pain. Options C and D are incorrect because pulp necrosis results in a non-responsive pulp to vitality testing, while apical periodontitis produces distinct tenderness to percussion and palpation.

oral-pathology-medicine-640.question: A 22-year-old female patient presents to your dental office with trismus, dysphagia, and severe pain in the mandibular right posterior region that developed rapidly over the past 24 hours. She reports a history of recurrent pericoronitis around her partially impacted mandibular right third molar (tooth #32). Clinical examination reveals significant swelling of the operculum and surrounding soft tissues, with purulent exudate expressed upon palpation. What is the MOST appropriate long-term definitive management after the acute infection is resolved?
options: Daily warm saline rinses and local debridement
Operculectomy of the overlying soft tissue
Long-term prophylactic systemic antibiotic therapy
Surgical extraction of the impacted mandibular third molar
oral-pathology-medicine-640.explanation: Option D is correct because surgical extraction of the partially impacted third molar (tooth #32) is the definitive standard of care to eliminate the source of infection and prevent recurrent pericoronitis once acute inflammation resolves. Options A and C are incorrect because warm saline rinses, local debridement, and antibiotics provide only temporary stabilization during the acute phase rather than definitive therapy. Option B is incorrect because operculectomy carries a high recurrence rate due to soft tissue regrowth over impacted alveolar bone and fails to resolve the underlying impaction.

oral-pathology-medicine-643.question: A 28-year-old male patient presents for a routine dental examination. A bitewing radiograph reveals a deep carious lesion on the mesial surface of permanent tooth #30 extending close to the pulp chamber. The tooth is asymptomatic, vital, and non-responsive to percussion or palpation. Clinically, complete excavation of caries is performed, leaving a thin layer of sound remaining dentin with no pulp exposure. What is the MOST appropriate pulp protection strategy prior to restoring the tooth?
options: Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide
Pulpotomy with formocresol
Placement of a resin-modified glass ionomer liner
Non-surgical root canal treatment
oral-pathology-medicine-643.explanation: Option C is correct because applying a resin-modified glass ionomer liner over thin remaining dentin seals dentinal tubules, provides chemical and thermal insulation, and releases fluoride beneath the definitive restoration without pulp exposure. Option A is incorrect because direct pulp capping is indicated only when there is a mechanical or carious pin-point exposure of the dental pulp. Options B and D are incorrect because coronal pulpotomy and root canal therapy are unnecessarily invasive and contraindicated for an asymptomatic, vital permanent tooth with an unexposed pulp.

oral-pathology-medicine-724.question: A 45-year-old male patient presents to your dental office with a chief complaint of severe, throbbing pain in his maxillary right posterior region that began spontaneously and wakes him at night. He reports sensitivity to hot and cold that lingers for several minutes. Clinical examination reveals that tooth #3 (maxillary right first molar) has a deep occlusal restoration. Percussion and palpation tests are positive for tooth #3, and cold testing elicits severe, lingering pain. Radiographic examination shows no periapical radiolucency but confirms a deep restoration close to the pulp chamber. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis
Reversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues
Pulp necrosis with acute apical abscess
Acute maxillary sinusitis of odontogenic origin
oral-pathology-medicine-724.explanation: Option A is correct because spontaneous nocturnal pain and severe lingering thermal sensitivity are pathognomonic for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, while localized tenderness to percussion and palpation confirms symptomatic apical periodontitis per AAE diagnostic terminology. Option B is incorrect because reversible pulpitis produces sharp, non-lingering pain without spontaneous aching or periapical tenderness. Options C and D are incorrect because the pulp remains responsive and vital (ruling out necrosis), and the clinical symptoms are localized directly to tooth #3 rather than the maxillary sinus.

oral-pathology-medicine-726.question: A 25-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of a slowly growing, painless swelling on the buccal aspect of her anterior maxilla in the canine and lateral incisor region. She reports that the swelling has been present for approximately 6 months without trauma or pain. Clinical examination reveals a firm, non-tender, sessile lesion covered by normal-appearing mucosa, measuring about 1.5 cm in diameter. The adjacent teeth (#6 and #7) are vital and show no signs of caries or periodontal disease. Radiographic examination reveals a well-defined unilocular radiolucency between the roots of tooth #6 and tooth #7, causing slight divergence of their roots. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Periapical granuloma
Lateral periodontal cyst
Radicular cyst
Nasopalatine duct cyst
oral-pathology-medicine-726.explanation: Option B is correct because a lateral periodontal cyst typically presents as an asymptomatic, well-defined unilocular radiolucency located along the lateral root surface of adjacent vital teeth, most commonly in the mandibular premolar or maxillary anterior canine-lateral incisor region. Options A and C are incorrect because periapical granulomas and radicular cysts arise as inflammatory sequelae of pulpal necrosis, whereas teeth #6 and #7 are vital. Option D is incorrect because a nasopalatine duct cyst develops in the incisive canal at the maxillary midline, not laterally between the canine and lateral incisor.

oral-pathology-medicine-734.question: A 9-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of an unerupted maxillary left front tooth. Clinical examination reveals that the permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8) has fully erupted, but the permanent maxillary left central incisor (tooth #9) is clinically absent. Radiographic examination reveals that tooth #9 is impacted in a high palatal position with its crown displaced superiorly and mesially, impinging on the root of the adjacent permanent lateral incisor (tooth #10). What is the MOST appropriate initial management plan?
options: Periodic observation for 12 months to allow for spontaneous eruption
Surgical extraction of impacted tooth #9 followed by prosthetic replacement
Surgical exposure of tooth #9 followed by orthodontic traction
Extraction of the permanent lateral incisor (tooth #10) to permit spontaneous eruption
oral-pathology-medicine-734.explanation: Option C is correct because an impacted permanent central incisor (tooth #9) demonstrating asymmetrical eruption exceeding 6 months, ectopic displacement, and root impingement requires surgical exposure and orthodontic traction to guide it into functional occlusion. Option A is incorrect because observation is ineffective for an ectopic, palatally impacted incisor and increases the risk of root resorption on adjacent tooth #10. Options B and D are incorrect because extracting an intact permanent central or lateral incisor in a growing child is unnecessarily destructive and violates standard orthodontic principles.

oral-pathology-medicine-781.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents to your dental office with his parents following a playground accident, reporting that his permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8) was completely knocked out approximately 30 minutes ago. The parents brought the tooth immersed in cold milk. Clinical examination reveals an empty alveolar socket at tooth site #8 with an intact socket wall and minimal soft tissue laceration. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management step for this avulsed tooth?
options: Replant the tooth immediately after gentle saline rinsing, then stabilize with a flexible splint
Scrub the root surface with a surgical brush and soap prior to replantation
Refer the patient immediately to an oral surgeon for dental implant placement
Perform extraoral root canal therapy prior to attempting replantation
oral-pathology-medicine-781.explanation: Option A is correct because AAE and IADT guidelines recommend immediate replantation after gentle saline rinsing for a permanent tooth avulsed within 60 minutes and stored in a physiologic medium like milk, followed by flexible splinting for 2 weeks.
