Option B is incorrect because scrubbing the root surface with a brush or soap mechanically destroys viable periodontal ligament (PDL) cells, precipitating replacement root resorption (ankylosis). Options C and D are incorrect because dental implants are strictly contraindicated in growing pediatric patients, and performing extraoral endodontics unnecessarily prolongs extraoral time and causes PDL cell death.

oral-pathology-medicine-800.question: A 30-year-old male patient presents to your dental office after experiencing a traumatic avulsion of tooth #9 (maxillary left central incisor) approximately 45 minutes ago. The tooth was found, rinsed briefly with tap water, and immediately placed in cold milk. Clinical examination reveals an intact alveolar socket. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management step?
options: Scrape the root surface thoroughly with a surgical curette before replantation
Replant the tooth immediately after gentle rinsing with saline and stabilize with a flexible splint
Wrap the tooth in dry sterile gauze and refer to an oral surgeon for delayed replantation
Perform an extraoral pulpectomy and obturate the root canal before replantation
oral-pathology-medicine-800.explanation: Option B is correct because AAE and IADT guidelines recommend immediate replantation after gentle saline rinsing and stabilization with a passive flexible splint for a permanent tooth avulsed for less than 60 minutes that was maintained in milk. Option A is incorrect because mechanical curettage strips away viable periodontal ligament cells and accelerates severe inflammatory or replacement root resorption. Options C and D are incorrect because storing the tooth in dry gauze causes rapid cell death, and performing extraoral root canal treatment increases extraoral dry time and reduces the likelihood of periodontal healing.

oral-pathology-medicine-807.question: A 10-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of an unusually discolored front tooth. His parents recall a fall on the playground approximately six months ago without immediate symptoms or treatment. Clinical examination reveals that tooth #8 (permanent maxillary right central incisor) is discolored greyish-brown, non-tender to percussion and palpation, and exhibits normal mobility. Radiographic examination reveals an immature root with a wide open apex and a slightly widened periodontal ligament space, with no periapical radiolucency. Adjacent teeth respond normally to cold testing. What is the MOST appropriate initial step in managing tooth #8?
options: Perform pulp vitality testing to assess pulpal status and determine treatment necessity
Perform immediate surgical extraction of the discolored permanent tooth
Initiate internal non-vital bleaching to resolve the aesthetic concern
Perform immediate conventional root canal treatment followed by a full-coverage crown
oral-pathology-medicine-807.explanation: Option A is correct because performing pulp vitality testing (thermal and electric testing) is essential to determine whether the pulp is vital or necrotic before deciding on apexification, pulp revascularization, or observation. Option B is incorrect because extraction of an intact, restorable permanent central incisor in a 10-year-old child is contraindicated. Options C and D are incorrect because internal bleaching and conventional endodontic treatment cannot be initiated without verifying necrosis, and traditional gutta-percha obturation is contraindicated in an immature tooth with an open apex.

oral-pathology-medicine-766.question: A 55-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of recurrent fracture of the acrylic resin denture teeth on her maxillary complete denture. She demonstrates severe nocturnal bruxism and heavy masticatory forces. What is the MOST appropriate prosthodontic modification to prevent future tooth fractures?
options: Reduce the vertical dimension of occlusion
Replace the acrylic teeth with porcelain denture teeth
Fabricate a new denture base using high-impact acrylic resin
Incorporate cast metal or wear-resistant composite occlusal surfaces
oral-pathology-medicine-766.explanation: Option D is correct because incorporating cast metal occlusal surfaces or wear-resistant composite provides superior fracture and wear resistance against excessive parafunctional loads in severe bruxers. Option A is incorrect because arbitrarily decreasing the vertical dimension of occlusion produces facial collapse, speech impediments, and temporomandibular joint discomfort without preventing fracture. Option B is incorrect because porcelain teeth are brittle and prone to chipping and catastrophic fracture under impact loads, and they do not chemically bond to acrylic. Option C is incorrect because high-impact acrylic resin reinforces the denture base against midline fracture, not the denture teeth against occlusal breakage.

oral-pathology-medicine-767.question: A 5-year-old male patient presents with deep occlusal caries in tooth L (primary mandibular left first molar). Clinical and radiographic examination reveals a carious pulp exposure upon excavation, vital radicular pulp, and no furcal or periapical radiolucency. The tooth is asymptomatic, and bleeding is controlled within 5 minutes of coronal pulp amputation. What is the MOST appropriate pulp treatment for this tooth?
options: Pulpectomy
Indirect pulp treatment
Direct pulp capping
Formocresol pulpotomy
oral-pathology-medicine-767.explanation: Option D is correct because according to American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) guidelines, pulpotomy (using formocresol, MTA, or ferric sulfate) is the standard of care for a vital primary molar with a carious pulp exposure when radicular pulp tissue remains vital and coronal hemostasis is achieved. Option A is incorrect because pulpectomy is indicated only when the pulp exhibits irreversible pulpitis or necrosis with radicular degeneration. Option B is incorrect because indirect pulp capping is performed before pulpal exposure by leaving a thin layer of affected dentin, not after exposure occurs. Option C is incorrect because direct pulp capping of a carious pulp exposure in primary teeth is contraindicated due to high failure rates and internal resorption.

oral-pathology-medicine-776.question: According to the American Dental Association (ADA) Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct, which core ethical principle directly governs a dentist's duty to maintain patient records and safeguard patient confidentiality?
options: Beneficence
Patient autonomy
Nonmaleficence
Justice
oral-pathology-medicine-776.explanation: Option B is correct because Section 1 of the ADA Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct (Patient Autonomy) explicitly codifies a dentist's obligation to maintain patient records and safeguard patient confidentiality. Beneficence (Option A) directs the practitioner to promote patient welfare and community well-being, Nonmaleficence (Option C) requires avoiding harm and preventing patient abandonment, and Justice (Option D) mandates fairness and non-discrimination in healthcare delivery.

oral-pathology-medicine-777.question: In dental radiography, which of the following modifications results in the GREATEST reduction in radiation exposure to the patient?
options: Switching from D-speed film to F-speed film
Decreasing the source-to-skin distance from 16 inches to 8 inches
Increasing the tube current-exposure time product (mAs)
Replacing a rectangular collimator with a standard round collimator
oral-pathology-medicine-777.explanation: Option A is correct because switching from D-speed film to F-speed film reduces patient radiation exposure by approximately 60% due to higher-sensitivity tabular silver halide grains. Decreasing source-to-skin distance to 8 inches (Option B) increases patient tissue dose due to greater beam divergence, while increasing mAs (Option C) directly increases total x-ray photon production and radiation dose. Replacing rectangular collimation with round collimation (Option D) nearly doubles the tissue area irradiated, increasing exposure rather than reducing it.

oral-pathology-medicine-753.question: A 9-year-old female patient presents for a routine dental check-up. Clinical examination reveals a caries-free permanent and mixed dentition, but dietary history reveals frequent consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages and processed snacks between meals. The family lives in an area with an optimally fluoridated community water supply. What is the MOST appropriate primary preventive measure to reinforce at this visit?
options: Prescribing daily 1.1% sodium fluoride (5,000 ppm) dentifrice
Placing pit and fissure sealants on all sound premolars
Scheduling routine dental recall appointments every 3 months
Providing dietary counseling focused on reducing the frequency of fermentable carbohydrate intake
oral-pathology-medicine-753.explanation: Option D is correct because nutritional counseling to reduce the frequency and duration of between-meal fermentable carbohydrate consumption directly targets this child's primary modifiable caries risk factor. High-concentration 1.1% sodium fluoride toothpaste (Option A) is indicated for high-caries-risk patients with active cavitation or xerostomia, not a caries-free 9-year-old in a fluoridated community. Routine sealing of all premolars (Option B) is not recommended by ADA/AAPD guidelines in low-risk anatomy, and a 3-month recall interval (Option C) is unwarranted without active decay or severe periodontal breakdown.

oral-pathology-medicine-757.question: Under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule (45 CFR § 164.502(g)) and ADA ethical principles, what is the dentist's legal and ethical responsibility when an unemancipated minor patient requests that their routine dental records and findings be withheld from their parents or legal guardians?
options: Inform the minor that parents or legal guardians possess legal rights to inspect the records as the minor's personal representatives
Maintain strict confidentiality from the parents if the minor demonstrates mature decision-making capacity
Withhold the dental treatment records from the parents until the minor reaches 18 years of age
Disclose dental findings to the parents only if the oral condition is immediately life-threatening
oral-pathology-medicine-757.explanation: Option A is correct because federal HIPAA regulations (45 CFR § 164.502(g)) and ADA ethics recognize parents or legal guardians as the personal representatives of an unemancipated minor, granting them legal authority to access the minor's dental records. The mature minor doctrine (Option B) does not supersede parental rights to routine dental records under US law. Withholding routine records until age 18 (Option C) violates parental rights to informed consent and proxy decision-making, and parental disclosure is not restricted solely to life-threatening conditions (Option D).

oral-pathology-medicine-765.question: A 70-year-old male patient taking propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker, requires surgical extraction of a mandibular molar. Administration of which of the following local anesthetic formulations carries the GREATEST risk of causing severe acute hypertension accompanied by reflex bradycardia?
options: 3% Mepivacaine plain
2% Lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine
4% Prilocaine plain
2% Lidocaine plain
oral-pathology-medicine-765.explanation: Option B is correct because epinephrine stimulates vascular alpha-1 receptors while non-selective beta-blockers block vasodilatory beta-2 receptors, resulting in unopposed peripheral vasoconstriction that precipitates severe hypertension and compensatory reflex vagal bradycardia. In contrast, 3% mepivacaine plain (Option A), 4% prilocaine plain (Option C), and 2% lidocaine plain (Option D) do not contain adrenergic vasoconstrictors and therefore do not elicit this dangerous pharmacodynamic interaction.

oral-pathology-medicine-817.question: A 3-year-old male patient presents for his first dental visit. His parents are concerned about caries because an older sibling has extensive restorations. Clinical examination reveals a caries-free primary dentition. The family consumes tap water from an optimally fluoridated municipal supply (0.7 mg/L). What is the MOST appropriate primary preventive oral hygiene recommendation for this patient?
options: Daily application of 5% sodium fluoride varnish at home by the parents
Prescription of a daily 0.50 mg systemic fluoride dietary supplement
Twice-daily brushing with a pea-sized amount of fluoridated toothpaste under parental supervision
Twice-daily brushing with a smear or rice-grain amount of fluoridated toothpaste
oral-pathology-medicine-817.explanation: Option C is correct because ADA and AAPD guidelines recommend twice-daily brushing with a pea-sized amount of fluoridated toothpaste with parental supervision for children aged 3 to 6 years. A smear or rice-grain amount (Option D) is reserved for infants and children younger than 3 years to minimize ingestion risk. Systemic fluoride supplements (Option B) are contraindicated because the child already drinks optimally fluoridated water (0.7 mg/L), and 5% sodium fluoride varnish (Option A) is a professional in-office application applied 2 to 4 times annually, not a daily home remedy.

oral-pathology-medicine-818.question: A 45-year-old female patient presents for restoration of a deep occlusal carious lesion on tooth #30 (mandibular right first molar). Pulpal sensibility tests are normal, and there is no tenderness to percussion. Radiographs show caries extending to within 0.5 mm of the pulp chamber without periapical pathosis. Following complete removal of infected dentin without pulpal exposure, which of the following is the MOST appropriate restorative management for this tooth in a high-stress, load-bearing area?
options: Conventional glass ionomer cement placed as the definitive restorative material
Direct placement of an etch-and-rinse composite restoration without a protective liner
Flowable composite resin placed as the sole bulk restorative material
Placement of a biocompatible protective liner and base followed by a definitive amalgam restoration
oral-pathology-medicine-818.explanation: Option D is correct because placing a protective liner/base (e.g., resin-modified glass ionomer or calcium silicate) over near-pulpal dentin insulates the pulp against thermal and mechanical stress before placing a definitive amalgam restoration designed to withstand heavy posterior occlusal forces. Conventional glass ionomer cement (Option A) lacks sufficient fracture toughness and wear resistance for permanent occlusal restorations in posterior teeth. Etching deep dentin without a protective liner (Option B) causes chemical irritation, pulpal inflammation, and post-operative sensitivity, while flowable composite (Option C) exhibits high polymerization shrinkage and low wear resistance, making it unsuitable as a sole occlusal material.

oral-pathology-medicine-820.question: A 45-year-old male non-smoker presents for a comprehensive periodontal evaluation. Clinical examination reveals generalized probing depths of 4 to 5 mm, bleeding on probing at 45% of sites, and interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm affecting 40% of teeth. Radiographs demonstrate generalized horizontal bone loss confined to the coronal third of the root length (15% to 33%), with no furcation involvement, tooth mobility, or tooth loss. What is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis according to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification?
options: Generalized Stage I, Grade A periodontitis
Generalized Stage II, Grade B periodontitis
Generalized Stage III, Grade C periodontitis
Biofilm-induced gingivitis on an intact periodontium
oral-pathology-medicine-820.explanation: Option B is correct because under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm with horizontal bone loss limited to the coronal third (15% to 33%) and maximum probing depths <=5 mm without tooth loss defines Stage II periodontitis; involvement of >=30% of teeth establishes a generalized extent, and a non-smoker with bone loss commensurate with plaque deposits corresponds to Grade B (moderate rate of progression). Stage I (Option A) features milder attachment loss of 1 to 2 mm and bone loss <15%, whereas Stage III (Option C) requires attachment loss >=5 mm with bone loss extending to the mid-root or apical third (>=33%). Biofilm-induced gingivitis (Option D) exhibits bleeding on probing without any clinical attachment loss or radiographic bone destruction.

oral-pathology-medicine-824.question: A 55-year-old male patient presents with a solitary, painless, non-healing ulcer on the lateral border of his tongue that has persisted for 3 months. He reports a 30 pack-year smoking history and heavy daily alcohol consumption. Clinical examination reveals an indurated, exophytic mass measuring 1.5 cm in diameter with rolled, elevated margins. What is the MOST appropriate next step in the clinical management of this patient?
options: Perform an incisional biopsy of the lesion margin
Perform a complete excisional biopsy with 1 mm margins
Prescribe high-potency topical corticosteroids for 2 weeks
Reassure the patient and schedule observation in 4 weeks
oral-pathology-medicine-824.explanation: Option A is correct because an indurated, chronic (>2 weeks) lateral tongue ulcer measuring >1 cm in a high-risk patient is highly suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma, requiring an incisional biopsy including the lesion margin to establish a definitive histopathologic diagnosis. Excisional biopsy (Option B) is contraindicated for large (>1 cm) malignant-appearing lesions because it compromises surgical oncologic margins and impedes optimal staging. Topical corticosteroids (Option C) can suppress local immunity and exacerbate malignancies, while observation (Option D) inappropriately delays urgent oncologic diagnosis and treatment.

oral-pathology-medicine-826.question: A 40-year-old male patient requires extraction of his maxillary right second premolar (tooth #4). The dentist plans to administer local infiltration anesthesia above the apex of the tooth. Which peripheral nerve branch provides the primary sensory innervation to the pulp of this tooth?
options: Posterior superior alveolar nerve
Middle superior alveolar nerve
Anterior superior alveolar nerve
Greater palatine nerve
oral-pathology-medicine-826.explanation: Option B is correct because the middle superior alveolar (MSA) nerve provides sensory innervation to the maxillary premolars (tooth #4 and tooth #5) and the mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar. The posterior superior alveolar (PSA) nerve (Option A) innervates the remaining roots of the first molar as well as the second and third molars (teeth #1, #2, and #3). The anterior superior alveolar (ASA) nerve (Option C) innervates the maxillary central incisors, lateral incisors, and canines (teeth #6 through #11), while the greater palatine nerve (Option D) innervates posterior palatal mucoperiosteum without providing pulpal sensory fibers.

oral-pathology-medicine-851.question: A 50-year-old male patient with a 30 pack-year smoking history presents for a periodontal evaluation. Clinical examination reveals generalized interdental clinical attachment loss of 5 to 6 mm, probing depths of 5 to 7 mm, and Class II mobility on multiple teeth, with fibrotic gingiva and minimal bleeding on probing. Radiographs show generalized bone loss extending into the middle third of root length (>33%). What is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis according to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification?
options: Generalized Stage I, Grade A periodontitis
Generalized Stage II, Grade B periodontitis
Generalized Stage III, Grade C periodontitis
Biofilm-induced gingivitis on a reduced periodontium
oral-pathology-medicine-851.explanation: Option C is correct because interdental clinical attachment loss >=5 mm, probing depths >=6 mm, radiographic bone loss extending into the middle third of the root (>=33%), and Class II tooth mobility satisfy the criteria for Stage III periodontitis under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification; heavy smoking (>=10 cigarettes/day) automatically designates Grade C due to rapid progression and impaired healing. Stage I (Option A) is characterized by minimal attachment loss (1 to 2 mm) and bone loss <15% in slow-progressing cases. Stage II (Option B) involves moderate attachment loss (3 to 4 mm) and coronal-third bone loss (15% to 33%), while gingivitis (Option D) does not present with progressive attachment loss, mobility, or radiographic bone destruction.

oral-pathology-medicine-857.question: A 32-year-old female patient at 28 weeks of gestation presents with severe, spontaneous, throbbing pain in her maxillary right first molar (tooth #3). Clinical and radiographic evaluations confirm a diagnosis of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis. What is the MOST appropriate management for this patient during her current stage of pregnancy?
options: Defer all dental interventions until after delivery to prevent fetal stress
Perform an immediate pulpectomy under local anesthesia to eliminate pain and infection
Prescribe systemic amoxicillin and ibuprofen without operative intervention
Prescribe opioid analgesics and defer endodontic debridement until the postpartum period
oral-pathology-medicine-857.explanation: Option B is correct because ADA and ACOG guidelines affirm that acute dental pain and pulpal infections should be treated during any trimester of pregnancy; an immediate pulpectomy under local anesthesia (e.g., 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine) safely eradicates pain and removes the infectious source. Deferring care until delivery (Option A) subjects the mother and fetus to severe physiologic pain and increases bacteremia risk. Prescribing antibiotics and ibuprofen (Option C) is ineffective for pulpal necrosis and dangerous in the third trimester due to premature ductus arteriosus closure, while opioid maintenance (Option D) fails to address the underlying pulpal infection and risks fetal harm.

oral-pathology-medicine-954.question: A 9-year-old female patient presents to the dental clinic with a chief complaint of a fractured upper front tooth sustained 2 hours ago from a fall. Clinical examination reveals a complicated crown fracture of the permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8) with a 1.5 mm vital pulp exposure. Radiographic examination reveals an immature root with an open apex and no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Apexogenesis using mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA)
Pulpectomy with conventional gutta-percha obturation
Pulpectomy followed by calcium hydroxide apexification
Immediate extraction and space maintenance
oral-pathology-medicine-954.explanation: Option A is correct because apexogenesis via partial or full pulpotomy with MTA preserves vital radicular pulp tissue in an immature permanent tooth with an open apex, allowing continued physiological root development and apical closure according to AAE guidelines. Option B is contraindicated because conventional obturation cannot establish an apical seal in an open apex and halts root wall thickening, leaving the root fragile and susceptible to cervical fracture. Options C and D are incorrect because apexification is indicated only for non-vital immature teeth, and extraction is unnecessarily aggressive when an immature permanent tooth is restorable.

oral-pathology-medicine-957.question: A 52-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of root exposure and cervical sensitivity on his maxillary right canine (tooth #6). He reports a history of aggressive horizontal toothbrushing. Clinical examination reveals 4 mm of facial gingival recession on tooth #6 without interproximal bone or soft-tissue loss (Miller Class I / Cairo RT1 defect). The adjacent premolar possesses a wide, thick band of keratinized tissue. What is the MOST appropriate surgical management to achieve root coverage?
options: Open flap debridement
Lateral pedicle flap
Free gingival graft
Distal wedge procedure
oral-pathology-medicine-957.explanation: Option B is correct because a lateral pedicle (sliding) flap maintains an intact vascular pedicle from adjacent donor keratinized tissue to achieve predictable root coverage over an isolated Miller Class I recession defect. Option A is incorrect because open flap debridement is indicated for subgingival debridement in periodontitis, not root coverage. Option C is less appropriate because free gingival grafts have lower aesthetic color matching and less predictable root coverage over avascular roots, being primarily used to augment the width of attached keratinized tissue. Option D is incorrect because a distal wedge procedure is utilized for periodontal pocket elimination distal to the terminal molar.

oral-pathology-medicine-976.question: A 45-year-old female patient presents for a comprehensive dental examination. She reports occasional bleeding during toothbrushing. Clinical examination reveals generalized marginal gingival erythema, probing depths of 3 to 4 mm with bleeding on probing, interdental clinical attachment loss of 1 to 2 mm at multiple non-adjacent teeth, and bitewing radiographs demonstrating horizontal alveolar bone loss confined to the coronal third (<15%). No teeth have been lost due to periodontitis. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification system, what is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Gingivitis on an intact periodontium
Stage I periodontitis
Stage III periodontitis
Necrotizing periodontitis
oral-pathology-medicine-976.explanation: Option B is correct because interdental clinical attachment loss of 1 to 2 mm, radiographic bone loss confined to the coronal third (<15%), and probing depths up to 4 mm without tooth loss satisfy the diagnostic criteria for Stage I periodontitis under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification. Option A is incorrect because gingivitis requires the complete absence of clinical attachment loss and radiographic bone loss. Option C is incorrect because Stage III periodontitis involves clinical attachment loss of 5 mm or greater, bone loss extending to the middle third of the root or beyond, and probing depths of 6 mm or greater. Option D is incorrect because necrotizing periodontitis presents with severe pain, ulcerated and punched-out papillae, and pseudomembrane formation.

oral-pathology-medicine-977.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic with a chief complaint of a fractured front tooth sustained 1 hour ago during a fall. Clinical examination reveals an uncomplicated crown fracture involving enamel and dentin on the permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8), with no pulpal exposure. The tooth is non-mobile, non-tender to percussion, and responds positively to cold testing. Periapical radiography confirms an open apex with no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide
Bonded composite resin restoration and periodic vitality monitoring
Pulpectomy with mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) apical barrier
Full-coverage ceramic crown preparation
oral-pathology-medicine-977.explanation: Option B is correct because uncomplicated crown fractures without pulpal exposure require immediate sealing of exposed dentinal tubules using a bonded composite resin restoration (or fragment reattachment) along with periodic pulp vitality monitoring under AAPD and AAE trauma guidelines. Option A is incorrect because direct pulp capping is indicated only when there is mechanical or traumatic exposure of the pulp tissue. Option C is incorrect because endodontic intervention is contraindicated in a vital tooth with continuing root development. Option D is contraindicated because full-coverage crown preparation in a 7-year-old risks iatrogenic pulp exposure due to the large pulp chamber and damages immature gingival architecture.

oral-pathology-medicine-906.question: A 9-year-old female patient presents for an orthodontic evaluation. Clinical examination reveals a skeletal Class II malocclusion characterized by mandibular retrognathia, an excessive overjet of 8 mm, and proclined maxillary incisors during the mixed dentition stage. What is the MOST appropriate initial orthodontic treatment approach for this patient?
options: Observation without intervention until all permanent teeth have erupted
Growth modification using a functional appliance
Serial extractions of primary canines and first molars
Orthognathic surgical mandibular advancement
oral-pathology-medicine-906.explanation: Option B is correct because Phase I growth modification using a functional appliance (such as a Twin Block or Herbst appliance) in a growing mixed-dentition patient postures the mandible forward to correct skeletal Class II discrepancy and reduce excessive overjet, minimizing the risk of incisal trauma. Option A is incorrect because postponing intervention leaves severely proclined incisors with an 8 mm overjet vulnerable to traumatic fracture during active childhood years. Option C is incorrect because serial extraction is indicated for severe arch-length tooth-size discrepancy and severe crowding, not skeletal mandibular retrognathia. Option D is contraindicated because orthognathic surgery must be delayed until skeletal growth is complete.

oral-pathology-medicine-907.question: A 25-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of a dull ache and discomfort upon mastication in his mandibular left quadrant. He reports a history of sports-related trauma to the region several years ago. Clinical examination reveals tooth #21 is discolored and tender to percussion. The tooth does not respond to thermal testing or electric pulp testing. Radiographic examination reveals a circumscribed periapical radiolucency associated with the apex of tooth #21. What is the MOST likely pulpal and periapical diagnosis according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) standards?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis
Pulp necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis
Pulp necrosis with asymptomatic apical periodontitis
Reversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues
oral-pathology-medicine-907.explanation: Option B is correct because the absence of response to both thermal and electric pulp testing confirms pulp necrosis, while pain upon mastication and percussion associated with a periapical radiolucency establishes the diagnosis of symptomatic apical periodontitis under AAE diagnostic terminology. Option A is incorrect because symptomatic irreversible pulpitis requires a vital pulp exhibiting heightened, lingering response to thermal stimuli. Option C is incorrect because asymptomatic apical periodontitis exhibits no clinical symptoms or pain to percussion and mastication. Option D is incorrect because reversible pulpitis presents with non-lingering sensitivity in a vital tooth without periapical radiolucency.

oral-pathology-medicine-913.question: A 28-year-old male presents for a comprehensive dental examination. He is systemically healthy, a non-smoker, and maintains good oral hygiene with minimal dental biofilm. Clinical examination reveals deep periodontal pockets (8 to 9 mm) localized to the maxillary incisors and mandibular first molars (teeth #19 and #30), with only mild marginal gingivitis. Radiographic examination demonstrates severe vertical angular bone loss restricted to these sites that is disproportionate to the amount of local plaque. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the MOST likely periodontal diagnosis?
options: Stage I, Grade A periodontitis, generalized
Stage III, Grade C periodontitis, molar-incisor pattern
Necrotizing periodontitis
Biofilm-induced gingivitis on an intact periodontium
oral-pathology-medicine-913.explanation: Option B is correct because severe interdental attachment loss with probing depths >= 6 mm, severe vertical bone loss disproportionate to low biofilm deposits, rapid disease progression (Grade C), and localization to the first molars and incisors defines Stage III, Grade C periodontitis with a molar-incisor pattern (formerly localized aggressive periodontitis) under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification. Option A is incorrect because Stage I, Grade A represents mild horizontal bone loss (<15%) with slow progression and shallow pockets. Option C is incorrect because necrotizing periodontitis is characterized by painful punched-out papillae, ulceration, and necrosis. Option D is incorrect because gingivitis presents without clinical attachment loss or alveolar bone destruction.

oral-pathology-medicine-1054.question: A 70-year-old female patient with a history of osteoporosis has been taking oral alendronate for 8 years. She presents with a non-restorable mandibular molar requiring extraction. According to ADA and AAOMS guidelines, which of the following is the MOST appropriate clinical management strategy to minimize the risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ)?
options: Discontinue alendronate for 3 months prior to surgery
Prescribe high-dose systemic corticosteroids for 2 weeks preoperatively
Perform minimally traumatic extraction, achieve primary soft-tissue closure, and provide perioperative antimicrobial coverage
Perform routine hyperbaric oxygen therapy prior to any surgical intervention
oral-pathology-medicine-1054.explanation: Option C is correct because the American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons (AAOMS) and American Dental Association (ADA) recommend conservative surgical technique with minimal periosteal trauma, elimination of sharp bony edges, tension-free primary wound closure, and perioperative antimicrobial therapy to minimize MRONJ risk. Option A is incorrect because routine 'drug holidays' for oral bisphosphonates are not supported by clinical evidence due to the long skeletal half-life of bisphosphonates (up to 10 years) and potential risk to bone density. Option B is contraindicated because corticosteroids are immunosuppressive and significantly elevate the risk of osteonecrosis. Option D is incorrect because hyperbaric oxygen therapy is not indicated as standard prophylaxis for dentoalveolar extractions in patients taking oral bisphosphonates.

oral-pathology-medicine-1025.question: A 40-year-old patient with a history of Crohn's disease presents for evaluation of persistent oral lesions. Clinical examination reveals non-tender, diffuse swelling of the upper and lower lips, cobblestone appearance of the buccal mucosa, and deep linear ulcers in the buccal vestibules. What is the MOST likely diagnosis for these oral manifestations?
options: Pyostomatitis vegetans
Orofacial granulomatosis
Oral squamous cell carcinoma
Erythema multiforme
oral-pathology-medicine-1025.explanation: Option B is correct because orofacial granulomatosis presents with non-tender persistent lip swelling (cheilitis granulomatosa), mucosal cobblestoning, and deep linear vestibule ulcers, which represent noncaseating granulomatous inflammation characteristically associated with Crohn's disease (Neville). Option A is incorrect because pyostomatitis vegetans presents as yellowish pustules that rupture into 'snail-track' ulcerations and is classically associated with ulcerative colitis. Option C is incorrect because oral squamous cell carcinoma typically manifests as a solitary, indurated ulcer or exophytic lesion with rolled margins, not diffuse cobblestoning. Option D is incorrect because erythema multiforme is an acute hypersensitivity reaction featuring crusting lip erosions and targetoid skin lesions rather than chronic granulomatous thickening.

oral-pathology-medicine-1076.question: A 65-year-old male with a 40 pack-year smoking history and heavy alcohol consumption presents with a persistent, painless ulcer on the lateral border of the tongue that has been present for 3 months. Clinical examination reveals an indurated ulcer measuring 2 cm with rolled borders. Palpation of the neck demonstrates a firm, fixed 2.5 cm lymph node in the ipsilateral submandibular region. What is the MOST appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: Prescribe empirical oral antibiotics and re-evaluate the lesion in 2 weeks
Perform an incisional biopsy of the tongue lesion and refer for fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of the lymph node
Perform an incisional biopsy of both the primary tongue lesion and the cervical lymph node
Perform an excisional biopsy of the tongue lesion and prescribe topical corticosteroids
oral-pathology-medicine-1076.explanation: Option B is correct because a chronic, indurated ulcer suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma requires an incisional biopsy of the primary mucosal lesion, whereas suspected cervical lymph node metastasis must be evaluated by fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or oncologic referral to avoid capsular rupture. Option C is contraindicated because an open incisional biopsy of a cervical lymph node breaches the nodal capsule and risks tumor seeding into adjacent neck compartments, worsening prognosis. Options A and D are incorrect because prescribing antibiotics or corticosteroids inappropriately delays definitive histopathological diagnosis of a highly suspicious malignancy, and excisional biopsy is inappropriate for a large, suspected malignant tumor.

oral-pathology-medicine-961.question: A 58-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of sharp pain upon chewing on her mandibular left first molar (tooth #19) and a sensation that 'something is broken.' The tooth has an existing extensive MOD amalgam restoration. Clinical examination reveals a crack extending across the distal marginal ridge and pulpal floor toward the distobuccal cusp. The tooth responds normally to cold without lingering, percussion sensitivity is mild, and a bite test on the distobuccal cusp elicits sharp pain upon release. Probing depths are 2 to 3 mm throughout. What is the MOST appropriate definitive restorative treatment?
options: Direct composite resin restoration
Replacement multi-surface amalgam restoration
Full-coverage crown
Pulpectomy followed by a post and core
oral-pathology-medicine-961.explanation: Option C is correct because a cracked tooth with a vital pulp exhibiting reversible symptoms requires a full-coverage crown to provide cuspal protection and circumferential ferrule, stabilizing the tooth segments and preventing catastrophic fracture. Options A and B are incorrect because direct intracoronal restorations (composite or amalgam) do not provide external cuspal splinting and wedging forces during mastication can accelerate crack propagation. Option D is incorrect because the pulp remains vital without signs of irreversible pulpitis; endodontic therapy is unnecessary unless pulpal symptoms fail to resolve after cuspal protection or irreversible pulpitis develops.

oral-pathology-medicine-968.question: A 70-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of difficulty chewing on his left side due to missing teeth. He requests a removable partial denture (RPD) and has a medical history of well-controlled hypertension. Clinical examination reveals missing teeth #18 and #19 with all other natural teeth present and periodontally sound, establishing a Kennedy Class II mandibular arch. The residual alveolar ridge is well-healed with adequate attached gingiva. What is the MOST critical biomechanical design consideration for this patient's distal extension RPD?
options: Maximizing the flexibility of the major connector
Selecting steep anatomic cusp angles for the prosthetic teeth
Achieving broad stress distribution between the abutment teeth and the residual ridge
Utilizing rigid cast circumferential clasps on the terminal abutment to eliminate movement
oral-pathology-medicine-968.explanation: Option C is correct because a Kennedy Class II RPD is a tooth-and-tissue-supported distal extension prosthesis subject to rotational dislodging forces due to differential compressibility between the periodontal ligament (0.2 mm) and residual mucosa (1-2 mm), making broad stress distribution critical to protect both the abutment teeth and residual ridge. Option A is incorrect because major connectors must be rigid to distribute masticatory forces evenly across the entire arch. Option B is incorrect because steep prosthetic cusp angles generate destructive lateral torquing forces on the residual ridge and abutment teeth. Option D is incorrect because rigid circumferential clasps engage undercut regions without stress-release, exerting harmful destructive cantilever forces on the terminal abutment during distal extension function.

oral-pathology-medicine-973.question: A 32-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of intermittent sharp pain in her maxillary left posterior region that is exacerbated by cold beverages and sweets, lingering for 10 to 15 seconds after stimulus removal. Percussion and palpation tests are negative. Radiographs reveal a deep carious lesion approximating the pulp chamber of tooth #14. What is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis?
options: Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Pulpal necrosis
Normal pulp
oral-pathology-medicine-973.explanation: Option B is correct because according to the American Association of Endodontists (AAE), prolonged thermal pain (lingering 10-15 seconds) after stimulus removal associated with deep caries into the pulp chamber characterizes symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, indicating vital inflamed pulp incapable of healing. Option A is incorrect because reversible pulpitis produces quick, transient sharp pain that resolves within seconds after stimulus removal. Option C is incorrect because a necrotic pulp is non-vital and does not respond to thermal vitality testing. Option D is incorrect because normal pulp responds mildly to cold and returns to baseline within 1 to 2 seconds without lingering pain.

oral-pathology-medicine-1037.question: A 33-year-old pregnant patient in her second trimester develops multiple exophytic, red, bleeding gingival masses consistent with pyogenic granulomas. The lesions cause mild discomfort during brushing but do not interfere with mastication. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate surgical excision of all lesions
Meticulous plaque control, scaling, and observation until postpartum
Prescription of systemic corticosteroids
Empiric systemic antibiotic therapy
oral-pathology-medicine-1037.explanation: Option B is correct because pregnancy pyogenic granulomas represent hyperplastic vascular responses to local irritants modulated by elevated estrogen and progesterone, which frequently regress or completely resolve postpartum after hormonal levels normalize. Option A is incorrect because surgical excision during pregnancy carries a high rate of recurrence and should be deferred until postpartum unless severe hemorrhage, ulceration, or masticatory interference occurs. Options C and D are incorrect because pyogenic granuloma is a reactive benign vascular hyperplasia that does not respond to corticosteroids or antibacterial pharmacotherapy.

oral-pathology-medicine-1039.question: A 72-year-old patient with a history of continuous, long-term complete denture wear presents with an asymptomatic, velvety erythematous patch on the hard palate strictly confined to the denture-bearing area. The lesion cannot be wiped off. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Traumatic ulcer
Denture stomatitis (erythematous candidiasis)
Erythroplakia
Allergic contact stomatitis
oral-pathology-medicine-1039.explanation: Option B is correct because asymptomatic, non-scrapable erythema strictly confined to the mucosal outline of a maxillary complete denture in a patient who wears dentures continuously is the classic clinical presentation of denture stomatitis (erythematous candidiasis). Option A is incorrect because traumatic ulcers present with painful mucosal discontinuities covered by a yellowish fibrinopurulent membrane and surrounded by an erythematous halo. Option C is incorrect because erythroplakia is a high-risk precancerous red patch diagnosed strictly by exclusion when all specific local inflammatory etiologies have been ruled out. Option D is incorrect because true contact allergy to cured methyl methacrylate denture base is exceedingly rare and produces diffuse mucosal burning and sloughing rather than confined, asymptomatic erythema.

oral-pathology-medicine-1048.question: A 42-year-old patient presents with recurrent pain and swelling in the right submandibular triangle, particularly before and during meals. Clinical examination reveals a firm, tender nodule palpable along the right Wharton duct near the sublingual caruncle, and milking the duct expresses scant, cloudy saliva. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Urgent surgical excision of the submandibular gland
Antibiotic therapy, hydration, and salivary stimulation
Systemic corticosteroid therapy
Incisional biopsy of the palpable nodule
oral-pathology-medicine-1048.explanation: Option B is correct because acute obstructive sialadenitis with purulent discharge secondary to sialolithiasis is initially managed conservatively with oral antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate), aggressive hydration, warm compresses, and sialogogues to resolve infection and promote calculus expulsion. Option A is incorrect because surgical gland extirpation is invasive and reserved for chronic, recurrent, or medically refractory sialadenitis after the acute infection has cleared. Option C is incorrect because corticosteroids do not treat the underlying bacterial infection or mechanical ductal blockage. Option D is incorrect because biopsy is contraindicated in acute suppurative sialadenitis and obstructive lithiasis.

oral-pathology-medicine-1099.question: A 48-year-old male complains of recurrent, acute painful swelling in the floor of the mouth while eating that subsides over several hours. Bimanual palpation reveals a firm, tender nodule in the anterior floor of the mouth along the course of the submandibular duct. What is the MOST appropriate initial diagnostic imaging modality?
options: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Cross-sectional mandibular occlusal radiograph
Diagnostic salivary gland ultrasound
oral-pathology-medicine-1099.explanation: Option C is correct because according to White & Pharoah, a cross-sectional mandibular occlusal radiograph is the primary, standard first-line chairside imaging modality for detecting suspected radiopaque sialoliths in the anterior portion of Wharton duct. Option A is incorrect because CBCT delivers a higher radiation dose and is unnecessary for a localized, superficial anterior calculus readily visualized on conventional dental films. Option B is incorrect because MRI is costly, indicated primarily for soft tissue neoplasms, and suboptimal for visualizing calcified salivary stones. Option D is incorrect because while ultrasound is useful for parenchymal gland evaluation, occlusal radiography is the standard, most accessible first-line chairside imaging technique in clinical dentistry.

oral-pathology-medicine-1140.question: A 48-year-old female presents with a persistent burning sensation of the oral mucosa, difficulty swallowing solid foods (dysphagia), and fatigue. Clinical examination reveals generalized atrophy of the dorsal tongue papillae with a smooth, erythematous appearance, accompanied by bilateral angular cheilitis. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypochromic microcytic anemia and low serum ferritin. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Sjögren syndrome
Plummer-Vinson syndrome
Pernicious anemia
Behçet syndrome
oral-pathology-medicine-1140.explanation: Option B is correct because Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by the classic clinical triad of iron deficiency anemia, atrophic glossitis (smooth, red tongue with mucosal burning), and dysphagia associated with esophageal webs, which carries an increased risk for upper aerodigestive squamous cell carcinoma. Option A is incorrect because Sjögren syndrome is an autoimmune disorder manifesting primarily with xerostomia and keratoconjunctivitis sicca rather than esophageal webs and microcytic anemia. Option C is incorrect because pernicious anemia involves vitamin B12 deficiency resulting in macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia rather than microcytic iron deficiency. Option D is incorrect because Behçet syndrome presents with recurrent aphthous stomatitis, genital ulcerations, and ocular inflammation.

oral-pathology-medicine-1210.question: A 40-year-old female patient presents with a diffuse, erythematous, depapillated tongue (atrophic glossitis) and bilateral angular cheilitis. She also reports chronic fatigue, exertional shortness of breath, and pale palpebral conjunctiva. Complete blood count and serum studies reveal low hemoglobin, low mean corpuscular volume (MCV), and low ferritin. What is the MOST likely underlying systemic diagnosis?
options: Pernicious anemia
Aplastic anemia
Iron deficiency anemia
Thalassemia minor
oral-pathology-medicine-1210.explanation: Option C is correct because atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, fatigue, and pallor occurring alongside microcytic hypochromic indices and depleted serum ferritin levels specifically define iron deficiency anemia. Option A is incorrect because pernicious anemia causes macrocytic megaloblastic anemia secondary to intrinsic factor deficiency and impaired vitamin B12 absorption, marked by an elevated MCV. Option B is incorrect because aplastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia secondary to bone marrow failure rather than isolated iron depletion. Option D is incorrect because thalassemia minor features microcytic anemia with normal or elevated serum ferritin levels.

oral-pathology-medicine-1198.question: A 70-year-old female with osteoporosis managed with subcutaneous denosumab presents three months following the extraction of tooth #19 with exposed, necrotic bone in the extraction socket. The area is painful, has failed to heal, and the patient has no history of radiation therapy to the head and neck. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic osteomyelitis
Osteoradionecrosis of the jaw
Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ)
Alveolar osteitis
oral-pathology-medicine-1198.explanation: Option C is correct because the American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons (AAOMS) defines MRONJ as exposed necrotic bone persisting for more than 8 weeks in patients receiving antiresorptive agents (such as denosumab, a RANKL inhibitor, or bisphosphonates) without a history of craniofacial radiation therapy. Option A is incorrect because chronic osteomyelitis presents with deep osseous infection, sequestrum formation, and draining sinus tracts without the prerequisite antiresorptive pharmacological etiology. Option B is incorrect because osteoradionecrosis specifically requires prior therapeutic head and neck radiation therapy. Option D is incorrect because alveolar osteitis (dry socket) occurs 3 to 5 days post-extraction and resolves within 1 to 2 weeks without persistent necrotic bone exposure.

oral-pathology-medicine-1199.question: An adult patient presents with creamy white plaques on the buccal mucosa and hard palate, accompanied by a mild burning sensation. The plaques are easily wiped off with a gauze sponge, revealing an erythematous, bleeding mucosal surface. The patient recently completed a 3-week course of broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics. What is the MOST appropriate first-line treatment for this condition?
options: Systemic fluconazole 100 mg daily for 14 days
Intravenous amphotericin B therapy
Surgical excision of the mucosal plaques
Topical nystatin oral suspension or clotrimazole troches
oral-pathology-medicine-1199.explanation: Option D is correct because topical antifungals, such as nystatin oral suspension or clotrimazole troches, represent the primary first-line therapeutic regimen for mild to moderate, uncomplicated pseudomembranous candidiasis (oral thrush) in an immunocompetent adult. Option A is incorrect because systemic fluconazole is typically reserved for refractory candidiasis, esophageal involvement, or immunocompromised hosts. Option B is incorrect because intravenous amphotericin B is reserved for severe, life-threatening systemic or invasive fungal infections due to substantial nephrotoxicity. Option C is incorrect because pseudomembranous candidiasis is a superficial fungal overgrowth that requires topical antifungal pharmacotherapy, not surgical excision.

oral-pathology-medicine-1294.question: According to the International Study Group criteria for Behçet syndrome, which of the following is the MANDATORY diagnostic criterion required to establish the diagnosis?
options: Recurrent oral aphthous ulcerations
Recurrent genital ulcerations
Ocular lesions (anterior or posterior uveitis)
Positive cutaneous pathergy test
oral-pathology-medicine-1294.explanation: Option A is correct because the International Study Group (ISG) diagnostic criteria for Behçet syndrome mandate the presence of recurrent oral aphthous ulcerations (at least three episodes within a 12-month period) as the prerequisite criterion, accompanied by at least two secondary criteria. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because recurrent genital ulceration, ocular inflammatory lesions, and a positive pathergy reaction are secondary criteria that support the diagnosis but are not individually mandatory.

oral-pathology-medicine-1269.question: A 65-year-old female presents with severe xerostomia, reporting difficulty speaking, swallowing, and recurrent oral candidiasis. Her medical history includes hypertension, depression, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia. Her daily medications include hydrochlorothiazide, amitriptyline, ibuprofen, and atorvastatin. Which of these medications is the MOST potent contributor to her severe xerostomia?
options: Amitriptyline
Ibuprofen
Hydrochlorothiazide
Atorvastatin
oral-pathology-medicine-1269.explanation: Option A is correct because amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant with potent anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) properties that directly inhibit parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands, resulting in profound hyposalivation. Option B is incorrect because ibuprofen is an NSAID with no significant xerogenic effects. Option C is incorrect because while hydrochlorothiazide can cause mild oral dryness through diuretic-induced fluid volume contraction, its effect is far less severe than direct muscarinic receptor blockade. Option D is incorrect because atorvastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor that is not associated with salivary hypofunction.

oral-pathology-medicine-1349.question: A 70-year-old edentulous patient wearing complete dentures with severely worn prosthetic teeth presents with bilateral erythema, painful fissuring, and maceration at the labial commissures. What is the PRIMARY local predisposing factor for this condition?
options: Loss of vertical dimension of occlusion
Excessive vertical dimension of occlusion
Contact allergy to denture base methyl methacrylate
Occlusal prematurities causing lateral tongue thrust
oral-pathology-medicine-1349.explanation: Option A is correct because loss of vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO) from denture tooth attrition causes mandibular overclosure and deep skin folding at the labial commissures, leading to chronic saliva accumulation, tissue maceration, and secondary opportunistic coinfection by Candida albicans and Staphylococcus aureus (angular cheilitis). Option B is incorrect because excessive vertical dimension leads to muscular fatigue, clicking of denture teeth, and inability to close the lips comfortably rather than commissural folding. Option C is incorrect because contact stomatitis to processed acrylic resin is exceedingly rare and produces generalized palatal or alveolar mucosal erythema rather than isolated commissural cheilitis. Option D is incorrect because occlusal prematurities and tongue thrusting do not cause labial commissure folding or salivary maceration.

oral-pathology-medicine-862.question: A 25-year-old male presents for the surgical extraction of an impacted maxillary third molar (#16). Following extraction, inspection of the socket reveals a 4 mm opening into the maxillary sinus, through which air can be seen bubbling upon gentle nasal exhalation. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management of this finding?
options: Administer oral antibiotics and dismiss the patient with sinus precautions alone
Pack the extraction socket tightly with non-resorbable gauze
Achieve primary closure of the socket using tension-free soft tissue flap advancement and sutures
Perform an immediate Caldwell-Luc procedure to seal the sinus floor
oral-pathology-medicine-862.explanation: Option C is correct because an acute moderate-sized (2 to 6 mm) oroantral communication following maxillary molar (#16) extraction requires tension-free primary soft tissue closure with sutures (often augmented with a collagen barrier or gelatin sponge) and sinus precautions to prevent epithelial tract formation and chronic sinusitis. Option A is incorrect because communications greater than 2 mm rarely heal spontaneously without primary surgical closure. Option B is incorrect because non-resorbable packing prevents clot organization and tissue closure, while Option D is incorrect because a Caldwell-Luc procedure is indicated for retrieving displaced roots or treating chronic sinusitis, not for routine immediate closure of an acute communication.

oral-pathology-medicine-863.question: A 38-year-old male presents with sensitivity to cold on his maxillary left first molar (#14). Clinical examination reveals a deep Class II carious lesion extending subgingivally on the distal surface, and radiographs confirm pulp proximity without periapical pathosis. What is the MOST appropriate technique to ensure adequate isolation and prevent gingival trauma during cavity preparation and restoration?
options: Rely on cotton roll isolation combined with high-volume evacuation alone
Place a standard dental dam clamp coronally without inverting the dam margins
Perform an electrosurgical gingivectomy to expose the margin prior to isolation
Utilize a deep-reach dental dam clamp and invert the dam below the subgingival cavity margin
oral-pathology-medicine-863.explanation: Option D is correct because isolating a subgingival Class II proximal box on a molar (#14) requires a deep-reach clamp with subgingivally directed jaws and careful inversion of the dental dam apical to the gingival cavosurface margin to achieve a moisture-tight seal without traumatizing the gingival attachment. Option A is incorrect because cotton roll isolation cannot reliably prevent crevicular fluid and saliva contamination during resin bonding procedures. Option B is incorrect because a standard clamp seated coronally without dam inversion will leak crevicular fluid and may impinge on the lesion margin. Option C is incorrect because an electrosurgical gingivectomy is unnecessary, invasive, and risks violating biological width and damaging bone when mechanical isolation is achievable.

oral-pathology-medicine-865.question: A 9-year-old male presents with a fractured maxillary right central incisor (#8) following a fall 2 hours ago. Clinical examination reveals an uncomplicated enamel-dentin fracture involving the incisal third of the crown, with normal mobility and no pulp exposure. The fractured fragment was not recovered. Radiographs demonstrate an open apex with no root fracture or periapical pathosis. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Initiate root canal treatment to prevent future pulpal complications
Restore the fractured crown with composite resin to seal exposed dentinal tubules
Perform a cervical pulpotomy to protect the underlying pulp tissue
Smooth the sharp enamel margins and postpone definitive restoration until root closure
oral-pathology-medicine-865.explanation: Option B is correct because according to American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) and International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an uncomplicated crown fracture (enamel and dentin without pulpal involvement) should be treated promptly by sealing exposed dentinal tubules with a bonded composite resin restoration to protect the vital pulp from bacterial ingress. Option A is incorrect because pulpectomy and root canal therapy are contraindicated in a vital, asymptomatic tooth with no pulp exposure. Option C is incorrect because a pulpotomy is indicated only when there is mechanical or traumatic pulp exposure. Option D is incorrect because leaving dentinal tubules unsealed allows microleakage and bacterial invasion, predisposing an immature pulp to necrosis.

oral-pathology-medicine-898.question: A 7-year-old female presents with a fractured maxillary right central incisor (#8) following a fall 3 hours ago. Clinical examination reveals a complicated crown fracture with a 1 mm vital pulp exposure that exhibits controlled, bright red hemorrhage. Radiographs demonstrate an immature root with a wide open apex and no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate initial treatment for this tooth?
options: Perform a complete pulpectomy and obturate with gutta-percha
Perform a Cvek pulpotomy (partial pulpotomy) with a biocompatible material
Place a direct pulp cap with calcium hydroxide and restore with composite resin
Extract the fractured tooth and fabricate a removable space maintainer
oral-pathology-medicine-898.explanation: Option B is correct because a Cvek pulpotomy (partial pulpotomy), involving the removal of 1 to 2 mm of inflamed coronal pulp tissue followed by placement of a biocompatible capping material (such as MTA or calcium hydroxide), preserves radicular pulp vitality to allow continued root development and apexogenesis in an immature permanent tooth. Option A is incorrect because complete pulpectomy halts dentin deposition, leaving an open apex and thin root walls susceptible to cervical fracture. Option C is incorrect because direct pulp capping in traumatic crown fractures has significantly lower success rates than partial pulpotomy due to superficial bacterial contamination. Option D is incorrect because extraction is contraindicated for a restorable permanent central incisor.

oral-pathology-medicine-871.question: A 60-year-old male with well-controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.4%) presents for a comprehensive periodontal evaluation. Clinical examination reveals generalized marginal erythema, bleeding on probing at 35% of sites, and localized probing depths of 6 mm limited to the first and second molars (affecting 15% of all teeth). Radiographs show horizontal bone loss of 30% to 40% (extending into the middle third of the root) localized to these molar sites, with no history of tooth loss from periodontitis. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis?
options: Generalized gingivitis on an intact periodontium
Localized Stage III, Grade B periodontitis
Generalized Stage II, Grade A periodontitis
Localized Stage IV, Grade C periodontitis
oral-pathology-medicine-871.explanation: Option B is correct because according to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, probing depths >= 6 mm with radiographic bone loss extending into the middle third of the root (30% to 40%) classify as Stage III, involvement of < 30% of teeth defines a localized extent, and well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c < 7.0%) designates Grade B progression. Option A is incorrect because gingivitis cannot be diagnosed in the presence of periodontal attachment and radiographic bone loss. Option C is incorrect because Stage II is characterized by probing depths <= 5 mm and bone loss limited to the coronal third (< 33%), and involvement of 15% of teeth is localized rather than generalized. Option D is incorrect because Stage IV requires severe tooth loss (>= 5 teeth) or masticatory dysfunction, and Grade C is indicated for poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c >= 7.0%).

oral-pathology-medicine-879.question: A 65-year-old male presents for scaling and root planing. His medical history includes hypertension managed with lisinopril, hyperlipidemia managed with atorvastatin, and gastroesophageal reflux disease managed with omeprazole; he also took 2 g of prophylactic oral amoxicillin 1 hour prior to treatment. Immediately following the appointment, he is rapidly returned from a supine to an upright position and complains of sudden lightheadedness and blurred vision, with a recorded blood pressure drop from 136/84 mmHg to 92/58 mmHg. Which of the patient's medications is MOST likely responsible for this acute orthostatic hypotensive episode?
options: Amoxicillin
Atorvastatin
Omeprazole
Lisinopril
oral-pathology-medicine-879.explanation: Option D is correct because lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) blunts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and reduces peripheral vascular resistance, impairing the sympathetic baroreceptor-mediated vasoconstrictive reflex required to maintain arterial pressure upon rapid upright repositioning. Option A is incorrect because amoxicillin has no autonomic or hemodynamic effects on vascular tone or blood pressure regulation. Options B and C are incorrect because neither atorvastatin (an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor) nor omeprazole (a proton-pump inhibitor) causes vasodilation or predisposes patients to postural hypotension.

oral-pathology-medicine-880.question: A 40-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of a dull, aching sensation across her left posterior maxilla accompanied by nasal congestion and left facial pressure that worsens when bending forward. Clinical examination reveals that all maxillary left teeth respond normally to cold vitality testing and are non-tender to percussion and palpation. Radiographs show generalized mucosal thickening and an air-fluid level within the left maxillary sinus, with no dental caries or periapical radiolucencies. What is the MOST probable diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Acute maxillary sinusitis
Cracked tooth syndrome
Acute apical abscess
oral-pathology-medicine-880.explanation: Option B is correct because acute maxillary sinusitis (of rhinogenic origin) classically presents with facial pressure, nasal obstruction, radiographic sinus opacification or air-fluid levels, and pain referred to multiple maxillary posterior teeth that worsens upon lowering the head, in the absence of localized odontogenic pathosis. Option A is incorrect because symptomatic irreversible pulpitis produces sharp, lingering thermal pain localized to a specific offending tooth. Option C is incorrect because cracked tooth syndrome is characterized by sharp pain upon mastication or release of biting pressure. Option D is incorrect because an acute apical abscess presents with marked percussion sensitivity, pulp necrosis, and localized periapical swelling.

oral-pathology-medicine-884.question: During coronal endodontic access cavity preparation of a permanent maxillary first molar (#14), which anatomical area is at the GREATEST risk of iatrogenic perforation if the bur is directed too deeply while searching for the pulp chamber floor?
options: Furcation floor of the pulp chamber
Lateral cervical root surface in the mesial concavity
Apical third of the mesiobuccal root canal
Palatal cortical plate of the alveolar process
oral-pathology-medicine-884.explanation: Option A is correct because excessive apical extension with a rotary bur past the pulpal roof without identifying the true pulpal chamber floor carries the highest risk of iatrogenic furcal perforation directly into the periodontal ligament of the interradicular space. Option B is incorrect because lateral strip perforations along the mesial cervical concavity occur during aggressive radicular instrumentation and flaring, not during coronal access preparation. Option C is incorrect because apical canal transportation and apical perforation occur during mechanical canal enlargement within the root canal system. Option D is incorrect because the palatal cortical bone is an external anatomical structure outside the tooth and is not at direct risk during coronal chamber access.

oral-pathology-medicine-937.question: A 35-year-old female presents with a persistent dull, aching pain in her left posterior maxilla. Clinical examination reveals no caries, defective restorations, or periodontal pockets, and the maxillary left first molar (#14) responds normally to cold testing and is non-tender to percussion and palpation. The patient reports increased stress, morning jaw tightness, and frequent clenching. Palpation of the left masseter and temporalis muscles reproduces the pain. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis of tooth #14
Myofascial pain dysfunction
Acute periodontal abscess
Cracked tooth syndrome
oral-pathology-medicine-937.explanation: Option B is correct because myofascial pain dysfunction (masticatory muscle disorder) characteristically manifests as dull, aching jaw pain, morning muscle stiffness, and tenderness upon palpation of the masseter and temporalis muscles in patients with stress-related clenching, in the absence of dental or pulpal pathosis. Option A is incorrect because normal pulp vitality testing and lack of percussion sensitivity rule out irreversible pulpitis on tooth #14. Option C is incorrect because a periodontal abscess presents with localized swelling, deep probing depths, and purulent exudate. Option D is incorrect because cracked tooth syndrome is characterized by sharp pain on chewing or releasing biting pressure rather than continuous dull muscular soreness.

oral-pathology-medicine-916.question: A 35-year-old male presents with sharp, spontaneous pain in his maxillary right quadrant that lingers for several minutes following exposure to cold beverages. Clinical examination reveals a deep amalgam restoration on the maxillary right first molar (#3) with no visible fracture. Cold testing of tooth #3 produces sharp pain that persists for 45 seconds after removal of the stimulus; percussion and palpation testing are negative. What is the MOST probable pulpal diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis
oral-pathology-medicine-916.explanation: Option A is correct because according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic terminology, spontaneous pain accompanied by exaggerated thermal sensitivity that lingers for prolonged periods (> 30 seconds) after stimulus removal is pathognomonic for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis. Option B is incorrect because reversible pulpitis produces quick, transient sensitivity that dissipates within seconds of stimulus removal. Option C is incorrect because a necrotic pulp lacks vital nerve fibers and yields no response to cold vitality testing. Option D is incorrect because asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis by definition presents without clinical symptoms, typically identified through deep caries or hyperplastic pulpitis.

oral-pathology-medicine-920.question: A 7-year-old male presents for treatment of his mandibular right primary first molar (tooth S). Radiographs demonstrate a deep occlusal carious lesion approximating the pulp chamber with normal periapical and furcation tissues. Clinically, the tooth has no history of spontaneous pain and is non-tender to percussion. During complete caries excavation, a small pinpoint pulpal exposure is encountered with bright red, easily arrestable hemorrhage. What is the MOST appropriate treatment for this tooth?
options: Pulpotomy followed by a stainless steel crown
Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide followed by composite resin
Extraction of the primary molar followed by space maintainer placement
Complete pulpectomy followed by zinc oxide-eugenol obturation
oral-pathology-medicine-920.explanation: Option A is correct because according to American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) guidelines, a vital pulpotomy (using MTA, ferric sulfate, or formocresol) followed by a stainless steel crown is the recommended treatment for a restorable primary molar with a vital carious exposure and healthy radicular pulp. Option B is incorrect because direct pulp capping is contraindicated in primary molars with carious pulp exposures due to high failure rates and subsequent internal root resorption. Option C is incorrect because extraction is premature and unnecessarily invasive for a restorable tooth that can be maintained to preserve space and arch integrity. Option D is incorrect because pulpectomy is indicated only for primary teeth exhibiting irreversible pulpitis or pulpal necrosis.

oral-pathology-medicine-929.question: A 12-year-old male undergoes a routine dental examination. During dental charting, the clinician notes a permanent tooth in the mandibular left quadrant with five distinct cusps—including a prominent distal cusp—and two widely separated roots on the periapical radiograph. Which permanent tooth is being described?
options: Maxillary left first molar (#14)
Mandibular left first molar (#19)
Mandibular left second premolar (#20)
Mandibular left second molar (#18)
oral-pathology-medicine-929.explanation: Option B is correct because the permanent mandibular left first molar (#19) characteristically possesses five cusps (mesiobuccal, distobuccal, distal, mesiolingual, and distolingual) with a distinct distal cusp and two divergent roots (mesial and distal). Option A is incorrect because the maxillary left first molar (#14) features four primary cusps, often a cusp of Carabelli, and three divergent roots (two buccal, one palatal). Option C is incorrect because the mandibular left second premolar (#20) is a bicuspid or tricuspid tooth with a single root. Option D is incorrect because the mandibular left second molar (#18) has four cusps with a cruciform occlusal groove pattern and two less divergent roots.

oral-pathology-medicine-1232.question: A 42-year-old male presents with intermittent swelling and pain in the left submandibular region that is particularly exacerbated during meal consumption and gradually subsides afterward. Intraoral examination reveals a firm, tender mass in the floor of the mouth lateral to the lingual frenum, with absent salivary flow from the left submandibular duct orifice. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ranula
Sialadenitis
Mucocele
Sialolithiasis
oral-pathology-medicine-1232.explanation: Option D is correct because mealtime-associated swelling and pain (salivary colic) of the submandibular gland, combined with a palpable calcified mass in Wharton's duct and obstructed salivary flow, is classic for sialolithiasis. Sialadenitis typically presents with continuous erythema, purulent ductal exudate, and systemic signs rather than intermittent mealtime obstruction. Ranulas and mucoceles are mucus extravasation or retention phenomena that lack episodic meal-related pain and palpable calcified ductal obstructions.

oral-pathology-medicine-1233.question: A 58-year-old female presents with bilateral, interlacing white lines (Wickham striae) on her buccal mucosa, accompanied by erythematous and erosive areas on her attached gingiva. She reports burning and discomfort, especially when eating spicy or acidic foods. A clinical diagnosis of symptomatic erosive lichen planus is established. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic therapy?
options: Topical acyclovir cream
Systemic antibiotic therapy
Topical corticosteroids
Systemic antifungal therapy
oral-pathology-medicine-1233.explanation: Option C is correct because high-potency topical corticosteroids (such as clobetasol propionate or fluocinonide) represent the first-line pharmacologic therapy for symptomatic erosive lichen planus to suppress T-cell-mediated mucosal destruction. Topical acyclovir is indicated for herpes simplex viral infections and has no efficacy against autoimmune dermatoses. Systemic antibiotics and antifungals do not treat lichen planus because it is an immune-mediated disorder rather than a bacterial or primary fungal infection.

oral-pathology-medicine-1234.question: A 25-year-old male presents with a cluster of small, painful vesicles and shallow ulcers on the vermilion border of his lower lip. He reports a tingling sensation at the site 2 days prior to the eruption and notes recurrent episodes typically triggered by sun exposure. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic treatment?
options: Oral prednisone
Topical antibacterial ointment
Systemic acyclovir
Excisional biopsy
oral-pathology-medicine-1234.explanation: Option C is correct because recurrent herpes labialis triggered by ultraviolet light is caused by reactivated herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and is effectively treated with antiviral agents such as acyclovir or valacyclovir. Corticosteroids like oral prednisone are contraindicated because immunosuppression can exacerbate viral replication and delay healing. Topical antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections, and an excisional biopsy is contraindicated for acute, self-limiting viral vesiculobullous lesions.

oral-pathology-medicine-1235.question: A 38-year-old male who is HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 150 cells/µL presents with multiple, white, corrugated, non-wipeable lesions on the bilateral lateral borders of his tongue. The lesions are completely asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pseudomembranous candidiasis
Idiopathic leukoplakia
Oral hairy leukoplakia
Oral lichen planus
oral-pathology-medicine-1235.explanation: Option C is correct because oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL), caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) replication in immunocompromised patients (especially HIV with CD4 < 200 cells/µL), characteristically presents as asymptomatic, corrugated, vertically folded, non-wipeable white patches on the lateral borders of the tongue. Pseudomembranous candidiasis produces curd-like plaques that wipe off to reveal an erythematous base. Idiopathic leukoplakia and oral lichen planus do not present as bilateral, vertically corrugated folds on the lateral tongue borders intimately associated with profound immunodeficiency.

oral-pathology-medicine-1236.question: A 19-year-old female presents with concern regarding "spots" on her tongue that repeatedly appear, disappear, and change location over time. Clinical examination reveals multiple irregular erythematous patches on the dorsal surface of the tongue surrounded by raised, yellowish-white circinate borders. The patient reports no pain other than mild sensitivity to spicy foods. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Fissured tongue
Median rhomboid glossitis
Geographic tongue
Erythematous candidiasis
oral-pathology-medicine-1236.explanation: Option C is correct because geographic tongue (erythema migrans) classically manifests as transient, wandering erythematous areas of depapillated filiform papillae rimmed by slightly elevated, yellowish-white circinate margins on the dorsal tongue. Fissured tongue features deep grooves on the dorsal surface, although it commonly coexists with geographic tongue.
