pharmacology-anesthesia-1321.question: An 8-year-old child presents 30 minutes following trauma to the anterior maxilla. Clinical examination reveals that the immature permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8) is displaced apically into the alveolar socket, appearing 3 mm shorter than the adjacent permanent maxillary left central incisor (tooth #9), and is immobile. Radiographs confirm an open apex and intrusion without alveolar fracture. According to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate initial management for tooth #8?
options: Immediate surgical repositioning and rigid splinting for 4 weeks
Immediate extraction to prevent damage to adjacent structures
Allow for spontaneous re-eruption and monitor periodically
Immediate pulpectomy with calcium hydroxide paste placement
pharmacology-anesthesia-1321.explanation: Option C is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an immature permanent tooth with an open apex and mild-to-moderate intrusion (<7 mm) retains remarkable eruptive and revascularization capacity, making spontaneous re-eruption the preferred initial conservative approach. Option A is incorrect because immediate surgical repositioning and rigid splinting are reserved for mature teeth with severe intrusions (>7 mm) and carry an increased risk of marginal bone loss and replacement resorption (ankylosis). Option B is incorrect because extraction is contraindicated when a traumatized immature permanent incisor has a favorable prognosis for re-eruption and survival. Option D is incorrect because immature teeth frequently retain pulp vitality or revascularize after intrusion, so prophylactic endodontic treatment is not indicated unless pulp necrosis is confirmed during follow-up.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1329.question: A 25-year-old male presents with severe pain and limited mouth opening (trismus of 18 mm). Intraoral examination reveals acute pericoronitis around a partially erupted mandibular left third molar (tooth #17), with an erythematous, edematous operculum that actively expresses purulent drainage upon gentle palpation. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate surgical extraction of tooth #17 under local anesthesia
Mechanical debridement with subopercular irrigation, systemic antibiotics, and warm saline rinses
Surgical incision and drainage of the dorsal surface of the operculum
Immediate operculectomy using a surgical scalpel or electrosurgery
pharmacology-anesthesia-1329.explanation: Option B is correct because the presence of trismus indicates extension of infection into the masticator space (e.g., pterygomandibular or masseteric space), which necessitates conservative local debridement and subopercular irrigation combined with systemic antibiotic therapy and warm saline rinses until acute symptoms subside. Option A is incorrect because immediate extraction in the presence of severe trismus and active spreading cellulitis is contraindicated due to limited surgical access, poor anesthetic efficacy, and risk of fascial space dissemination. Option C is incorrect because incising an already draining operculum does not provide additional drainage, traumatizes inflamed tissue, and fails to address deep infection. Option D is incorrect because surgical operculectomy during acute infection causes severe bleeding and pain, and definitive management requires extraction once the acute phase resolves.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1334.question: A 45-year-old female who is a heavy cigarette smoker presents for a routine dental checkup. Clinical examination reveals an asymptomatic, 1.5 cm white, corrugated patch on the right buccal mucosa that cannot be wiped away with gauze. What is the MOST appropriate initial management step?
options: Perform an immediate incisional biopsy of the lesion
Prescribe an oral nystatin suspension for 14 days
Provide tobacco cessation counseling and re-evaluate the lesion in 10 to 14 days
Reassure the patient that the lesion is benign and schedule a 1-year recall
pharmacology-anesthesia-1334.explanation: Option C is correct because according to ADA clinical practice guidelines and oral pathology standards, an asymptomatic, non-wipeable keratotic lesion associated with an identifiable local irritant (such as tobacco use) should be managed initially by eliminating the irritant and re-evaluating in 10 to 14 days to observe for resolution. Option A is incorrect because immediate incisional biopsy is premature prior to assessing whether the lesion regresses following removal of the etiologic factor. Option B is incorrect because non-wipeable keratotic plaques are not candidiasis and will not resolve with antifungal therapy. Option D is incorrect because potentially malignant disorders such as leukoplakia cannot simply be dismissed or deferred for annual monitoring without verifying resolution or obtaining a histologic diagnosis.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1290.question: A 50-year-old male requires a full-coverage crown on his permanent maxillary left first molar (tooth #14). The tooth is prepared, isolated, and completely dried. During the final impression using a hydrophilic polyvinyl siloxane (PVS) material, several small rounded voids are noted on the occlusal surface of the prepared tooth on the impression. What is the MOST probable cause of these voids?
options: Exceeding the maximum working time of the impression material
Air entrapment caused by lifting the syringe tip during material dispensing
Excessive moisture contamination from gingival crevicular fluid
Inadequate seating pressure on the custom impression tray
pharmacology-anesthesia-1290.explanation: Option B is correct because the most common cause of localized, rounded voids on the occlusal or critical surfaces of an elastomeric impression when the preparation is dry is air entrapment, which occurs when the clinician lifts the dispensing tip out of the material while syringing around the tooth. Option A is incorrect because exceeding the working time results in generalized dragging, tearing, and distorted margins rather than isolated rounded bubbles. Option C is incorrect because the vignette explicitly notes that the tooth was completely isolated and thoroughly dried before impression taking. Option D is incorrect because inadequate seating pressure leads to thick, incomplete margins and incomplete tray adaptation rather than isolated occlusal voids.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1352.question: A 38-year-old female presents with severe, spontaneous pain in her maxillary right quadrant that worsens at night and lingers for several minutes following cold exposure. Clinical examination reveals a deep mesio-occlusal composite restoration on the permanent maxillary right first molar (tooth #3). The tooth is tender to percussion and displays an exaggerated, prolonged response to cold testing. What is the MOST appropriate pulpal diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis
pharmacology-anesthesia-1352.explanation: Option A is correct because according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic standards, spontaneous radiating pain, nighttime awakenings, and prolonged lingering pain to thermal stimuli (>30 seconds) are classic diagnostic criteria for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis. Option B is incorrect because reversible pulpitis is characterized by non-lingering thermal sensitivity that resolves within seconds of stimulus removal. Option C is incorrect because a necrotic pulp has a complete absence of vital sensory innervation and does not respond to thermal testing. Option D is incorrect because asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis has no clinical symptoms despite deep pulpal compromise.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1356.question: A 9-year-old male presents to the dental clinic 45 minutes after completely avulsing his permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8) during a playground accident. The tooth was found immediately, rinsed gently under tap water, and transported in a glass of cold milk. Clinical examination shows an intact alveolar socket. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Replant the tooth immediately and stabilize with a flexible splint
Scrub the root surface thoroughly with a surgical brush before replanting
Perform extraoral root canal therapy prior to repositioning the tooth
Administer systemic antibiotics and delay replantation for 48 hours
pharmacology-anesthesia-1356.explanation: Option A is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an avulsed permanent incisor with an extraoral time under 60 minutes stored in a physiologic medium (milk) should be replanted immediately and stabilized with a flexible splint for up to 2 weeks to maximize periodontal ligament (PDL) healing. Option B is incorrect because scrubbing or mechanically abrading the root surface destroys viable PDL cells and induces aggressive replacement resorption (ankylosis). Option C is incorrect because extraoral endodontics increases extraoral dry time and kills remaining PDL cells; endodontic therapy should instead be initiated 7 to 14 days after replantation if indicated. Option D is incorrect because delaying replantation leads to total PDL necrosis; systemic antibiotics are an adjunctive measure, not a reason to defer replantation.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1361.question: A 19-year-old female presents with a complicated crown-root fracture of her permanent maxillary left central incisor (tooth #9) following an athletic injury. The fracture extends 2 mm subgingivally on the facial aspect, exposing the pulp, but the remaining root has adequate length and no periapical pathology. What is the MOST appropriate initial conservative management sequence to preserve the natural tooth while respecting biologic width and anterior esthetics?
options: Immediate extraction with socket preservation followed by single-tooth implant placement
Direct resin composite restoration without endodontic therapy or margin exposure
Surgical crown lengthening followed by endodontic therapy and full-coverage crown
Orthodontic extrusion followed by endodontic therapy and definitive crown restoration
pharmacology-anesthesia-1361.explanation: Option D is correct because orthodontic extrusion (forced eruption) successfully moves the subgingival fracture margin coronal to the alveolar crest to re-establish the biologic width and provide adequate ferrule, while maintaining the marginal bone height and gingival symmetry critical in the maxillary anterior esthetic zone. Option A is incorrect because extraction and implant placement are unnecessarily aggressive when the natural root possesses sufficient periodontal support and length to be preserved. Option B is incorrect because placing a direct restoration without addressing the pulpal exposure and subgingival margin leads to pulpal necrosis and chronic periodontal breakdown from biologic width violation. Option C is incorrect because surgical crown lengthening on a single maxillary anterior incisor removes supporting crestal bone and causes severe gingival asymmetry and unesthetic gingival recession.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1372.question: A 9-year-old male presents 2 hours after a fall with a complicated crown fracture of his permanent maxillary left central incisor (tooth #9). Clinical examination reveals a 1.5 mm vital pulpal exposure, and periapical radiographs demonstrate an open, immature root apex with no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate treatment to preserve pulpal vitality and promote continued root apex development?
options: Partial pulpotomy (Cvek pulpotomy) using a biocompatible hydraulic calcium silicate or calcium hydroxide
Complete pulpectomy and root canal obturation with gutta-percha
Placement of a direct composite resin restoration without pulp capping
Immediate extraction followed by a temporary removable partial denture
pharmacology-anesthesia-1372.explanation: Option A is correct because according to American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) and AAE guidelines, a partial (Cvek) pulpotomy with a bioceramic material (e.g., MTA) or calcium hydroxide is the treatment of choice for an immature permanent tooth with a traumatic pulp exposure, as it preserves healthy radicular pulp tissue to permit physiological root completion and apical closure (apexogenesis). Option B is incorrect because complete pulpectomy halts dentin deposition, leaving thin, fragile root walls that are highly susceptible to subsequent cervical fracture. Option C is incorrect because restoring over an exposed pulp without vital pulp therapy causes persistent bacterial microleakage, pulpal necrosis, and periapical pathology. Option D is incorrect because extraction is contraindicated for a restorable traumatic crown fracture in a growing child.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1491.question: A 65-year-old male patient presents to your dental office with a chief complaint of difficulty speaking and chewing due to persistent dry mouth. His medical history includes Sjögren's syndrome, and he takes hydrochlorothiazide and an antidepressant daily. Clinical examination reveals generalized xerostomia, diminished salivary flow, and scattered small carious lesions at the cervical margins of several teeth. What is the MOST appropriate long-term preventive management strategy for this patient's oral health?
options: Recommend over-the-counter saliva substitutes alone and standard annual dental recall visits
Prescribe pilocarpine tablets and schedule daily in-office professional fluoride varnish applications
Instruct on meticulous oral hygiene, prescribe 1.1% sodium fluoride (5,000 ppm) dentifrice, and schedule frequent recall intervals
Advise immediate discontinuation of hydrochlorothiazide and refer the patient for salivary gland gene therapy
pharmacology-anesthesia-1491.explanation: Option C is correct because patients with severe xerostomia and high caries risk from Sjögren's syndrome and xerogenic medications require intensive preventive protocols, specifically daily high-concentration prescription fluoride dentifrice (1.1% sodium fluoride / 5,000 ppm), meticulous plaque control, and frequent recall intervals (every 3–4 months) per ADA guidelines. Option A is incorrect because over-the-counter substitutes and annual recalls are insufficient to arrest rampant cervical decay in severe xerostomia. Option B is incorrect because in-office professional fluoride varnish cannot feasibly be applied daily by a dentist, and Option D is incorrect because dentists should not unilaterally discontinue prescribed antihypertensive medications.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1493.question: A 25-year-old male patient presents to your dental office with a chief complaint of sensitivity to cold and sweets on his maxillary left first molar (#14). He reports no spontaneous pain, and the sensitivity is sharp and subsides immediately upon removal of the stimulus. Clinical examination reveals a deep occlusal composite restoration placed two years ago, with no visible recurrent caries or marginal breakdown. Probing depths are within normal limits, and the tooth is not tender to percussion. What is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Dentin hypersensitivity
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
Reversible pulpitis
pharmacology-anesthesia-1493.explanation: Option D is correct because according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic criteria, sharp, transient discomfort provoked by thermal and sweet stimuli that resolves immediately upon stimulus removal in a deeply restored tooth without periapical symptoms indicates reversible pulpitis. Option A is incorrect because irreversible pulpitis features lingering thermal pain after stimulus removal or spontaneous, unprovoked pain. Option B is incorrect because dentin hypersensitivity classically occurs on exposed cervical root surfaces rather than under intact coronal restorations, and Option C is incorrect because apical periodontitis presents with tenderness to percussion or mastication.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1498.question: In the United States, what is the maximum annual occupational whole-body effective radiation dose limit for a dental healthcare professional, as established by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP)?
options: 1 mSv (0.1 rem)
5 mSv (0.5 rem)
20 mSv (2.0 rem)
50 mSv (5.0 rem)
pharmacology-anesthesia-1498.explanation: Option D is correct because in the United States, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (10 CFR § 20) and NCRP Report No. 145 set the annual occupational whole-body effective dose limit for radiation workers, including dental personnel, at 50 mSv (5 rem or 0.05 Sv) per calendar year. Option A is incorrect because 1 mSv/year is the maximum permissible dose limit for the general non-occupationally exposed public. Option B is incorrect because 5 mSv is the dose limit for an embryo/fetus of a declared pregnant worker over the entire gestation period, and Option C is incorrect because 20 mSv/year is an international recommendation (ICRP) that has not been adopted into US federal regulatory standards.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1502.question: A 55-year-old female patient presents to your dental office with a chief complaint of swelling and redness around her maxillary right central incisor (#8) that developed over the past few days. She reports mild tenderness to palpation. Her medical history is significant for poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Clinical examination reveals a localized, fluctuant, erythematous swelling on the facial gingiva of tooth #8, with purulent exudate upon palpation. Tooth #8 responds normally to electric pulp testing and thermal testing, with no restorations or history of trauma. Periodontal probing depths around tooth #8 reveal an 8 mm pocket on the distofacial aspect with bleeding on probing. What is the MOST appropriate initial diagnosis?
options: Acute periapical abscess
Acute periodontal abscess
Gingival abscess
Ludwig angina
pharmacology-anesthesia-1502.explanation: Option B is correct because the clinical combination of a localized purulent gingival swelling, deep periodontal pocketing (8 mm), bleeding on probing, and a vital response to thermal and electric pulp testing in tooth #8 is diagnostic of an acute periodontal abscess. Option A is incorrect because a periapical abscess stems from pulpal necrosis and would yield a negative response to pulp vitality testing. Option C is incorrect because a gingival abscess is a localized, acute inflammatory lesion confined to the marginal gingiva or interdental papilla without pre-existing periodontal breakdown or deep pockets, and Option D is incorrect because Ludwig angina is a rapid, bilateral, space-infecting cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental fascial spaces.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1509.question: A 42-year-old male patient presents for a recall examination with generalized bleeding on probing, probing depths ranging from 4 to 6 mm, and radiographic evidence of horizontal bone loss affecting 20% to 30% of root length across multiple quadrants. He reports no pain but notices occasional gingival bleeding during brushing. His medical history is non-contributory. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification system, what is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis?
options: Necrotizing periodontitis
Biofilm-induced gingivitis on an intact periodontium
Localized periodontitis, Stage I, Grade A
Generalized periodontitis, Stage II, Grade B
pharmacology-anesthesia-1509.explanation: Option D is correct because according to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, horizontal bone loss of 15% to 33% (coronal third of the root) corresponds to Stage II periodontitis, involvement of multiple quadrants (>30% of teeth) defines generalized extent, and an expected moderate rate of progression relative to age (bone loss / age ≈ 0.6) qualifies as Grade B. Option A is incorrect because necrotizing periodontitis presents with severe pain, ulcerated interdental papillae, and pseudomembrane formation. Option B is incorrect because gingivitis does not exhibit clinical attachment loss or radiographic alveolar bone loss, and Option C is incorrect because Stage I involves <15% bone loss and localized disease involves fewer than 30% of teeth.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1512.question: Which of the following amide-type local anesthetics produces the least intrinsic vasodilation and is commonly administered in dental practice as a 3% plain formulation (without a vasoconstrictor)?
options: Procaine
Lidocaine
Articaine
Mepivacaine
pharmacology-anesthesia-1512.explanation: Option D is correct because according to Malamed's Handbook of Local Anesthesia, mepivacaine produces the least intrinsic vasodilation among dental amide local anesthetics, allowing 3% mepivacaine plain to provide reliable pulpal anesthesia (20–40 minutes) without the addition of a vasoconstrictor. Option A is incorrect because procaine is an ester-type local anesthetic with potent vasodilating properties. Option B is incorrect because 2% plain lidocaine is a significant vasodilator that is rapidly absorbed into systemic circulation, yielding inadequate and brief pulpal anesthesia, and Option C is incorrect because articaine is a vasodilator formulated exclusively with epinephrine in commercial dental cartridges.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1513.question: A 9-year-old male patient presents to your dental office 45 minutes after falling from his skateboard, resulting in a lateral luxation of his maxillary right central incisor (#8). The crown is displaced palatally and locked into the alveolar bone, is not mobile, and exhibits no crown or root fractures on periapical radiographs. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Perform immediate extraction of tooth #8
Initiate immediate pulpectomy and root canal therapy
Reposition the tooth into its anatomical socket and stabilize with a flexible splint for 4 weeks
Observe the tooth for 4 weeks without repositioning to avoid further trauma
pharmacology-anesthesia-1513.explanation: Option C is correct because according to the International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) and AAE guidelines, a laterally luxated permanent tooth (#8) must be gently disengaged from the bone plate, repositioned into its anatomical position, and stabilized with a flexible splint for 4 weeks due to concurrent alveolar bone fracture. Option A is incorrect because traumatized permanent teeth in growing pediatric patients should be preserved whenever possible. Option B is incorrect because immature permanent teeth have substantial potential for pulpal revascularization and should be monitored rather than treated with immediate pulpectomy, and Option D is incorrect because leaving a displaced tooth unreduced leads to malocclusion and ankylosis in an ectopic position.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1515.question: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS), what is the optimal recommended concentration of fluoride in community drinking water for the prevention of dental caries?
options: 0.2 ppm (0.2 mg/L)
0.7 ppm (0.7 mg/L)
1.2 ppm (1.2 mg/L)
2.0 ppm (2.0 mg/L)
pharmacology-anesthesia-1515.explanation: Option B is correct because the U.S. Public Health Service and CDC updated community water fluoridation guidelines in 2015 to establish a single optimal target concentration of 0.7 mg/L (0.7 ppm), maximizing dental caries prevention while minimizing the risk of dental fluorosis. Option A is incorrect because 0.2 ppm is sub-optimal and confers negligible protective anticaries benefits. Option C is incorrect because 1.2 ppm was the upper boundary of the obsolete 1962 temperature-dependent range (0.7–1.2 ppm) that has since been replaced, and Option D is incorrect because 2.0 ppm represents the EPA secondary maximum contaminant level, a non-enforceable cosmetic benchmark for dental fluorosis.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1472.question: A 50-year-old female patient presents with persistent discomfort and tenderness to percussion on her mandibular right lateral incisor (#26), which received root canal treatment 5 years ago. Periapical radiographs reveal an intact, apparently well-obturated canal with an apical radiolucency that has slightly enlarged compared to post-treatment films. The tooth has no thermal sensitivity and probing depths are 2 to 3 mm. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Nonsurgical root canal retreatment
Extraction and replacement with an immediate implant
Surgical apicoectomy with retrograde root-end filling
Prescription of systemic amoxicillin and clinical observation
pharmacology-anesthesia-1472.explanation: Option A is correct because according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) guidelines, nonsurgical root canal retreatment is the initial standard of care for post-treatment apical periodontitis to eliminate persistent intraradicular microorganisms and identify untreated anatomy, such as a missed second (lingual) canal commonly present in mandibular incisors like #26. Option B is incorrect because the tooth is structurally restorable and extraction should only be considered after endodontic options fail. Option C is incorrect because apical surgery does not address persistent coronal or mid-root intraradicular bacterial contamination, and Option D is incorrect because localized chronic endodontic lesions cannot be cured with systemic antibiotics.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1518.question: According to the American Dental Association (ADA) Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct, which ethical principle states that the dentist has a primary duty to promote the patient's welfare and actively serve both the public-at-large and the profession?
options: Beneficence
Patient Autonomy
Nonmaleficence
Justice
pharmacology-anesthesia-1518.explanation: Option A is correct because under the ADA Code of Ethics, Beneficence ('do good') dictates that dentists have a duty to promote the patient's welfare, obligating practitioners to act for the benefit of others through competent, timely care, public service, and stewardship of the profession. Option B is incorrect because Patient Autonomy ('self-governance') concerns the duty to respect the patient's right to self-determination and confidentiality. Option C is incorrect because Nonmaleficence ('do no harm') focuses on protecting the patient from harm, and Option D is incorrect because Justice ('fairness') deals with delivering dental care without prejudice and treating all patients equitably.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1523.question: A 48-year-old male patient requires a full-coverage crown on his maxillary left first molar (#14). Following tooth preparation and retraction cord placement, the preparation margins are slightly subgingival with minor sulcular moisture. Which of the following impression materials is MOST suitable for capturing an accurate definitive master impression in this clinical scenario?
options: Polyether
Irreversible hydrocolloid
Polysulfide
Zinc oxide-eugenol impression paste
pharmacology-anesthesia-1523.explanation: Option A is correct because polyether is an elastomeric impression material with intrinsic hydrophilicity (low contact angle), high tear strength, and excellent dimensional accuracy, making it exceptionally well-suited for recording subgingival margins in the presence of minor residual moisture. Option B is incorrect because irreversible hydrocolloid (alginate) lacks the tear strength and fine detail reproduction necessary for fixed prosthodontic master casts. Option C is incorrect because polysulfide is hydrophobic, has a prolonged setting time, and exhibits dimensional instability due to water byproduct loss, and Option D is incorrect because zinc oxide-eugenol paste is an inelastic, rigid material that fractures when withdrawn over undercuts in dentate arches.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1525.question: A 45-year-old male patient presents to your dental office for an initial new-patient comprehensive examination. Clinical examination reveals multiple existing restorations with intact margins and no visible carious lesions, but the patient reports intermittent cold sensitivity in the posterior quadrants. His last dental radiographs were taken 5 years ago. According to ADA/FDA guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate radiographic examination for this patient?
options: Periapical radiographs of the posterior teeth only
Four posterior bitewing radiographs alone
Maxillary and mandibular occlusal radiographs
A full-mouth radiographic series (FMX)
pharmacology-anesthesia-1525.explanation: Option D is correct because according to ADA/FDA radiographic guidelines, a new adult patient presenting with active symptoms (cold sensitivity), a history of extensive dental treatment (multiple restorations), and no radiographs for 5 years requires a comprehensive baseline evaluation with a full-mouth series (or panoramic radiograph combined with bitewings). Option A is incorrect because posterior periapicals fail to image anterior teeth and provide inadequate interproximal projection geometry. Option B is incorrect because bitewings alone evaluate only coronal and crestal alveolar structures, omitting root apices and periapical pathology, and Option C is incorrect because occlusal radiographs are indicated for trauma, foreign bodies, or large bony lesions rather than comprehensive dental screening.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1528.question: A 55-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of a constant dull ache in her maxillary left posterior region for several weeks, exacerbated by chewing. She reports no sensitivity to hot or cold liquids. Clinical examination reveals a large amalgam restoration with recurrent decay on the distal aspect of tooth #14. Percussion and palpation elicit mild tenderness, and endodontic cold testing produces no response. A periapical radiograph shows a widened periodontal ligament space and a subtle periapical radiolucency associated with the distobuccal root of tooth #14. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Placement of a temporary sedative restoration and observation
Prescription of systemic antibiotics and analgesics alone
Immediate surgical extraction of tooth #14
Root canal therapy followed by a full-coverage crown
pharmacology-anesthesia-1528.explanation: Option D is correct because tooth #14 exhibits pulpal necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis (non-responsive to cold testing, tender to percussion, and periapical radiolucency), requiring non-surgical root canal therapy followed by a full-coverage crown to restore function and protect against coronal fracture in a posterior tooth. Option A is incorrect because pulpal necrosis cannot be resolved with temporary sedative restorations or pulp capping. Option B is incorrect because localized endodontic infections without systemic spread (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, or fascial space involvement) do not warrant systemic antibiotics, which cannot reach the necrotic root canal system. Option C is incorrect because the tooth has adequate remaining tooth structure and periodontal support, making extraction an unnecessarily aggressive treatment.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1531.question: A 7-year-old female patient presents for a routine check-up. Her last dental visit was 18 months ago. Clinical examination reveals sound permanent first molars (teeth #3, #14, #19, and #30) with deep, retentive occlusal fissures but no clinical or radiographic evidence of caries. The patient's caries risk is assessed as moderate, based on limited fluoride exposure and infrequent sugary snack consumption. What is the MOST appropriate preventive measure for her permanent first molars at this appointment?
options: Placement of pit and fissure sealants
Application of topical fluoride varnish without sealants
Prescription of a daily 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate rinse
Prophylactic odontotomy and composite resin placement
pharmacology-anesthesia-1531.explanation: Option A is correct because the American Dental Association (ADA) and American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) recommend pit and fissure sealants as the primary evidence-based preventive intervention for sound permanent molars with deep, retentive fissures in children at moderate to high caries risk. Option B is incorrect because although topical fluoride varnish protects smooth surfaces, sealants provide significantly superior protection against pit and fissure caries by creating a physical barrier against biofilm accumulation. Option C is incorrect because chlorhexidine rinses are not indicated for routine caries prophylaxis in pediatric patients and cause adverse effects such as extrinsic tooth staining and taste alteration. Option D is incorrect because prophylactic cavity preparation on sound, caries-free enamel violates modern principles of minimally invasive dentistry.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1533.question: A 48-year-old male patient with a known history of stable angina pectoris experiences sudden substernal chest pain and shortness of breath during an operative dental procedure. He appears pale and diaphoretic. His blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, and his pulse is 95 bpm. The patient has his prescribed nitroglycerin tablets with him. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Discontinue the procedure, position the patient comfortably upright, and administer his sublingual nitroglycerin
Place the patient in a supine position with feet elevated and administer high-flow oxygen
Immediately activate emergency medical services before administering any medication
Initiate high-quality chest compressions and prepare the automated external defibrillator
pharmacology-anesthesia-1533.explanation: Option A is correct because according to AHA and emergency dental guidelines (Malamed), an awake patient with known stable angina experiencing acute chest pain should have the procedure terminated immediately, be placed in a comfortable upright or semi-reclined position, and receive their prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin along with supplemental oxygen. Option B is incorrect because placing an anginal patient in a supine position increases venous return, preload, and myocardial oxygen demand, which exacerbates ischemic chest pain and pulmonary congestion. Option C is incorrect because immediate EMS activation is indicated if chest pain is unrelieved after three doses of nitroglycerin over 15 minutes, if symptoms acutely worsen, or if the patient has no prior history of angina. Option D is incorrect because chest compressions and defibrillation are indicated only for an unconscious, pulseless patient in cardiac arrest.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1539.question: A 40-year-old female patient presents for a periodontal evaluation. Her medical history includes well-controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (HbA1c = 6.8%). Clinical examination reveals bleeding on probing (BOP) at 55% of sites, probing depths of 4 to 5 mm in multiple quadrants, and interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm on more than 30% of teeth. Radiographs confirm horizontal bone loss confined to the coronal third of the roots (15% to 33%). There is no furcation involvement, tooth mobility, or tooth loss due to periodontitis. According to the 2018 AAP/EFP World Workshop classification, what is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis?
options: Generalized gingivitis on an intact periodontium
Generalized Stage II, Grade B periodontitis
Localized Stage III, Grade C periodontitis
Generalized Stage I, Grade A periodontitis
pharmacology-anesthesia-1539.explanation: Option B is correct because under the 2018 AAP/EFP classification, interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm, probing depths ≤5 mm, and radiographic bone loss within the coronal third (15% to 33%) with no tooth loss define Stage II periodontitis; involving >30% of teeth denotes generalized extent, and Grade B is assigned due to moderate rate of progression and well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c < 7.0%). Option A is incorrect because active interdental attachment loss and radiographic bone loss rule out gingivitis. Option C is incorrect because Stage III requires interdental attachment loss ≥5 mm, probing depths ≥6 mm, and bone loss extending to the middle third of the root or beyond. Option D is incorrect because Stage I is characterized by only 1 to 2 mm of attachment loss and <15% coronal bone loss.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1551.question: A 40-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of intermittent, dull discomfort in her maxillary right posterior region, localized to tooth #3. She had root canal treatment completed on tooth #3 five years ago. Radiographic examination reveals a persistent periapical radiolucency associated with the distobuccal and mesiobuccal roots of tooth #3; the existing obturation appears dense but slightly under-extended, with an untreated second mesiobuccal (MB2) canal visible. The tooth has sound margins on a full-coverage crown, normal mobility, and normal periodontal probing depths. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-surgical endodontic retreatment of tooth #3
Surgical periapical resection (apicoectomy) with retrograde filling of tooth #3
Immediate extraction of tooth #3 and alveolar ridge preservation
Long-term prescription of broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics and radiographic monitoring
pharmacology-anesthesia-1551.explanation: Option A is correct because according to the American Association of Endodontists (AAE), non-surgical root canal retreatment is the primary and most predictable initial intervention for post-treatment apical periodontitis when coronal access is feasible and identifiable deficiencies (such as an untreated MB2 canal and under-extended obturation) can be addressed non-surgically. Option B is incorrect because apical microsurgery is indicated when non-surgical retreatment is unsuccessful, contraindicated, or unable to access the etiology (e.g., irretrievable posts or canal obstructions). Option C is incorrect because the tooth has intact periodontal support and is restorable, making extraction prematurely aggressive. Option D is incorrect because systemic antibiotics cannot eradicate intraradicular microbial biofilms in a necrotic root canal system and are contraindicated for localized, non-disseminating apical periodontitis.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1556.question: A 16-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department after sustaining a direct blow to the right side of his mandible during a hockey game. Clinical examination reveals preauricular tenderness, swelling over the right temporomandibular joint, premature occlusal contact on the right posterior teeth, an anterior and contralateral (left) open bite, and marked deviation of the mandible toward the right upon maximal opening. What is the MOST probable diagnosis?
options: Left condylar fracture
Right condylar fracture
Isolated mandibular symphysis fracture
Anterior dislocation of the right temporomandibular joint
pharmacology-anesthesia-1556.explanation: Option B is correct because a unilateral right condylar fracture causes loss of vertical ramus height on the ipsilateral side, resulting in premature posterior contact on the right, a contralateral left open bite, and deviation of the mandible toward the injured (right) side upon opening due to unopposed translation by the intact contralateral (left) lateral pterygoid muscle. Option A is incorrect because a left condylar fracture would result in premature contact on the left posterior dentition, a right open bite, and mandibular deviation to the left upon opening. Option C is incorrect because an isolated symphysis fracture typically causes a step defect in the lower anterior region and generalized malocclusion without isolated unilateral TMJ dysfunction or translation failure. Option D is incorrect because anterior TMJ dislocation fixes the jaw in a widely open position and causes deviation toward the unaffected side if unilateral, rather than ipsilateral deviation upon opening with premature posterior contact.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1562.question: A 9-year-old female patient presents for an orthodontic evaluation. Clinical examination reveals an Angle Class I molar relationship, but permanent tooth #6 (maxillary right canine) is palpable high in the buccal vestibule and is ectopically erupting mesially. A panoramic radiograph confirms significant mesial angulation of the crown of tooth #6 overlapping the distal root contour of adjacent permanent tooth #7 (maxillary right lateral incisor). Tooth C (primary maxillary right canine) is non-mobile and caries-free. What is the MOST appropriate initial interceptive management strategy?
options: Interceptive extraction of primary tooth C
Immediate surgical exposure and bracket bonding to permanent tooth #6
Extraction of permanent tooth #7 to provide space for tooth #6
Observation without intervention until all permanent teeth erupt at age 12
pharmacology-anesthesia-1562.explanation: Option A is correct because according to established orthodontic guidelines (Ericson and Kurol), interceptive extraction of the primary canine (tooth C) normalizes the eruption path of a mesially displaced permanent canine (tooth #6) in the majority of cases and prevents resorption of the lateral incisor root (tooth #7). Option B is incorrect because surgical exposure and orthodontic traction are invasive second-line interventions reserved for when interceptive primary extraction fails or when severe impaction persists. Option C is incorrect because sacrificing a sound permanent lateral incisor is contraindicated when timely removal of the primary canine can guide the permanent canine into proper alignment. Option D is incorrect because unmonitored observation allows the ectopically migrating canine to cause irreversible root resorption of adjacent tooth #7 and worsening impaction.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1565.question: A 10-year-old male patient presents for a routine recall appointment. He resides in a non-fluoridated community and is assessed as having moderate caries risk based on past caries history and dietary habits. Clinical examination reveals deep, retentive occlusal fissures on his permanent first molars (teeth #3, #14, #19, and #30), which are sound and caries-free. What is the MOST appropriate primary preventive intervention for these specific teeth at this visit?
options: Prescription of a daily 0.05% sodium fluoride mouthrinse for home use
Biannual application of 5% sodium fluoride varnish without occlusal sealants
Placement of resin-based pit and fissure sealants on teeth #3, #14, #19, and #30
Prophylactic enameloplasty followed by composite resin restorations
pharmacology-anesthesia-1565.explanation: Option C is correct because ADA and AAPD clinical practice guidelines strongly recommend the placement of pit and fissure sealants on sound occlusal surfaces of permanent first molars (teeth #3, #14, #19, and #30) in children at moderate or high caries risk to create a physical barrier against cariogenic plaque biofilm. Option A is incorrect because daily sodium fluoride mouthrinses primarily remineralize smooth enamel surfaces and provide minimal protection against deep fissure caries. Option B is incorrect because while topical fluoride varnish provides systemic and surface caries benefits, pit and fissure sealants demonstrate significantly superior efficacy in arresting and preventing occlusal decay. Option D is incorrect because prophylactic cavity cutting (preventive restorations) on sound enamel causes irreversible tooth structure loss and violates minimally invasive dentistry standards.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1572.question: A 6-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of spontaneous pain and difficulty chewing on the lower right side. Clinical examination reveals a deep, cavitated carious lesion on tooth T (mandibular right primary second molar) that is tender to percussion. Radiographic examination reveals caries extending into the pulp chamber, a widened periodontal ligament space around the roots, and intact root structure with no pathologic root resorption. Permanent tooth #30 has not yet erupted. What is the MOST appropriate immediate treatment for tooth T?
options: Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide
Indirect pulp therapy with glass ionomer cement
Pulpectomy followed by a stainless steel crown
Extraction of tooth T without space maintenance
pharmacology-anesthesia-1572.explanation: Option C is correct because according to AAPD guidelines, a pulpectomy followed by a stainless steel crown is indicated for restorable primary molars presenting with irreversible pulpitis or pulpal necrosis (spontaneous pain and widened PDL) in order to retain the tooth and prevent mesial drift of the unerupted permanent first molar (#30). Option A is incorrect because direct pulp capping is contraindicated in primary teeth with carious pulpal exposures due to high rates of internal resorption and subsequent failure. Option B is incorrect because indirect pulp therapy is indicated exclusively for asymptomatic teeth or those with reversible pulpitis, not for teeth with spontaneous pain and apical pathology. Option D is incorrect because extracting tooth T without space maintenance would lead to rapid loss of arch space due to mesial drifting of the developing tooth #30, resulting in severe impaction of the second premolar.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1575.question: A 40-year-old male patient presents with severe, spontaneous, throbbing pain in his maxillary right posterior quadrant that radiates to his right temple. Cold testing of tooth #3 (maxillary right first molar) elicits an intense, sharp pain that lingers for over 30 seconds after removal of the stimulus. Radiographic examination reveals a deep composite restoration approaching the pulp on tooth #3, with a normal periodontal ligament space and no periapical radiolucency. Percussion and palpation tests on tooth #3 are non-tender. What is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis for tooth #3?
options: Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
pharmacology-anesthesia-1575.explanation: Option B is correct because according to the American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic standards, spontaneous pain and an exaggerated, prolonged painful response to cold testing (>30 seconds) are classic diagnostic hallmarks of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, indicating that the pulp is irreversibly damaged and requires endodontic therapy. Option A is incorrect because reversible pulpitis manifests as sharp, non-lingering discomfort that subsides within seconds after stimulus removal. Option C is incorrect because necrotic pulps do not respond to thermal or electrical pulp testing. Option D is incorrect because asymptomatic apical periodontitis is a periapical diagnosis characterized by radiographic apical radiolucency without clinical symptoms, whereas this tooth exhibits an acute pulpal response with normal periapical tissues.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1581.question: According to current CDC and OSHA infection control guidelines for dental health-care settings, which method is recommended for processing heat-sensitive semi-critical dental instruments that cannot withstand heat sterilization?
options: Immersion in an intermediate-level hospital disinfectant with tuberculocidal claim for 10 minutes
Sterilization using an unsaturated chemical vapor sterilizer cycle
Sterilization using a dry heat oven at reduced temperature and extended cycle
High-level disinfection using an FDA-cleared liquid chemical sterilant (e.g., glutaraldehyde)
pharmacology-anesthesia-1581.explanation: Option D is correct because CDC and OSHA guidelines dictate that semi-critical instruments that are heat-sensitive and cannot tolerate steam or dry heat sterilization must, at a minimum, undergo high-level disinfection using an FDA-cleared liquid chemical sterilant/disinfectant (such as glutaraldehyde) according to manufacturer-specified immersion contact times. Option A is incorrect because intermediate-level disinfectants are indicated solely for clinical contact surfaces, not for reprocessing semi-critical instruments that contact mucous membranes. Options B and C are incorrect because unsaturated chemical vapor (operating at 132°C/270°F) and dry heat (160°C–170°C/320°F–340°F) are high-temperature heat sterilization techniques that will melt, degrade, or destroy heat-sensitive instruments.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1587.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic after falling from his bicycle 30 minutes ago, resulting in the complete avulsion of permanent tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor). The parents retrieved the intact tooth immediately and transported it immersed in cold milk. Examination shows an intact alveolar socket without extensive bone fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management for tooth #8?
options: Gently rinse the root with saline, replant into the socket, and stabilize with a flexible splint for 2 weeks
Scrape the root surface to remove contaminated periodontal ligament cells, rinse with chlorhexidine, and replant
Perform extraoral endodontic treatment, replant the tooth, and place a rigid archwire splint for 6 weeks
Store the tooth in sterile saline and fabricate an immediate removable partial denture
pharmacology-anesthesia-1587.explanation: Option A is correct because according to the American Association of Endodontists (AAE) and International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an avulsed permanent tooth with an open apex and short extraoral dry time (<60 minutes) stored in a physiologic storage medium (milk) should be gently rinsed with sterile saline without disturbing root surface cells, replanted immediately, and stabilized with a passive, flexible splint for approximately 2 weeks. Option B is incorrect because scraping or chemical disinfection of the root surface strips viable periodontal ligament cells, precipitating ankylosis and progressive replacement root resorption. Option C is incorrect because immediate extraoral root canal therapy is contraindicated when replantation is performed promptly (especially in an immature tooth with open apex, where revascularization is possible), and rigid prolonged splinting increases the likelihood of ankylosis. Option D is incorrect because delaying or abandoning replantation in favor of a removable prosthesis leads to rapid alveolar ridge resorption and fails to preserve the natural tooth.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1594.question: A 58-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of a fractured porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown on tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor), exposing the underlying metal coping. The crown was cemented 15 years ago. The patient is concerned about esthetics and function. Clinical examination confirms a large buccal fracture of the porcelain extending to the metal coping. The abutment tooth is periodontally sound with no recurrent caries, and the pulp was previously treated with a satisfactory root canal filling. What is the MOST appropriate definitive management?
options: Repair the fractured porcelain with intraoral composite resin
Extract tooth #8 and place an implant-supported crown
Fabricate a full-coverage cast gold crown
Fabricate and place a new full-coverage crown
pharmacology-anesthesia-1594.explanation: Option D is correct because fabricating a new full-coverage crown is the definitive treatment of choice for an aged prosthesis with an extensive porcelain fracture exposing the metal framework in the esthetic zone. Direct composite resin repair has poor bond strength to metal copings and high failure rates for large fractures, cast gold crowns are esthetically unacceptable in the anterior maxilla, and extraction is overly aggressive and contraindicated when the abutment tooth is structurally and periodontally sound.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1596.question: A 38-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of constant, dull, aching pain in the mandibular left quadrant for the past 2 weeks. She reports intense pain when chewing on tooth #19 (mandibular left first molar). Clinical examination reveals a deep composite restoration on tooth #19, exquisite tenderness to percussion and biting, and no response to cold or electric pulp testing. Radiographs reveal a distinct periapical radiolucency associated with the mesial root of tooth #19. What is the MOST likely periapical diagnosis according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) standards?
options: Symptomatic apical periodontitis
Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
Acute apical abscess
Chronic apical abscess
pharmacology-anesthesia-1596.explanation: Option A is correct because symptomatic apical periodontitis is defined by the American Association of Endodontists (AAE) as inflammation of the apical periodontium producing clinical symptoms of pain to biting, percussion, or palpation, which may or may not be accompanied by a periapical radiolucency. Asymptomatic apical periodontitis is characterized by periapical radiolucency without clinical symptoms of pain or percussion tenderness, an acute apical abscess requires rapid-onset severe spontaneous pain with purulent swelling, and a chronic apical abscess requires continuous sinus tract drainage.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1609.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic after falling from his bicycle 1 hour ago, complaining of pain in his maxillary anterior teeth. Clinical examination reveals tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor) is displaced palatally and slightly extruded, causing occlusal interference, but responds positively to pulp sensibility testing. Radiographs reveal an intact root with an open apex and no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Observation and monitoring without active intervention
Rigid splinting of the tooth without repositioning
Gentle repositioning of the tooth and application of a flexible splint
Immediate extraction of the tooth
pharmacology-anesthesia-1609.explanation: Option C is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) and AAPD guidelines, the immediate management for an extruded or laterally luxated permanent incisor is gentle digital repositioning into the anatomic socket followed by flexible splinting for 2 weeks to allow periodontal healing. Splinting without repositioning locks the tooth in traumatic malocclusion, observation alone allows the tooth to heal in a displaced position, and extraction is contraindicated because salvageable permanent incisors can be preserved.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1610.question: A 55-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of severe dry mouth, difficulty swallowing dry foods, and recurrent episodes of oral candidiasis. Her medical history is significant for rheumatoid arthritis, which is managed with methotrexate. Clinical examination reveals a visibly reduced salivary pool, a dry, erythematous mucosal surface, and bilateral enlargement of the parotid glands. What is the MOST likely underlying cause of her xerostomia?
options: Medication-induced salivary gland hypofunction
Secondary Sjögren syndrome
Nutritional deficiency stomatitis
Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
pharmacology-anesthesia-1610.explanation: Option B is correct because secondary Sjögren syndrome is an autoimmune disorder defined by keratoconjunctivitis sicca and profound xerostomia occurring in the presence of an underlying autoimmune connective tissue disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis. Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic antimetabolite that does not cause marked xerostomia or parotid enlargement, unlike anticholinergics or antidepressants. Uncontrolled diabetes and nutritional deficiencies can produce mucosal burning or candidiasis but do not account for the classic autoimmune presentation of chronic xerostomia and parotid involvement in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1617.question: A 28-year-old female patient presents with an acute onset of severe oral pain, fever, malaise, and difficulty eating that began 2 days ago. Clinical examination reveals generalized marginal and attached gingival erythema and edema, alongside multiple small vesicles and coalescing punctate ulcers distributed across the gingiva, labial mucosa, buccal mucosa, and hard palate. She has no skin or genital lesions. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis
Recurrent aphthous stomatitis
Erythema multiforme minor
Pemphigus vulgaris
pharmacology-anesthesia-1617.explanation: Option A is correct because primary herpetic gingivostomatitis characteristically presents with an acute viral prodrome (fever and malaise) followed by diffuse marginal gingival inflammation and widespread, coalescing vesicles and ulcers across both keratinized and non-keratinized oral mucosa. Recurrent aphthous stomatitis presents without systemic fever prodromes and almost exclusively affects non-keratinized movable mucosa while sparing the attached gingiva, erythema multiforme classically spares the attached gingiva and presents with targetoid skin lesions and hemorrhagic crusting of the lips, and pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering condition characterized by flaccid bullae and a positive Nikolsky sign without an acute febrile viral onset.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1619.question: A 48-year-old male patient requires periodontal regenerative surgery to treat a deep, 3-wall infrabony defect on the mesial aspect of tooth #26 (mandibular right lateral incisor). The surgical objective is to achieve debridement of the root surface and placement of a bone graft with a barrier membrane. Which of the following flap designs is MOST appropriate to facilitate access and ensure complete, tension-free primary closure over the regenerative site?
options: Internal bevel incision with a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap
Modified Widman flap
Apically positioned flap
Gingivectomy
pharmacology-anesthesia-1619.explanation: Option A is correct because an internal bevel incision with reflection of a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap (such as a papilla preservation flap) preserves maximal soft tissue volume and vascularity, facilitating tension-free primary closure over the bone graft and barrier membrane. An apically positioned flap is a resective procedure designed to reduce pocket depths by exposing root surfaces and alveolar crest, which leaves regenerative biomaterials uncovered and doomed to failure; a modified Widman flap removes the pocket lining and is designed for intimate root adaptation via long junctional epithelium rather than regenerative space maintenance; and a gingivectomy excises the soft tissue pocket wall entirely, completely precluding flap reflection or graft coverage.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1633.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents with his mother after falling on the playground 2 hours ago. He complains of mild sensitivity to cold in his upper front teeth. Clinical examination reveals an uncomplicated crown fracture involving enamel and dentin on tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor) without pulpal exposure. The tooth is firm, non-displaced, and not mobile. Radiographs confirm an immature open apex with no root fracture or periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide
Cvek partial pulpotomy with mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA)
Placement of a full-coverage stainless steel crown
Restoration with composite resin to seal exposed dentinal tubules
pharmacology-anesthesia-1633.explanation: Option D is correct because an uncomplicated crown fracture involving enamel and dentin without pulpal exposure requires prompt sealing of exposed dentinal tubules and restoration of esthetics and function with composite resin (or fragment reattachment) according to IADT and AAPD guidelines. Direct pulp capping is contraindicated because the dental pulp is not exposed, a Cvek partial pulpotomy is reserved for complicated crown fractures with pulpal exposure, and a stainless steel crown requires excessive tooth preparation and is esthetically unacceptable for an anterior permanent incisor.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1653.question: A 7-year-old female patient presents to the dental clinic immediately after falling from her scooter. Clinical examination reveals that tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor) is displaced palatally and locked behind the mandibular incisors, with slight intrusion. The tooth is firm with no crown fracture, and radiographs confirm an open apex with no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Monitor the tooth without intervention to allow spontaneous repositioning
Gently reposition the tooth into its anatomic alignment and apply a flexible splint
Extract the tooth immediately to avoid ankylosis
Perform immediate pulpectomy and root canal obturation
pharmacology-anesthesia-1653.explanation: Option B is correct because lateral luxation of a permanent incisor with palatal displacement and bony lock requires gentle digital disengagement and repositioning back into its normal anatomic position, followed by stabilization with a flexible splint for 2 to 4 weeks according to IADT guidelines. Spontaneous repositioning is only indicated for mild intrusion in immature teeth without lateral displacement or occlusal interference, extraction of a restorable permanent incisor is contraindicated, and immediate pulpectomy is inappropriate for an immature tooth with an open apex because revascularization and continued root development (apexogenesis) can occur.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1654.question: A 60-year-old male agricultural worker presents with a chief complaint of a persistent, non-healing ulcer on the vermilion border of his lower lip that has been present for 2 months. He reports a 40 pack-year smoking history and moderate alcohol intake. Clinical examination reveals an indurated, crusted, painless ulcer measuring 8 mm in diameter on the lower lip vermilion. A biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. What is the MOST significant etiological risk factor for this patient's lesion?
options: Chronic solar ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure
High-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection
Combined tobacco and alcohol consumption
Chronic mechanical trauma from lip biting
pharmacology-anesthesia-1654.explanation: Option A is correct because chronic cumulative ultraviolet (UV-B) solar radiation is the single most significant etiological risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip vermilion, often preceded by actinic cheilitis. Although tobacco and alcohol abuse are the primary synergistic drivers of intraoral mucosal squamous cell carcinomas (such as the floor of mouth and ventrolateral tongue), their etiological contribution to lip vermilion carcinoma is minor compared to sunlight. High-risk HPV (HPV-16) is primarily associated with oropharyngeal carcinoma, and chronic mechanical trauma does not induce malignant transformation.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1659.question: A 9-year-old male patient presents for a 6-month follow-up evaluation after tooth #9 (maxillary left central incisor) sustained an avulsion injury. The tooth was replanted within 30 minutes, stabilized with a flexible splint for 2 weeks, and endodontic treatment was completed 4 weeks post-injury. Clinical examination reveals a normal percussion sound, physiological mobility, and an intact coronal restoration. Radiographs demonstrate a well-adapted root canal filling and intact root contours with no external root resorption, but a distinct periapical radiolucency is noted. What is the MOST likely cause of this periapical radiolucency?
options: Internal root resorption within the root canal system
Dentoalveolar ankylosis (replacement resorption)
Persistent intraradicular microbial infection
Inflammatory external root resorption
pharmacology-anesthesia-1659.explanation: Option C is correct because the development or persistence of a periapical radiolucency following endodontic obturation is primarily caused by persistent intraradicular microbial infection, untreated canal space, or coronal microleakage. Internal root resorption requires vital pulp tissue and cannot occur after complete pulpectomy and root canal obturation, dentoalveolar ankylosis results in obliteration of the periodontal ligament space and replacement of root structure by bone without a distinct radiolucency, and inflammatory external root resorption was explicitly ruled out by the intact root contours on radiographs.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1664.question: Which of the following bone graft materials is considered the clinical gold standard because it uniquely exhibits osteogenesis, osteoinduction, and osteoconduction through viable transplanted cells and the release of Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (BMPs)?
options: Autogenous bone graft
Demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft (DFDBA)
Anorganic bovine bone mineral xenograft
Beta-tricalcium phosphate alloplast
pharmacology-anesthesia-1664.explanation: Option A is correct because an autogenous bone graft (autograft) is the only graft material that possesses all three regenerative properties: osteogenesis (living osteogenic cells), osteoinduction (native growth factors including BMPs), and osteoconduction (trabecular scaffold). Demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft (DFDBA) is osteoinductive and osteoconductive but completely lacks viable donor cells (non-osteogenic), while anorganic bovine xenografts and synthetic beta-tricalcium phosphate alloplasts serve solely as osteoconductive passive scaffolds.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1685.question: An 8-year-old male patient presents with his mother, who is concerned about a dark gray discoloration of his permanent maxillary left central incisor (tooth #9) that developed 3 months after a fall. Clinical examination reveals tooth #9 is intact, non-mobile, tender to percussion, and completely unresponsive to cold and electric pulp testing. A periapical radiograph reveals an immature root with a wide, open blunderbuss apex and a distinct periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis and management plan?
options: Calcific metamorphosis; monitor clinically and radiographically without intervention
Internal root resorption; initiate surgical periapical curettage
Pulp necrosis; perform apexification with an apical mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) plug
Reversible pulpitis; perform indirect pulp capping and composite resin restoration
pharmacology-anesthesia-1685.explanation: Option C is correct because the combination of gray tooth discoloration, negative sensibility tests, percussion tenderness, and periapical radiolucency establishes a diagnosis of pulp necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis; in an immature tooth with an open blunderbuss apex, apexification with an apical MTA plug (or regenerative endodontic therapy) is the treatment of choice to establish an apical seal. Calcific metamorphosis results in yellow crown discoloration and canal obliteration without periapical pathosis, internal resorption requires a vital pulp and appears as a ballooning radiolucency within the canal, and reversible pulpitis features a vital pulp that responds normally or hypersensitively to vitality testing without periapical radiolucency.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1666.question: In the United States, according to the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP Report No. 145) and federal regulatory standards, what is the maximum permissible annual effective dose limit for occupationally exposed dental personnel, excluding medical and natural background radiation?
options: 1 mSv (0.1 rem)
5 mSv (0.5 rem)
20 mSv (2.0 rem)
50 mSv (5.0 rem)
pharmacology-anesthesia-1666.explanation: Option D is correct because the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP) and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC/OSHA) establish the maximum permissible annual occupational effective dose limit at 50 mSv (5 rem or 0.05 Sv) for radiation workers. In contrast, 1 mSv is the annual effective dose limit for the general public, 5 mSv represents the embryo/fetus gestation limit or the public limit for infrequent exposure, and 20 mSv is the international guideline recommended by the ICRP rather than the US regulatory limit.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1668.question: A 48-year-old male presents with a chief complaint of a dull ache in his left posterior maxilla that is exacerbated by cold and sweets. Clinical examination reveals tooth #14 with a deep composite restoration. Thermal testing of tooth #14 elicits sharp pain that lingers for over 30 seconds after stimulus removal, accompanied by mild tenderness to percussion. Periapical radiography shows the restoration approximating the pulp space with a normal periodontal ligament space and no periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis?
options: Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Pulpal necrosis
Previously initiated therapy
pharmacology-anesthesia-1668.explanation: Option B is correct because prolonged, lingering pain to thermal testing persisting longer than 30 seconds after stimulus removal is diagnostic of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) standards. Reversible pulpitis presents with sharp, transient discomfort that ceases within seconds of stimulus removal without lingering. Pulpal necrosis results in a complete absence of response to vitality testing, whereas previously initiated therapy refers to a tooth that has previously received partial endodontic debridement such as a pulpotomy or pulpectomy.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1675.question: A 25-year-old male presents with recurrent swelling and discomfort associated with his maxillary right canine (tooth #6). He reports a history of facial trauma at age 9 resulting in arrested root development. Clinical examination reveals tooth #6 is discolored, non-responsive to thermal and electric pulp tests, and associated with a buccal draining sinus tract. Periapical radiography confirms an open (blunderbuss) apex with a wide root canal space and a large periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate definitive treatment for tooth #6?
options: Conventional root canal therapy with warm vertical condensation
Immediate extraction with dental implant placement
Surgical apicoectomy with retrofill without canal debridement
Apexification or a regenerative endodontic procedure
pharmacology-anesthesia-1675.explanation: Option D is correct because a non-vital permanent tooth with an open blunderbuss apex lacks an apical stop and cannot be obturated conventionally; it requires apexification (e.g., an apical mineral trioxide aggregate [MTA] barrier) or regenerative endodontics to stimulate periapical repair. Conventional root canal obturation is contraindicated because filling materials will inadvertently extrude into the periapical tissues. Immediate extraction with implant placement is excessively aggressive for a restorable tooth, and periapical surgery is inappropriate as initial therapy without prior canal disinfection.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1680.question: A 7-year-old female presents following a fall from her skateboard resulting in trauma to her maxillary anterior teeth. Clinical examination reveals permanent tooth #8 is slightly extruded and mobile. Radiographic examination shows a horizontal root fracture in the apical third of tooth #8 with minimal displacement of the coronal segment. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for tooth #8?
options: Immediate extraction of both coronal and apical fragments
Immediate conventional root canal therapy on the coronal fragment
Surgical root resection of the apical fragment and retrograde fill
Reposition the coronal fragment and stabilize with a flexible splint
pharmacology-anesthesia-1680.explanation: Option D is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, the initial treatment of choice for a horizontal root fracture with fragment displacement is gentle repositioning of the coronal segment followed by stabilization with a flexible splint for 4 weeks. Immediate endodontic therapy is contraindicated because the coronal pulp frequently maintains vitality or revascularizes; endodontics is only indicated if pulpal necrosis is confirmed on follow-up. Extraction and surgical root resection are contraindicated because apical third fractures demonstrate an excellent healing prognosis with conservative splinting.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1700.question: A 48-year-old female presents with sensitivity to cold and biting discomfort in her maxillary left quadrant. She recalls having a deep composite restoration placed on tooth #14 several weeks ago. Clinical examination reveals intact restoration margins without secondary caries. Thermal testing of tooth #14 elicits sharp, non-lingering pain that subsides within 2 seconds of cold removal, and the tooth is tender to percussion and occlusal loading. Radiographs reveal a deep restoration with a normal apical periodontium. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Initiate immediate non-surgical root canal therapy
Prepare the tooth for a full-coverage crown
Evaluate for occlusal interferences and perform selective occlusal adjustment
Extract the tooth due to structural failure
pharmacology-anesthesia-1700.explanation: Option C is correct because sharp, transient cold sensitivity that resolves immediately combined with tenderness to percussion and biting indicates reversible pulpitis secondary to occlusal trauma (hyperocclusion), which is appropriately resolved with conservative occlusal evaluation and adjustment. Endodontic therapy and full-coverage crown preparation are overly invasive and contraindicated for a vital pulp that displays reversible symptoms. Extraction is entirely unjustified for a structurally sound, restorable tooth with a reversible inflammatory condition.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1702.question: A 30-year-old female presents for follow-up three days after an uncomplicated extraction of tooth #17. She reports moderate postoperative pain that is bothersome, but she prefers to avoid NSAIDs due to a documented history of severe gastritis and gastric ulceration. She has no known drug allergies and no other medical conditions. According to ADA clinical practice guidelines for acute dental pain management, what is the MOST appropriate analgesic regimen for this patient?
options: Ibuprofen 600 mg orally every 6 hours
Naproxen sodium 500 mg orally every 12 hours
Ketorolac tromethamine 10 mg orally every 6 hours
Acetaminophen 650 to 1000 mg orally every 6 hours
pharmacology-anesthesia-1702.explanation: Option D is correct because American Dental Association (ADA) clinical guidelines recommend acetaminophen (650 to 1000 mg every 6 hours, not to exceed 3000 to 4000 mg daily) as the preferred first-line non-opioid analgesic when NSAIDs are contraindicated due to active gastrointestinal ulceration or severe gastritis. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and ketorolac are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit COX-1 and increase the risk of gastric bleeding and mucosal ulcer exacerbation. Routine opioid prescribing is inappropriate for mild-to-moderate post-extraction pain given the risks of sedation, nausea, and dependency when non-opioid alternatives are suitable.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1703.question: A 45-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of a dull ache across her left posterior maxilla that has persisted for several weeks and worsens when she bends forward. Clinical examination reveals sound restorations without recurrent caries or periodontal pocketing. Cold vitality, percussion, and palpation tests on teeth #14 and #15 are within normal limits. A panoramic radiograph demonstrates generalized mucosal thickening and haziness in the left maxillary sinus with no periapical radiolucencies. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Refer the patient to a physician or otolaryngologist for evaluation of maxillary sinusitis
Initiate non-surgical root canal therapy on tooth #14
Prescribe empirical clindamycin for an occult odontogenic infection
Perform surgical exploration of teeth #14 and #15 to detect root fractures
pharmacology-anesthesia-1703.explanation: Option A is correct because the clinical findings of non-odontogenic midface discomfort exacerbated by postural changes, normal vitality and percussion responses on teeth #14 and #15, and radiographic sinus opacification point to maxillary sinusitis of non-odontogenic origin, warranting medical referral. Initiating endodontic therapy on vital, asymptomatic teeth without pulpal or periapical pathosis violates standard of care. Antibiotics are contraindicated without evidence of a bacterial odontogenic infection, and surgical exploration is needlessly invasive in the absence of focal periodontal or radiographic pathology.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1704.question: A 7-year-old male presents with his mother immediately after sustaining a bicycle accident resulting in facial trauma. Clinical examination reveals permanent tooth #8 is displaced palatally and slightly extruded, exhibiting moderate mobility. Periapical radiographs reveal widening of the periodontal ligament space with an open apex, and confirm no root or alveolar fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management for tooth #8?
options: Perform an immediate pulpotomy on tooth #8 to preserve pulp vitality
Gently reposition the tooth with digital pressure and stabilize with a flexible splint
Extract tooth #8 and place an immediate removable space maintainer
Allow the tooth to re-erupt and reposition spontaneously over several months
pharmacology-anesthesia-1704.explanation: Option B is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, acute management of an extruded or laterally luxated permanent incisor requires gentle digital repositioning into its anatomic socket followed by stabilization with a flexible splint for 2 weeks. Immediate pulpotomy is contraindicated because immature luxated teeth retain exceptional capacity for pulpal revascularization and should be monitored for healing. Extraction is inappropriate for a salvageable permanent anterior tooth, and spontaneous repositioning applies exclusively to intruded teeth with open apices, not extruded or displaced incisors.

pharmacology-anesthesia-1715.question: A 55-year-old male with a history of stage 1 hypertension controlled with lisinopril requires a crown preparation on tooth #3. What is the maximum recommended dose (MRD) of 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine for this patient at a single appointment?
options: 7.0 mg/kg of lidocaine, with a maximum of 0.20 mg of epinephrine
2.0 mg/kg of lidocaine, with a maximum of 0.08 mg of epinephrine
4.4 mg/kg of lidocaine, with a maximum of 0.04 mg of epinephrine
1.0 mg/kg of lidocaine, with a maximum of 0.02 mg of epinephrine
