Conventional glass ionomer cement (Option C) has low tensile strength and inadequate fracture toughness to withstand heavy occlusal masticatory stresses on molar surfaces.

operative-materials-999.question: A 45-year-old female patient presents with a large MOD (mesial-occlusal-distal) carious lesion in tooth #14 (maxillary left first molar). During restorative preparation of the proximal boxes, a matrix band and wedge are placed prior to condensation of the restorative material. What is the primary purpose of placing the matrix band and wedge?
options: To isolate the operative field from salivary and gingival crevicular fluid contamination
To recreate the anatomical proximal contour and seal the gingival margin to prevent overhangs
To provide mechanical retention for the restorative material through internal undercuts
To protect the pulp from exothermic polymerization heat and chemical toxicity
operative-materials-999.explanation: Option B is correct because the matrix band establishes the missing proximal wall and anatomical contour of tooth #14 (maxillary left first molar), while the wedge closely adapts the band against the cervical cavosurface margin to prevent gingival overhangs and provides slight tooth separation to ensure tight proximal contact. Isolation from saliva and moisture (Option A) is achieved using a rubber dam, not a matrix band and wedge. Cavity retention (Option C) is created by cavity preparation design, not the matrix system. Pulpal thermal and chemical protection (Option D) is achieved using cavity liners or bases.

operative-materials-1000.question: A 28-year-old male patient presents with an unesthetic, non-cavitated white spot lesion on the facial surface of tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor) following orthodontic treatment. Clinical examination reveals that the enamel surface is smooth and intact. The patient requests conservative aesthetic management. What is the MOST appropriate initial management strategy?
options: Full-coverage porcelain laminate veneer preparation
Conventional Class V preparation and composite resin restoration
Placement of a resin-modified glass ionomer surface sealant
Resin infiltration of the porous enamel lesion
operative-materials-1000.explanation: Option D is correct because resin infiltration (e.g., Icon) is the minimally invasive treatment of choice for smooth-surface, non-cavitated enamel white spot lesions on anterior teeth (#8); the low-viscosity resin penetrates the porous enamel body, matching the refractive index of sound enamel (1.62) and restoring natural translucency without cavity preparation. Porcelain veneers (Option A) and Class V composite preparations (Option B) involve unnecessary, irreversible removal of sound tooth structure for an intact, non-cavitated lesion. Glass ionomer sealants (Option C) are opaque, wear rapidly on smooth facial surfaces, and fail to esthetically blend with surrounding enamel.

operative-materials-1025.question: A dental laboratory technician is preparing a dental stone (Type IV) die cast and wishes to minimize setting expansion to achieve optimal dimensional accuracy. Which modification to the mixing procedure will MOST effectively reduce setting expansion?
options: Increasing the water-to-powder ratio
Decreasing the water-to-powder ratio
Increasing the spatulation time and rate
Using warm water to accelerate crystallization
operative-materials-1025.explanation: Option A is correct because increasing the water-to-powder (W/P) ratio increases the physical distance between developing calcium sulfate dihydrate crystals, thereby reducing crystal impingement and outward thrust, which directly decreases setting expansion. Decreasing the W/P ratio (Option B) increases the density of crystallization nuclei, resulting in greater crystal impingement and increased setting expansion. Increasing spatulation time and rate (Option C) breaks up forming crystals into a greater number of nuclei, which increases setting expansion. Modifying water temperature (Option D) alters setting time rather than reliably reducing setting expansion.

operative-materials-1008.question: A dentist is selecting a cast gold alloy for a single full-coverage crown on a mandibular molar. To ensure adequate yield strength and hardness to resist high occlusal masticatory forces, which type of cast gold alloy is preferred according to ADA specifications?
options: Type I (soft) gold alloy
Type II (medium) gold alloy
Type III (hard) gold alloy
Type IV (extra-hard) gold alloy
operative-materials-1008.explanation: Option C is correct because ADA Specification No. 5 designates Type III (hard) gold alloy as the standard material for single posterior full crowns, onlays, and short-span fixed partial dentures exposed to high occlusal loads. Type I (soft) and Type II (medium) alloys (Options A and B) have lower yield strength and hardness, making them suitable only for non-stress-bearing inlays or small onlays. Type IV (extra-hard) gold alloy (Option D) is reserved for high-stress applications such as removable partial denture frameworks, clasps, and long-span fixed prostheses, not routine single posterior crowns.

operative-materials-1090.question: During the laboratory processing of a heat-cured polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) complete denture base, spherical gaseous porosity is observed localized exclusively within the thickest portions of the denture. What is the MOST common cause of this defect?
options: Overheating during the polymerization cycle exceeding monomer boiling point
Insufficient packing pressure maintained during flask closure
Rapid bench cooling of the denture flask following processing
An insufficient monomer-to-polymer ratio during dough preparation
operative-materials-1090.explanation: Option A is correct because gaseous porosity characteristically occurs in the thickest sections of a heat-cured acrylic denture base when rapid heating during processing causes the exothermic polymerization reaction to exceed the boiling temperature of unreacted methyl methacrylate monomer (100.3°C), causing monomer vaporization. Insufficient packing pressure (Option B) produces contraction porosity distributed throughout the entire thickness of the denture base. Rapid cooling (Option C) generates internal thermal stress and denture base warpage rather than gaseous porosity. An insufficient monomer-to-polymer ratio (Option D) produces granular, chalky porosity due to incomplete polymer bead wetting.

operative-materials-1229.question: During the chairside fabrication of a custom provisional crown on tooth #19, the clinician observes significant heat generation and high volumetric shrinkage during the chemically activated polymerization reaction. Which provisional material is characteristically associated with these properties?
options: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA)
Bis-acryl composite resin
Polyethyl methacrylate (PEMA)
Polycarbonate
operative-materials-1229.explanation: Option A is correct because polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) undergoes an exothermic addition polymerization reaction that generates substantial heat capable of causing thermal pulpal injury, accompanied by high volumetric shrinkage of approximately 6% to 8%. In contrast, bis-acryl composite resins generate minimal exothermic heat and lower shrinkage, polyethyl methacrylate produces significantly less exothermic heat than PMMA, and polycarbonate crowns are preformed thermoplastic shells that do not undergo chairside polymerization.

operative-materials-1239.question: A 32-year-old male presents for the replacement of an old, discolored Class III restoration on tooth #9. The patient desires an esthetic, tooth-colored restoration with high polishability and excellent mechanical strength. Which composite resin filler type provides the best combination of these properties for this anterior restoration?
options: Nanohybrid composite
Microfilled composite
Macrofilled composite
Flowable composite
operative-materials-1239.explanation: Option A is correct because nanohybrid composites incorporate both submicron glass particles and nanoscale filler particles, providing the optimal balance of mechanical strength, high initial polishability, and long-term gloss retention required for anterior Class III restorations on tooth #9. Microfilled composites offer excellent polishability but exhibit inferior mechanical strength and fracture toughness, macrofilled composites have poor polishability and wear into a rough surface, and flowable composites possess reduced filler loading with inferior wear resistance and mechanical strength.

operative-materials-1258.question: A 28-year-old female patient presents for the restoration of a Class III carious lesion on the mesial surface of tooth #9. The clinician desires a tooth-colored restorative material that achieves true chemical adhesion to tooth structure via ionic bonding to hydroxyapatite, while providing superior esthetics and physical properties compared to conventional glass ionomer. Which of the following restorative materials best satisfies these requirements?
options: Microfilled composite resin
Resin-modified glass ionomer cement
Conventional glass ionomer cement
Zinc polycarboxylate cement
operative-materials-1258.explanation: Option B is correct because resin-modified glass ionomer cement (RMGIC) achieves true chemical adhesion to enamel and dentin via ionic carboxylate chelation with calcium in hydroxyapatite, while its resin component provides greater translucency, polishability, and flexural strength than conventional glass ionomer. Microfilled composite resin bonds strictly through micromechanical retention via adhesive resins rather than true chemical bonding, conventional glass ionomer has inferior esthetics and lower physical properties, and zinc polycarboxylate lacks esthetic tooth-colored translucency.

operative-materials-1282.question: A pediatric patient requires a preformed stainless steel crown on a severely decayed primary mandibular right second molar (tooth T). Which mechanical property of stainless steel allows the clinician to crimp and contour the cervical margins without fracturing the metal?
options: Low modulus of elasticity permitting flexible elastic recovery
High ductility allowing permanent plastic deformation
Low proportional limit causing brittle fracture under stress
High coefficient of thermal expansion matching natural enamel
operative-materials-1282.explanation: Option B is correct because high ductility allows stainless steel to undergo substantial permanent plastic deformation without fracture when crimped and contoured with pliers, enabling precise cervical adaptation to the cervical constriction of tooth T. Stainless steel actually has a high modulus of elasticity (~200 GPa), meaning it is very stiff, and elastic recovery would cause crimped margins to spring back rather than remain adapted. A low proportional limit would imply poor resistance to functional deformation, and thermal expansion properties do not govern margin crimping.

operative-materials-1288.question: A dentist is selecting a permanent luting agent for a conventional cast high-noble metal crown on tooth #30, which exhibits adequate clinical crown height and retention form. Which of the following luting cements provides ionic chemical adhesion to tooth structure via chelation to calcium AND sustained fluoride release?
options: Resin-modified glass ionomer cement
Zinc phosphate cement
Zinc polycarboxylate cement
Conventional bis-GMA resin cement
operative-materials-1288.explanation: Option A is correct because resin-modified glass ionomer cement (RMGIC) contains fluoroaluminosilicate glass and polyalkenoic acid, allowing it to form ionic chemical bonds with calcium in tooth hydroxyapatite while providing continuous fluoride release. Zinc phosphate provides purely micromechanical retention without chemical adhesion or fluoride release, zinc polycarboxylate forms a chemical bond with calcium but does not release fluoride, and conventional bis-GMA resin cement relies on micromechanical interlocking via bonding agents without chemical chelation or significant fluoride release.

operative-materials-1291.question: According to the American Dental Association (ADA) classification of dental casting alloys, which of the following alloy compositions is classified as a 'High Noble' alloy?
options: 35% Gold, 30% Palladium, 20% Silver, 15% Copper
55% Gold, 10% Palladium, 20% Silver, 15% Copper
15% Gold, 15% Palladium, 50% Silver, 20% Copper
2% Gold, 10% Palladium, 68% Nickel, 20% Chromium
operative-materials-1291.explanation: Option B is correct because the ADA classifies casting alloys as High Noble if they contain a noble metal content (gold, platinum, palladium) of at least 60% by weight, with at least 40% of the total alloy being gold; this composition contains 65% noble metal (55% Au + 10% Pd) and meets both requirements. Option A contains 65% noble metal but fails the gold requirement by containing only 35% gold, classifying it as Noble. Option C has 30% noble metal (Noble), and Option D contains only 12% noble metal, classifying it as Predominantly Base Metal.

operative-materials-1309.question: During the manipulation of zinc polycarboxylate cement for luting a cast crown on tooth #19, the clinician observes that the mixture has lost its initial glossy sheen and appears dull. What does this physical change signify regarding the cement, and what is the proper clinical management?
options: The cement has reached its initial gel stage, indicating that the restoration must be seated immediately.
The powder-to-liquid ratio was insufficient, which can be corrected by quickly mixing in additional powder.
Available carboxylic acid groups have been bound, causing loss of adhesion and excessive film thickness; the mix must be discarded.
The cement has achieved its final crystallization, indicating optimal compressive strength for seating.
operative-materials-1309.explanation: Option C is correct because the glossy appearance of zinc polycarboxylate cement indicates the presence of free, unreacted polyacrylic acid chains needed to chelate calcium in tooth structure; loss of gloss indicates that cross-linking has consumed these groups and increased viscosity beyond acceptable film thickness, which clinically contraindicates seating and requires the mix to be discarded. Option A is incorrect because attempting to seat a crown after gloss is lost causes incomplete seating and lack of chemical adhesion. Options B and D are incorrect because adding powder or liquid disrupts matrix formation and final setting takes hours to complete.

operative-materials-1312.question: A 50-year-old female patient returns 2 weeks after the placement of a large, deep Class II composite resin restoration on tooth #13. She reports sharp pain localized to the tooth specifically upon the release of biting pressure while chewing. Percussion and palpation tests are negative, and thermal testing elicits a normal transient response. Targeted bite testing on the buccal cusp using a Tooth Slooth reproduces the sharp pain upon release. What is the most likely cause of this patient's postoperative sensitivity?
options: Hyperocclusion causing acute apical periodontitis
Inadequate depth of cure of the composite resin
Microleakage resulting in recurrent caries
Cuspal deflection caused by polymerization shrinkage stress
operative-materials-1312.explanation: Option D is correct because polymerization shrinkage in large Class II composite restorations (high configuration factor or C-factor) exerts inward tensile stress on remaining cuspal walls, and subsequent masticatory forces further bend the weakened cusp; releasing bite pressure causes rapid fluid movement in dentinal tubules, producing characteristic sharp rebound pain. Option A is incorrect because hyperocclusion causes pain on initial contact and direct percussion tenderness. Options B and C are incorrect because incomplete curing produces diffuse dentin sensitivity rather than isolated cusp rebound pain, and recurrent caries requires months to develop.

operative-materials-1369.question: An irreversible hydrocolloid (alginate) impression is taken of the maxillary arch for diagnostic casts. Due to a clinical interruption, the impression is inadvertently left exposed to ambient room air on the laboratory bench for 2 hours before pouring with dental stone. What physical process and dimensional change will occur within the alginate impression material?
options: Expansion and swelling due to imbibition of atmospheric water vapor
Shrinkage and distortion due to syneresis and water evaporation
Liquefaction and loss of detail due to reversible thermal hysteresis
Linear expansion due to ongoing cross-linking polymerization
operative-materials-1369.explanation: Option B is correct because alginate hydrocolloid contains approximately 80% water; when exposed to ambient air, it rapidly loses fluid through both evaporation and syneresis (the spontaneous exudation of liquid from the gel matrix), resulting in substantial volumetric shrinkage and irreversible dimensional distortion. Option A is incorrect because imbibition refers to the absorption of liquid water when immersed, not water vapor uptake from air. Option C is incorrect because alginate is an irreversible hydrocolloid that sets by chemical reaction and cannot undergo thermal hysteresis. Option D is incorrect because the setting reaction and dehydration cause contraction, not expansion.

operative-materials-1469.question: A 65-year-old male patient presents for evaluation of a loose mandibular complete denture that was fabricated 10 years ago. Clinical examination reveals severe residual alveolar ridge resorption, severely underextended posterior denture borders, extensive occlusal wear of the acrylic teeth, and a loss of vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO). What is the MOST appropriate management to restore retention, stability, and function?
options: Perform a laboratory hard reline of the existing denture
Place a resilient (soft) chairside liner in the existing denture
Equilibrate the existing occlusion and extend borders with cold-cure acrylic
Fabricate a new mandibular complete denture
operative-materials-1469.explanation: Option D is correct because fabricating a new complete denture is indicated when an existing 10-year-old prosthesis exhibits severely worn artificial teeth, loss of vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO), and significantly underextended borders, none of which can be corrected by relining. Options A and B are contraindicated because relines and soft liners only adapt the intaglio surface to the current ridge morphology and cannot restore worn occlusal anatomy, correct lost VDO, or properly extend deficient borders. Option C is incorrect because chairside border addition and equilibration cannot reconstruct collapsed vertical dimension or address severe denture base fatigue.

operative-materials-1477.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic 1 hour after sustaining facial trauma from a bicycle fall. Clinical examination reveals tooth #8 (permanent maxillary right central incisor) is displaced lingually, locked into alveolar bone, and tender to percussion. Radiographic examination demonstrates an open, immature apex with widened apical periodontal ligament space and no root fracture. According to IADT and AAE guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate immediate management for tooth #8?
options: Extract the tooth due to the imminent risk of pulp necrosis and ankylosis
Splint the tooth in its displaced position for 4 weeks without repositioning
Reposition the tooth gently into the socket and stabilize with a flexible splint for 2 to 4 weeks
Perform immediate pulp extirpation and initiate apexification with calcium hydroxide
operative-materials-1477.explanation: Option C is correct because according to IADT and AAE trauma guidelines, the definitive immediate management of a lateral luxation is to gently disengage and reposition the tooth into its anatomical socket, followed by stabilization with a flexible splint for 2 weeks (or up to 4 weeks if associated with alveolar bone fracture). In an immature tooth with an open apex at age 7, immediate root canal treatment (Option D) is contraindicated because the pulp has significant revascularization potential and must be monitored clinically and radiographically. Splinting without repositioning (Option B) prevents proper periodontal and bone healing, while extraction (Option A) is unnecessarily destructive.

operative-materials-1456.question: A 45-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of sharp, localized pain in his maxillary right premolar region that occurs only when chewing. He reports no spontaneous pain and no thermal sensitivity. Clinical examination of tooth #5 (maxillary right first premolar) reveals an existing large amalgam restoration with a fracture line extending across the marginal ridge. Palpation and percussion tests are negative, cold testing elicits a normal transient response, and a bite test using a Tooth Slooth on the buccal cusp reproduces the sharp pain upon release. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Cracked tooth syndrome
Periodontal abscess
operative-materials-1456.explanation: Option C is correct because cracked tooth syndrome characteristically presents with sharp pain elicited upon chewing or release of biting pressure (reproduced by targeted cusp flexure with a Tooth Slooth), typically in a restored posterior tooth (such as tooth #5) with normal pulpal and periapical responses. Reversible pulpitis (Option A) presents with thermal sensitivity without localized mechanical pain on cusp release. Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (Option B) features lingering thermal pain and spontaneous throbbing pain, and a periodontal abscess (Option D) presents with deep pocketing, purulence, and continuous localized swelling.

periodontics-80.question: A 45-year-old male presents for a comprehensive periodontal evaluation. Examination reveals generalized bleeding on probing, interdental probing depths ranging from 5 to 7 mm, and radiographic bone loss extending into the middle third of the root across multiple teeth. The patient has no history of tooth loss, does not smoke, and has no systemic medical conditions. Based on the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: Stage II, Grade B Periodontitis
Stage III, Grade C Periodontitis
Stage II, Grade C Periodontitis
Stage III, Grade B Periodontitis
periodontics-80.explanation: Option D is correct because radiographic bone loss extending into the middle third of the root (33% to 50%) and probing depths ≥6 mm establish Stage III disease severity and complexity under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification. In a patient with no diabetes, no smoking history, and bone loss consistent with local plaque accumulation, the progression rate is categorized as Grade B (moderate rate, with bone loss/age ratio between 0.25 and 1.0). Stage II is incorrect because it is restricted to bone loss in the coronal third (<33%) and probing depths ≤5 mm, while Grade C is incorrect because it requires rapid progression or major risk factors like heavy smoking or uncontrolled diabetes.

periodontics-179.question: When evaluating a maxillary first molar for furcation involvement, from which direction is the mesial furcation entrance best accessed and evaluated using a Nabers probe?
options: Direct buccal approach
Mesiopalatal approach
Direct occlusal approach
Distopalatal approach
periodontics-179.explanation: Option B is correct because the mesial furcation entrance of a maxillary first molar is situated approximately two-thirds of the buccolingual width toward the palatal surface, requiring a mesiopalatal probing approach. Option A is incorrect because the direct buccal approach accesses the buccal furcation between the mesiobuccal and distobuccal roots. Options C and D are incorrect because an occlusal approach cannot negotiate the cervical furcation anatomy, and a distopalatal approach is used to instrument the distal, not the mesial, furcation.

periodontics-181.question: A 55-year-old male presents for periodontal treatment. Clinical examination reveals generalized interdental clinical attachment loss of 5 mm with probing depths of 6 mm and bleeding on probing at the most severe sites, including the mesial aspect of tooth #14. Radiographs demonstrate bone loss extending into the middle third of the root (approximately 35%). The patient is a non-smoker with no diabetes or other systemic risk factors. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the correct diagnosis?
options: Stage I, Grade A Periodontitis
Stage II, Grade A Periodontitis
Stage III, Grade B Periodontitis
Stage IV, Grade C Periodontitis
periodontics-181.explanation: Option C is correct because interdental clinical attachment loss ≥5 mm, probing depths ≥6 mm, and radiographic bone loss extending into the middle third of the root (33% to 50%) define Stage III periodontitis under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification. Grade B is established because the indirect evidence of progression (percentage bone loss divided by age: ~35% / 55 = 0.64) falls within the moderate progression range of 0.25 to 1.0. Stages I and II are incorrect because they are limited to probing depths ≤5 mm and coronal-third bone loss, whereas Stage IV is incorrect because it requires advanced tooth loss (≥5 teeth) or masticatory dysfunction.

periodontics-222.question: During periodontal maintenance therapy, which specific Gracey curette design is indicated for scaling and root planing the facial and lingual surfaces of maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth?
options: Gracey 11/12
Gracey 1/2
Gracey 13/14
Gracey 15/16
periodontics-222.explanation: Option B is correct because the Gracey 1/2 curette (along with the 3/4) is an area-specific instrument featuring a slight shank angulation designed specifically for all surfaces of anterior teeth. Options A and D are incorrect because Gracey 11/12 and 15/16 curettes are engineered specifically for the mesial surfaces of posterior teeth. Option C is incorrect because the Gracey 13/14 curette is designed specifically for the distal surfaces of posterior teeth.

periodontics-213.question: Which histological principal fiber group of the periodontal ligament is the most numerous and primarily responsible for resisting vertical, intrusive forces during mastication?
options: Apical fibers
Oblique fibers
Alveolar crest fibers
Horizontal fibers
periodontics-213.explanation: Option B is correct because oblique fibers represent the largest and most abundant principal fiber group of the periodontal ligament, extending coronally and obliquely from cementum to alveolar bone to convert vertical, intrusive masticatory forces into tensile load on the alveolar bone. Option A is incorrect because apical fibers radiate from the root apex to resist extrusive forces and protect apical neurovascular structures. Options C and D are incorrect because alveolar crest and horizontal fibers primarily function to resist lateral, horizontal, and tipping movements.

periodontics-249.question: In the classic Page and Schroeder model of periodontal pathogenesis, an early gingival lesion developing 4 to 7 days after the initiation of plaque accumulation is histologically characterized by a predominant infiltrate of which inflammatory cell type?
options: Neutrophils
Plasma cells
B-lymphocytes
T-lymphocytes
periodontics-249.explanation: Option D is correct because the early gingival lesion (developing 4 to 7 days after plaque accumulation) is characterized histologically by a lymphoid infiltrate dominated by T-lymphocytes (comprising up to 75% of the infiltrate) accompanied by localized loss of collagen. Option A is incorrect because polymorphonuclear neutrophils predominate in the initial lesion (2 to 4 days) within the junctional epithelium and gingival sulcus. Options B and C are incorrect because B-lymphocytes and plasma cells predominate later in the established lesion (2 to 3 weeks) and advanced lesion (periodontitis).

periodontics-268.question: According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, which primary clinical finding distinguishes a stable, treated periodontium (periodontal health on a reduced periodontium) from active periodontitis?
options: Bleeding on probing at less than 10% of sites with no probing depths ≥4 mm that bleed
Complete eradication of all subgingival bacterial microbiota
Complete radiographic regeneration of original alveolar bone height
Absence of any clinical attachment loss across the dentition
periodontics-268.explanation: Option A is correct because the 2017 AAP/EFP classification defines periodontal health on a reduced periodontium by the absence of clinical inflammation, specifically bleeding on probing at less than 10% of sites with no probing depths of ≥4 mm displaying bleeding. Option B is incorrect because complete elimination of subgingival microbiota is biologically unachievable and unnecessary for tissue health. Options C and D are incorrect because a reduced periodontium retains permanent loss of alveolar bone height and clinical attachment from past disease, healing primarily via a long junctional epithelium rather than total tissue regeneration.

periodontics-272.question: During a periodontal examination, a 6 mm probing depth is measured on the facial aspect of tooth #19. The mucogingival junction is identified 2 mm apical to the base of the periodontal pocket. What is the width of the keratinized gingiva and the width of the attached gingiva at this site?
options: Keratinized gingiva: 6 mm; Attached gingiva: 0 mm
Keratinized gingiva: 8 mm; Attached gingiva: 2 mm
Keratinized gingiva: 4 mm; Attached gingiva: 2 mm
Keratinized gingiva: 8 mm; Attached gingiva: 6 mm
periodontics-272.explanation: Option B is correct because the width of keratinized gingiva is the total distance from the gingival margin to the mucogingival junction (6 mm probing depth + 2 mm apical to the pocket base = 8 mm), and the width of attached gingiva is the distance from the base of the pocket to the mucogingival junction (8 mm - 6 mm = 2 mm). Option A is incorrect because it mistakenly equates keratinized gingiva with probing depth and assumes zero attached gingiva. Options C and D are incorrect because they result from incorrect subtraction or confusing attached gingiva with the probing depth.

periodontics-277.question: What is the average dimension of the biologic width (supracrestal tissue attachment), and what are its histological components coronal to the alveolar bone crest?
options: Approximately 2.04 mm, composed of the junctional epithelium and supracrestal connective tissue attachment
Approximately 2.04 mm, composed of the sulcular epithelium and junctional epithelium
Approximately 3.00 mm, composed of the sulcular epithelium and free gingival fibers
Approximately 1.07 mm, composed exclusively of the junctional epithelium
periodontics-277.explanation: Option A is correct because the biologic width (classified as the supracrestal tissue attachment in the 2017 AAP/EFP workshop), according to Gargiulo's landmark measurements, averages approximately 2.04 mm, consisting of the junctional epithelium (~0.97 mm) and supracrestal connective tissue attachment (~1.07 mm). Option B is incorrect because sulcular epithelium lines the gingival crevice and does not form an attachment to the tooth surface. Options C and D are incorrect because 3.00 mm describes the total dentogingival complex when including the gingival sulcus (~0.69 mm), while 1.07 mm accounts only for the connective tissue component.

periodontics-289.question: A 60-year-old male with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with severe oral pain, rapid tissue necrosis, and fetor oris. Clinical examination reveals punched-out, cratered interdental papillae covered by a prominent pseudomembrane between teeth #8, #9, and #10. Which microbial group is most characteristically implicated in this acute presentation?
options: Actinomyces species and Streptococcus mutans
Red complex bacteria (Porphyromonas gingivalis and Tannerella forsythia)
Spirochetes (Treponema species) and fusiform bacteria
Orange complex bacteria (Fusobacterium nucleatum and Prevotella intermedia)
periodontics-289.explanation: Option C is correct because necrotizing periodontal diseases (necrotizing gingivitis and necrotizing periodontitis) are classically driven by an opportunistic fuso-spirochetal complex consisting of Treponema species (spirochetes) and fusiform bacteria. Option A is incorrect because Actinomyces species and Streptococcus mutans are associated with root caries and plaque biofilm maturation, not necrotizing lesions. Options B and D are incorrect because while red and orange complex anaerobes are associated with chronic adult periodontitis, the hallmark invasive organisms defining acute necrotizing ulcerative lesions are spirochetes and fusiform bacilli.

periodontics-294.question: A patient presents for periodontal evaluation. Periodontal probing reveals a 7 mm probing depth on the mesial aspect of tooth #15, with the base of the pocket located apical to the adjacent alveolar bone crest. There is no furcation involvement. How is this specific defect classified?
options: Infrabony (intra-alveolar) pocket
Gingival pocket
Pseudopocket
Suprabony pocket
periodontics-294.explanation: Option A is correct because an infrabony (intra-alveolar or subcrestal) pocket is defined specifically by the base of the pocket being located apical to the crest of the surrounding alveolar bone, typically accompanied by vertical bone defects. Option D is incorrect because a suprabony (supracrestal) pocket has its base located coronal to the alveolar bone crest, typically associated with horizontal bone loss. Options B and C are incorrect because gingival pockets (pseudopockets) result from coronal gingival enlargement without apical migration of the junctional epithelium or loss of alveolar bone.

periodontics-299.question: Which local anatomical risk factor is most commonly associated with localized severe clinical attachment loss and plaque retention on the mesial aspect of maxillary first molars?
options: Mesial root concavity and proximal furcation entrance
Enamel pearl
Cervical enamel projection
Palatogingival groove
periodontics-299.explanation: Option A is correct because the maxillary first molar characteristically possesses a prominent longitudinal developmental concavity on its mesial root trunk that leads directly into the mesial furcation entrance (located ~3 mm apical to the CEJ), creating a plaque-retentive niche that complicates periodontal instrumentation. Option B is incorrect because enamel pearls are rare developmental anomalies (occurring in <2-4% of molars) located predominantly in second and third molar furcations. Option C is incorrect because cervical enamel projections, though predisposing to furcation involvement, are less prevalent than standard root concavities. Option D is incorrect because palatogingival grooves are developmental anomalies characteristically found on maxillary lateral incisors (teeth #7 and #10).

operative-materials-1458.question: A 32-year-old male presents 3 days after the uneventful extraction of tooth #32 complaining of severe, throbbing pain radiating to his ear and a foul odor in his mouth. Clinical examination reveals an empty extraction socket with exposed bone, absence of a blood clot, and normal surrounding gingival tissues without fever, swelling, or lymphadenopathy. What is the MOST appropriate clinical management?
options: Prescribe a 7-day course of systemic amoxicillin and warm saline mouth rinses.
Gently irrigate the socket with warm saline and place a medicated sedative dressing.
Administer local anesthesia and vigorously curette the socket to induce fresh bleeding.
Debride the socket and tightly suture the mucosal margins over the exposed bone.
operative-materials-1458.explanation: Option B is correct because the definitive management of alveolar osteitis (dry socket) consists of gentle irrigation with warm saline to flush necrotic debris followed by the placement of a medicated sedative dressing (such as eugenol-impregnated gauze) for pain relief. Aggressive curettage of the socket (Option C) is strictly contraindicated because it removes residual viable tissue, increases bone exposure, and significantly delays healing while worsening pain. Systemic antibiotics (Option A) and primary closure with sutures (Option D) are inappropriate because alveolar osteitis is a localized, non-purulent osteolytic condition rather than a spreading bacterial infection.

operative-materials-1460.question: A 72-year-old male presents with difficulty chewing due to loose lower front teeth. Clinical examination reveals generalized interdental clinical attachment loss ≥5 mm, probing depths ranging from 5 to 7 mm with bleeding on probing, and Class II mobility on teeth #23, #24, #25, and #26. Full-mouth radiographs confirm generalized horizontal and vertical bone loss extending into the apical third of the roots (greater than 50% bone loss) affecting more than 30% of teeth. According to the 2018 AAP/EFP classification system, what is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis?
options: Generalized periodontitis, Stage IV
Generalized periodontitis, Stage II
Localized periodontitis, Stage III
Generalized gingivitis on a reduced periodontium
operative-materials-1460.explanation: Option A is correct because the 2018 AAP/EFP classification designates periodontitis as Stage IV when interdental clinical attachment loss is ≥5 mm, radiographic bone loss extends into the mid-to-apical third of the root (≥50%), and tooth hypermobility (Class II or greater) or masticatory dysfunction causes potential dentition loss across ≥30% of teeth (generalized). Stage II periodontitis (Option B) is characterized by coronal-third bone loss (15% to 33%) and probing depths ≤5 mm without hypermobility. Localized Stage III periodontitis (Option C) involves <30% of teeth and lacks complex masticatory dysfunction, while gingivitis (Option D) exhibits no progressive attachment loss.

operative-materials-1461.question: A 60-year-old female presents for scaling and root planing in the maxillary anterior sextant. Her medical history is significant for stage 2 hypertension well managed with lisinopril, and her blood pressure today is 140/90 mmHg. Which local anesthetic formulation is MOST appropriate to achieve adequate pulpal and soft tissue anesthesia as well as necessary hemostasis for this procedure?
options: Lidocaine 2% with 1:50,000 epinephrine
Mepivacaine 3% without vasoconstrictor
Articaine 4% with 1:100,000 epinephrine
Bupivacaine 0.5% with 1:200,000 epinephrine
operative-materials-1461.explanation: Option C is correct because Articaine 4% with 1:100,000 epinephrine provides rapid diffusion, profound pulpal and soft tissue anesthesia, and excellent local hemostasis for scaling and root planing, while staying well within the 0.04 mg cardiac epinephrine limit for patients with medically managed hypertension (Malamed). Mepivacaine 3% plain (Option B) lacks vasoconstriction, leading to inadequate duration and poor hemostatic control in bleeding periodontal pockets. Lidocaine with 1:50,000 epinephrine (Option A) poses unnecessary cardiovascular risk without clinical advantage, while bupivacaine 0.5% (Option D) has a delayed onset and is reserved for lengthy surgical procedures or prolonged postoperative analgesia.

operative-materials-1462.question: An 8-year-old male presents to the dental clinic 30 minutes after completely avulsing his permanent maxillary right central incisor (#8) during a playground fall. The tooth was immediately recovered, placed in cold milk, and transported to the clinic with an intact crown and open root apex. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management for this avulsed tooth?
options: Scrape the root surface with dry gauze to remove coagulum before replanting.
Perform extraoral pulpectomy and root canal obturation prior to replantation.
Gently rinse the root with saline, administer local anesthesia, irrigate the socket, and replant the tooth.
Place the tooth in sterile saline and defer replantation until an acrylic splint is fabricated.
operative-materials-1462.explanation: Option C is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) and AAPD guidelines, an avulsed permanent tooth with an open apex and short extraoral dry time (<60 minutes) should be gently rinsed with saline to preserve viable periodontal ligament cells, followed by gentle socket irrigation and immediate replantation. Mechanically scraping the root surface with gauze (Option A) strips viable periodontal ligament cells and precipitates severe replacement resorption and ankylosis. Performing extraoral endodontics (Option B) unnecessarily destroys periodontal cells and eliminates the potential for pulp revascularization in an immature tooth, while deferring replantation (Option D) drastically reduces periodontal ligament cell survival.

operative-materials-1464.question: A 52-year-old female presents with severe pain localized to tooth #19 (mandibular left first molar). Clinical and radiographic examinations reveal extensive subgingival caries and vertical bone loss rendering the mesial root non-restorable, whereas the distal root exhibits intact coronal structure, excellent periodontal bone support, and a favorable crown-to-root ratio. The patient strongly prefers to preserve the viable portion of the tooth as a functional abutment. What is the MOST appropriate management strategy?
options: Complete endodontic treatment on the distal root, perform hemisection with removal of the mesial root, and restore the distal root with a full-coverage crown.
Perform immediate surgical hemisection and mesial root extraction, followed by direct pulp capping of the remaining distal pulp chamber.
Perform complete root canal therapy on both roots, followed by an apicoectomy and retrofilling of the mesial root.
Perform periodontal flap surgery and tunnel preparation to maintain both roots intact beneath a splinted restoration.
operative-materials-1464.explanation: Option A is correct because retaining the distal root of a mandibular first molar via hemisection requires completing endodontic therapy on the retained root prior to surgical division and removal of the non-restorable mesial root, followed by full-coverage prosthodontic restoration. Performing hemisection with direct pulp capping (Option B) is biologically invalid because sectioning the pulp chamber creates massive irreversible pulpal exposure and inevitable necrosis. Apicoectomy (Option C) cannot resolve extensive coronal and cervical subgingival caries, and tunnel preparation (Option D) is reserved for cleansable furcation defects between two restorable roots rather than a structurally compromised, non-restorable root.

operative-materials-1484.question: A 30-year-old male is receiving local anesthesia for the surgical removal of an impacted tooth #17 (mandibular left third molar). During needle advancement for a conventional inferior alveolar nerve block, the patient suddenly reports an acute, 'electric shock' sensation radiating to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the left side, followed by prolonged sensory alteration. Which nerve sustained direct needle contact?
options: Lingual nerve
Inferior alveolar nerve
Long buccal nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
operative-materials-1484.explanation: Option A is correct because the lingual nerve runs anterior and medial to the inferior alveolar nerve in the pterygomandibular space; direct needle trauma causes an immediate electric shock sensation and persistent paresthesia along its sensory distribution in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (Malamed). Direct needle contact with the inferior alveolar nerve (Option B) produces electric shock sensations and paresthesia radiating to the lower lip, chin, and mandibular dentition rather than the tongue. The long buccal nerve (Option C) supplies the buccal gingiva of mandibular molars, and the mylohyoid nerve (Option D) provides primarily motor innervation to the mylohyoid and anterior digastric muscles without innervating the tongue.

operative-materials-1489.question: A 9-year-old female presents 4 months following the premature extraction of her primary mandibular left second molar (tooth K) due to severe caries. Clinical examination and bitewing radiographs confirm that succedaneous tooth #20 is developing normally, but permanent tooth #19 (mandibular left first molar) has tipped mesially, resulting in 3 mm of localized arch length loss. The mandibular permanent incisors are fully erupted. What is the MOST appropriate initial orthodontic intervention?
options: Place a passive mandibular lingual holding arch to maintain the remaining space.
Insert a distal shoe space maintainer along the mesial surface of tooth #19.
Utilize an active space-regaining appliance to distalize tooth #19 into its original position.
Perform serial extraction of the adjacent primary mandibular left first molar (tooth L).
operative-materials-1489.explanation: Option C is correct because once a permanent first molar has drifted mesially following premature primary molar loss, an active space-regaining appliance (such as an open-coil spring or cantilever appliance) must be used to distalize the molar and recover lost arch length before a passive maintainer is placed. A passive lingual holding arch (Option A) cannot recover lost space and would merely lock the permanent molar in its mesially tipped position, causing impaction or ectopic eruption of succedaneous premolar #20. A distal shoe (Option B) is indicated only prior to the eruption of the permanent first molar to guide its emergence, and serial extraction (Option D) is contraindicated in localized premature tooth loss without generalized tooth-size/arch-length discrepancy.

periodontics-108.question: A 54-year-old male with generalized periodontitis presents with a 6 mm probing depth and a Class II furcation defect on the buccal aspect of tooth #19 (mandibular left first molar). Radiographs reveal adequate adjacent interproximal bone crest height and no periapical pathology. Which surgical intervention provides the MOST predictable outcome for achieving periodontal regeneration in this defect?
options: Tunnel preparation through the bifurcation
Mandibular molar hemisection with extraction of the distal root
Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) with a barrier membrane and bone graft
Gingivectomy and apically repositioned flap without osseous grafting
periodontics-108.explanation: Option C is correct because mandibular buccal Class II furcation defects (such as on tooth #19) possess a favorable anatomical defect morphology (retained buccal and lingual bony walls with intact interproximal bone) that yields high, predictable clinical success for periodontal regeneration using guided tissue regeneration (GTR) with a barrier membrane and bone replacement graft (AAP guidelines). Tunnel preparation (Option A) is a resective procedure reserved for Class III furcations that creates an open plaque trap prone to root caries. Hemisection (Option B) is an aggressive resective approach indicated only when one root has catastrophic bone loss or non-restorable caries, while gingivectomy (Option D) is strictly resective and cannot regenerate lost periodontal attachment.

periodontics-23.question: A 30-year-old patient presents with localized gingival recession on the facial aspect of tooth #22 (mandibular left canine), exposing 3 mm of root surface. Clinical examination reveals that the margin of the recession does not extend to the mucogingival junction, there is an adequate band of attached gingiva apical to the defect, and interdental papillae and bone levels are completely intact. According to the Miller classification of marginal tissue recession, which category best describes this defect?
options: Class I
Class II
Class III
Class IV
periodontics-23.explanation: Option A is correct because Miller Class I recession is defined as marginal tissue recession that does not extend to the mucogingival junction, with no interdental bone or soft tissue loss, allowing 100% root coverage to be anticipated with periodontal plastic surgery. Miller Class II (Option B) extends to or beyond the mucogingival junction but also exhibits intact interproximal structures. Miller Class III (Option C) involves interdental attachment loss apical to the cementoenamel junction or tooth malposition where only partial coverage is possible, and Miller Class IV (Option D) displays severe interdental bone loss precluding root coverage.

periodontics-24.question: Which cellular component of the periodontal ligament is the most abundant and primarily responsible for the continuous synthesis, phagocytosis, and rapid physiological turnover of collagen fibers within the ligament?
options: Osteoblasts
Fibroblasts
Cementoblasts
Epithelial cell rests of Malassez
periodontics-24.explanation: Option B is correct because fibroblasts are the predominant cells within the periodontal ligament and are uniquely capable of both synthesizing collagen and intracellularly degrading it via matrix metalloproteinases and phagocytosis, driving the ligament's exceptionally high turnover rate (Ten Cate's Oral Histology). Osteoblasts (Option A) are specialized for the synthesis and mineralization of alveolar bone matrix rather than soft tissue ligament turnover. Cementoblasts (Option C) deposit cementum in an appositional manner without continuous physiological remodeling, and epithelial cell rests of Malassez (Option D) are quiescent developmental remnants of Hertwig's epithelial root sheath.

periodontics-73.question: A 40-year-old patient presents with an isolated, narrow 8 mm probing defect on the mid-facial aspect of tooth #19 (mandibular left first molar). Electric pulp testing and cold testing reveal that tooth #19 is completely non-vital, and periapical radiographs demonstrate a distinct periapical radiolucency isolated to the mesial root. Adjacent teeth exhibit normal 2 to 3 mm probing depths and intact crestal bone without generalized attachment loss. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis for this lesion?
options: Primary periodontal lesion
Primary endodontic lesion
Primary endodontic lesion with secondary periodontal involvement
True combined endodontic-periodontal lesion
periodontics-73.explanation: Option B is correct because an isolated, narrow probing defect on a non-vital tooth with periapical pathology in an otherwise healthy periodontium represents a sinus tract or pseudopocket of necrotic pulpal origin draining coronally through the periodontal ligament, defining a primary endodontic lesion (Simon/AAE classification). Primary periodontal lesions (Option A) present with vital pulps and generalized calculus-associated bone loss. Primary endodontic with secondary periodontal involvement (Option C) occurs only when a long-standing untreated necrotic tract accumulates marginal plaque and calculus, creating chronic periodontal pocketing. True combined lesions (Option D) develop when independent endodontic and periodontal defects coalesce along the root surface.

periodontics-77.question: What is the primary physiological function of the oblique fiber group of the periodontal ligament?
options: Resist rotational forces and maintain tight contact with adjacent teeth.
Resist extrusive forces and prevent tooth dislodgement from the socket.
Attach the gingival connective tissue directly to the junctional epithelium.
Resist vertical intrusive masticatory forces and transmit them as tensile stress to the alveolar bone.
periodontics-77.explanation: Option D is correct because oblique fibers are the most numerous principal fibers of the periodontal ligament, extending coronally and obliquely from cementum to alveolar bone to absorb axial masticatory loads and convert intrusive vertical forces into tension on the alveolar bone (Carranza's Clinical Periodontology). Resisting extrusive displacement (Option B) is the primary responsibility of alveolar crest and apical fiber groups. Resisting rotational and tipping forces (Option A) is mediated by horizontal and transeptal fiber groups, whereas attaching the gingiva to cementum (Option C) is performed by the gingival fiber groups (such as dentogingival fibers) rather than the dentoalveolar principal fibers.

periodontics-322.question: During histological examination of a healthy gingival sulcus, which primary defense mechanism of the junctional epithelium prevents bacterial penetration into the underlying connective tissue?
options: Continuous coronal migration and rapid desquamation of epithelial cells into the sulcus
Dense keratinization of the sulcular epithelial surface creating an impermeable barrier
Continuous apical migration of epithelial cells along the root surface
High density of tight junctions that completely seal the intercellular spaces
periodontics-322.explanation: Option A is correct because the junctional epithelium exhibits a rapid cellular turnover rate with continuous coronal migration and desquamation of cells into the gingival sulcus, constantly shedding adherent bacteria. Option B is incorrect because the junctional and sulcular epithelia are non-keratinized stratified squamous tissues that permit fluid exchange. Option C is incorrect because apical migration of the junctional epithelium represents a pathological hallmark of periodontitis and attachment loss rather than a physiological defense in health. Option D is incorrect because the junctional epithelium features wide intercellular spaces and relatively few desmosomes and tight junctions, facilitating neutrophil transmigration and gingival crevicular fluid flow.

periodontics-324.question: A 42-year-old female presents with localized acute pain and spontaneous bleeding in her anterior gingiva. Clinical examination reveals 'punched-out' cratered interdental papillae covered by a grayish pseudomembrane and a distinct fetid odor. She is afebrile with no regional lymphadenopathy or systemic signs. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Gentle superficial debridement of necrotic pseudomembrane combined with chlorhexidine or warm saline rinses
Prescription of systemic metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours without mechanical debridement
Aggressive full-mouth subgingival scaling and root planing under local anesthesia
Immediate surgical gingivectomy to excise the cratered interdental papillae
periodontics-324.explanation: Option A is correct because the initial therapy for acute necrotizing gingivitis in a patient without systemic involvement consists of gentle mechanical debridement of necrotic tissue and local antimicrobial rinses (e.g., 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate or warm saline). Option B is incorrect because systemic antibiotics are contraindicated in localized necrotizing disease without systemic signs (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy) under ADA antibiotic stewardship guidelines. Option C is incorrect because aggressive subgingival instrumentation during the acute ulcerative stage causes severe pain and tissue trauma and may disseminate bacteria into deeper tissues. Option D is incorrect because surgical gingivectomy is contraindicated during acute infection and is considered only after resolution if gingival craters persist.

periodontics-253.question: A 50-year-old female presents for re-evaluation of mandibular left first molar #19 following completion of Phase I periodontal therapy. Clinical examination reveals residual 5 mm probing depths, an isolated buccal Grade II (Class II) furcation defect, and adequate keratinized tissue. Radiographs confirm bone loss confined to the furcation without through-and-through involvement. What is the most appropriate definitive surgical intervention?
options: Extraction of tooth #19 and immediate implant placement
Periodontal regenerative therapy using guided tissue regeneration and bone replacement grafting
Osseous resective surgery with an apically positioned flap
Tunnel preparation through the furcation for interproximal cleansing
periodontics-253.explanation: Option B is correct because guided tissue regeneration (GTR) combined with bone grafting is the evidence-based gold standard for mandibular Class II furcation defects, offering predictable bone fill and clinical attachment gain. Option A is incorrect because the tooth has a favorable prognosis and is salvageable with regenerative therapy. Option C is incorrect because osseous resective surgery removes supporting alveolar bone and fails to address the horizontal component of a Class II furcation. Option D is incorrect because tunnel preparation is indicated for through-and-through Class III furcations with severe bone loss where regeneration is impossible.

periodontics-254.question: Which of the following is classified as an iatrogenic local contributing factor that promotes periodontal disease progression primarily by enhancing subgingival plaque retention and impeding effective oral hygiene?
options: Primary occlusal trauma
Overhanging restorative margin
Palatogingival developmental groove
Cervical enamel projection
periodontics-254.explanation: Option B is correct because an overhanging restorative margin is a clinician-induced (iatrogenic) local factor that creates a retentive niche for dental plaque biofilm, facilitates an anaerobic shift in the microflora, and prevents effective interproximal cleaning. Option A is incorrect because occlusal trauma represents an excessive mechanical force on supporting structures and does not act as a plaque-retentive factor or initiate gingival inflammation. Options C and D are incorrect because palatogingival grooves and cervical enamel projections are anatomical developmental anomalies of the tooth rather than iatrogenic factors.

periodontics-256.question: A 42-year-old female presents with acute gingival pain, spontaneous bleeding, and a fetid oral odor. Clinical examination reveals 'punched-out' cratered interdental papillae covered by a grayish pseudomembrane on her anterior teeth. She is afebrile with no regional lymphadenopathy. In addition to gentle mechanical debridement, which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antimicrobial therapy?
options: 0.12% Chlorhexidine gluconate oral rinse twice daily
Systemic amoxicillin 500 mg orally every 8 hours
Systemic metronidazole 500 mg orally every 8 hours
Systemic doxycycline 100 mg orally once daily
periodontics-256.explanation: Option A is correct because first-line adjunctive antimicrobial management of necrotizing gingivitis without systemic signs consists of topical antiseptic rinses, specifically 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate or warm dilute hydrogen peroxide rinses. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because systemic antibiotics (such as amoxicillin, metronidazole, or doxycycline) are contraindicated in localized necrotizing disease when systemic involvement (e.g., fever, lymphadenopathy, malaise) is absent, in accordance with ADA antibiotic stewardship guidelines.

periodontics-263.question: A 55-year-old male presents for a comprehensive periodontal examination. Clinical findings reveal interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm and probing depths up to 5 mm across multiple posterior teeth. Full-mouth radiographs demonstrate horizontal bone loss confined to the coronal third of the roots (20% to 25%), with no missing teeth due to periodontitis. The patient has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily (20 cigarettes/day) for 20 years. According to the 2018 AAP/EFP World Workshop classification, what is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: Stage II, Grade C periodontitis
Stage II, Grade B periodontitis
Stage III, Grade B periodontitis
Stage III, Grade C periodontitis
periodontics-263.explanation: Option A is correct because interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm, radiographic bone loss within the coronal third (15% to 33%), probing depths <= 5 mm, and no tooth loss from periodontitis define Stage II periodontitis. Additionally, smoking 20 cigarettes per day (>= 10 cigarettes/day) is an explicit risk factor modifier that automatically assigns the patient to Grade C (rapid rate of progression). Options B and C are incorrect because smoking >= 10 cigarettes/day precludes a Grade B designation. Option D is incorrect because the patient lacks the attachment loss (>= 5 mm), bone loss extending into the middle or apical third, or deep probing depths (>= 6 mm) required for Stage III.

periodontics-264.question: A 42-year-old female presents with localized gingival recession on the facial surface of maxillary right canine #6. Clinical examination reveals 3 mm of marginal tissue recession extending apical to the mucogingival junction with 1 mm probing depth. Interdental examination reveals moderate interdental bone loss and 4 mm probing depths, with the interproximal bone crest located apical to the CEJ but coronal to the apical base of the facial recession. According to the Miller Classification of Gingival Recession, what is the classification of this defect?
options: Miller Class I
Miller Class II
Miller Class III
Miller Class IV
periodontics-264.explanation: Option C is correct because Miller Class III recession is defined by marginal tissue recession extending to or beyond the mucogingival junction with loss of interdental bone or soft tissue coronal to the apical base of the facial defect (partial root coverage can be anticipated). Options A and B are incorrect because Miller Class I and Class II recessions present with intact interproximal bone and papillae without interdental attachment loss. Option D is incorrect because Miller Class IV recession involves severe interdental bone loss extending apically to or beyond the base of the facial recession margin, where no root coverage can be anticipated.

periodontics-356.question: According to the 2017/2018 AAP/EFP World Workshop classification of periodontal diseases, which of the following is explicitly incorporated into the grading matrix as a primary risk factor modifier to evaluate the rate of periodontal progression?
options: Cigarette smoking status
Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome
Down syndrome
Rheumatoid arthritis
periodontics-356.explanation: Option A is correct because cigarette smoking status (along with diabetes mellitus/glycemic control measured by HbA1c) is explicitly designated as a primary risk factor grade modifier in the 2017/2018 AAP/EFP classification matrix to assess biological rate of progression. Options B and C are incorrect because Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome and Down syndrome are categorized under systemic genetic disorders that manifest severe periodontitis rather than serving as grade modifiers. Option D is incorrect because rheumatoid arthritis is classified as a systemic inflammatory disease that influences periodontal pathogenesis but is not an explicit grading criterion.

periodontics-395.question: According to the 2017/2018 AAP/EFP World Workshop classification, which of the following conditions can cause destruction of periodontal supporting tissues independently of dental plaque biofilm-induced inflammation?
options: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency
Poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes mellitus
periodontics-395.explanation: Option A is correct because Langerhans cell histiocytosis is an osteolytic neoplastic disorder classified under systemic disorders that cause loss of periodontal supporting tissues independently of dental plaque biofilm, characteristically presenting as alveolar bone destruction with teeth 'floating in air'. Options B and C are incorrect because Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome and leukocyte adhesion deficiency cause severe attachment loss by dysregulating host immune-inflammatory responses to dental plaque biofilm rather than destroying tissues independently of biofilm. Option D is incorrect because diabetes mellitus acts as a metabolic modifier that exacerbates plaque-induced periodontal inflammation and tissue destruction.

periodontics-414.question: According to the Page and Schroeder model of periodontal disease pathogenesis, which inflammatory cell type predominates within the connective tissue infiltrate of the established lesion (chronic gingivitis, 14 to 21 days of plaque accumulation)?
options: Neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes)
T-lymphocytes
Plasma cells
Macrophage foam cells
periodontics-414.explanation: Option C is correct because the established lesion (chronic gingivitis, developing after 14 to 21 days of undisturbed plaque accumulation) is histologically characterized by an inflammatory infiltrate dominated by B-lymphocytes and plasma cells producing immunoglobulins. Option A is incorrect because neutrophils (PMNs) predominate in the initial lesion (2 to 4 days) and in the junctional epithelium and gingival crevicular fluid. Option B is incorrect because T-lymphocytes predominate in the early lesion (4 to 7 days). Option D is incorrect because macrophages act as antigen-presenting cells throughout all lesion stages but do not constitute the dominant cell population.

periodontics-371.question: During a lateral window sinus floor elevation procedure in the maxillary left posterior sextant, a clinician encounters a localized 3 mm perforation in the Schneiderian membrane. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Cover the perforation with a resorbable collagen membrane and proceed with the bone grafting procedure
Perform primary closure of the perforation using 4-0 silk interrupted sutures
Abort the procedure immediately, close the flap, and reschedule after 6 to 9 months of healing
Pack particulate bone graft material directly against the perforation to seal the sinus floor defect
periodontics-371.explanation: Option A is correct because small Schneiderian membrane perforations (< 5 mm) are safely managed by elevating the membrane around the defect to relieve tension, placing a resorbable collagen barrier membrane over the tear, and proceeding with the bone graft. Option B is incorrect because the Schneiderian membrane is extremely thin (0.3 to 0.8 mm) and friable, making suturing contraindicated as the needle and suture material tear the membrane further. Option C is incorrect because aborting the procedure is indicated only for large, unmanageable perforations (> 5 to 10 mm) that cannot be sealed with a barrier. Option D is incorrect because packing particulate bone directly into an unsealed perforation causes graft extrusion into the maxillary sinus, leading to severe foreign-body maxillary sinusitis and graft failure.

periodontics-377.question: Which of the following pharmacotherapeutic agents is most frequently implicated in drug-induced gingival enlargement through the alteration of cellular sodium/calcium influx and downregulation of active collagenase (matrix metalloproteinase-1)?
options: Phenytoin
Lisinopril
Cyclosporine
Amlodipine
periodontics-377.explanation: Option A is correct because phenytoin induces gingival enlargement in approximately 50% of patients by altering fibroblast sodium and calcium influx, decreasing folic acid uptake, and significantly downregulating active collagenase (MMP-1), resulting in dense collagen accumulation. Option B is incorrect because lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) does not cause gingival overgrowth and is instead associated with adverse effects like a dry cough and angioedema. Option C is incorrect because cyclosporine induces gingival enlargement primarily by calcineurin inhibition and upregulation of transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) rather than direct collagenase downregulation. Option D is incorrect because amlodipine causes gingival enlargement via blockade of L-type calcium channels with a substantially lower incidence (approximately 10%).

periodontics-495.question: A 68-year-old patient with severe ischemic heart disease and recent coronary stent placement requires a restorative dental procedure. The clinician seeks to avoid administering a vasoconstrictor while still achieving effective pulpal anesthesia. Which of the following local anesthetic formulations is most appropriate to administer plain because it produces minimal vasodilation compared to other dental amides?
options: 3% Mepivacaine plain
2% Lidocaine plain
4% Articaine plain
0.5% Bupivacaine plain
periodontics-495.explanation: Option A is correct because 3% mepivacaine plain exhibits the weakest vasodilating properties among commonly used dental amide anesthetics, allowing it to provide reliable pulpal anesthesia (20 to 40 minutes) without a vasoconstrictor like epinephrine. In contrast, plain formulations of lidocaine, articaine, and bupivacaine are moderate-to-potent vasodilators that are rapidly absorbed into the systemic circulation, resulting in inadequate pulpal anesthesia, shorter duration, and increased systemic toxicity risk.

periodontics-498.question: A 45-year-old systemically healthy nonsmoker presents for a comprehensive periodontal evaluation. Clinical examination reveals generalized probing depths of 4 to 5 mm with bleeding on probing and 3 to 4 mm of clinical attachment loss across 35% of sites. Full-mouth periapical radiographs demonstrate horizontal bone loss affecting approximately 25% of root length in the coronal third with no missing teeth due to periodontitis. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP World Workshop classification, what is the most accurate periodontal diagnosis?
options: Generalized Stage I, Grade A periodontitis
Generalized Stage II, Grade B periodontitis
Generalized Stage II, Grade C periodontitis
Generalized Stage III, Grade B periodontitis
periodontics-498.explanation: Option B is correct because clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm, probing depths <=5 mm, and horizontal bone loss of 15% to 33% (coronal third) without tooth loss define Stage II periodontitis affecting >30% of teeth (generalized); the bone loss-to-age ratio (25 / 45 = 0.56) falls within the 0.25 to 1.0 range, establishing Grade B in a nonsmoking, nondiabetic patient. Stage I is incorrect because it involves CAL of 1 to 2 mm and <15% bone loss, Grade C is incorrect because it requires a ratio >1.0 or significant risk factors like heavy smoking or uncontrolled diabetes, and Stage III requires >=5 mm CAL and bone loss extending to the mid-root third.

endodontics-2.question: Which of the following intracanal medicaments exerts its antimicrobial activity primarily through a sustained release of hydroxyl ions that creates a highly alkaline environment (pH approximately 12.5), causing lipid peroxidation of bacterial membranes and protein denaturation?
options: 2% Chlorhexidine gluconate gel
Formocresol
Calcium hydroxide
Triple antibiotic paste
endodontics-2.explanation: Option C is correct because calcium hydroxide dissociates into calcium and hydroxyl ions, generating a high alkaline pH of approximately 12.5 that damages bacterial cell membranes, denatures structural proteins, and inactivates essential enzymes. Chlorhexidine exerts antimicrobial action by electrostatic binding to negatively charged bacterial cell walls causing membrane leakage, formocresol acts via aldehyde fixation and protein cross-linking, and triple antibiotic paste relies on specific antibacterial mechanisms of ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and minocycline rather than alkaline pH.

endodontics-78.question: During endodontic access cavity preparation on a permanent mandibular first molar (tooth #30), the clinician seeks to unroof the pulp chamber while conserving tooth structure. Which geometric outline form is classically recommended to accommodate the widely spaced mesiobuccal and mesiolingual canal orifices and the distal canal anatomy?
options: Rectangular, with equal buccolingual widths at both mesial and distal margins
Triangular, with the base positioned along the distal marginal ridge and apex pointing mesially
Oval, centered along the central groove between the cusps
Trapezoidal (or rhomboidal), with the broad base oriented toward the mesial
endodontics-78.explanation: Option D is correct because the classic access outline form for a mandibular first molar is trapezoidal (or rhomboidal) with the broad base oriented toward the mesial to accommodate the widely spaced mesiobuccal and mesiolingual canal orifices and the narrower base oriented toward the distal canal(s). A rectangular outline overprepares distal coronal dentin, an inverted triangle (base distal) fails to expose the mesial orifices while removing excess distal structure, and an oval outline is characteristic of premolars or incisors and fails to encompass multi-canal molar anatomy.

endodontics-82.question: During endodontic evaluation of a two-rooted premolar, initial orthogonal periapical radiographs show superimposed canals in the buccolingual plane. Which of the following radiographic principles or techniques is most appropriate to separate the superimposed canals and identify their spatial orientation?
options: Clark's tube-shift technique applying the SLOB (Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal) rule
Standard bisecting-angle projection taken without tube angulation change
Cone-beam computed tomography acquired with maximum slice thickness
Standard bitewing radiography with zero-degree vertical angulation
endodontics-82.explanation: Option A is correct because Clark's tube-shift technique utilizes the SLOB rule (Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal) by altering horizontal or vertical x-ray beam angulation, causing the lingual object to move in the same direction as the tube shift and the buccal object to move in the opposite direction, thereby separating superimposed canals. The standard bisecting-angle and bitewing projections without horizontal tube shift project buccolingual structures directly on top of each other, while CBCT with maximum slice thickness degrades spatial resolution and volume averaging, obscuring fine endodontic anatomy.

endodontics-95.question: A 25-year-old patient presents with a history of anterior facial trauma sustained 2 years ago. Tooth #8 responds negatively to cold and electric pulp testing, demonstrates normal mobility, and exhibits normal probing depths of 2 to 3 mm. Periapical radiography reveals a well-circumscribed 4-mm radiolucency surrounding the root apex of tooth #8. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Surgical extraction followed by immediate dental implant placement
Nonsurgical root canal treatment
Vital pulp therapy using a full coronal pulpotomy
Clinical and radiographic observation with a 6-month recall
endodontics-95.explanation: Option B is correct because tooth #8 is diagnosed with pulp necrosis (negative response to thermal and electric pulp testing) and asymptomatic apical periodontitis (apical radiolucency), for which conventional nonsurgical root canal treatment is the gold standard initial therapy to disinfect the root canal system and promote periapical healing. Surgical extraction and implant placement are unnecessarily aggressive for a restorable tooth with a high endodontic success rate, vital pulp therapy is contraindicated in nonvital necrotic teeth, and observation allows the periapical infection to expand.

endodontics-53.question: During coronal flaring and endodontic access preparation on a permanent maxillary first premolar (tooth #5), which anatomical feature represents the most critical consideration to avoid an iatrogenic strip perforation?
options: A prominent developmental groove on the buccal surface of the buccal root
A shallow depression restricted exclusively to the lingual aspect of the lingual root
A pronounced developmental concavity on the mesial surface of the crown and root
A divergent apical third of the distobuccal root canal
endodontics-53.explanation: Option C is correct because the maxillary first premolar (tooth #5 or #12) characteristically exhibits a deep developmental concavity on its mesial surface extending from the crown onto the root trunk, which significantly thins the mesial dentin and creates a high risk of mesial strip perforation during coronal flaring. The buccal and lingual root surfaces possess greater dentin thickness and lack this deep anatomical groove, and maxillary first premolars typically have two roots (buccal and lingual) rather than a distobuccal root.

endodontics-62.question: A 42-year-old patient presents with severe, lingering pain to cold on tooth #30. Diagnostic testing confirms symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues. During cleaning and shaping of the mesiolingual canal, a nickel-titanium rotary file separates in the apical third after thorough irrigation. The separated fragment cannot be bypassed or safely retrieved without risking perforation. What is the most appropriate management strategy?
options: Perform an immediate apical surgery (apicoectomy) and retrofill
Schedule the tooth for intentional replantation within 24 hours
Extract the tooth immediately due to an untreatable endodontic prognosis
Clean, shape, and obturate the canal to the level of the fragment, followed by periodic radiographic monitoring
endodontics-62.explanation: Option D is correct because in a tooth with vital pulp tissue (symptomatic irreversible pulpitis) and normal apical tissues, the canal space apical to the separated instrument is largely uninfected; cleaning, shaping, and obturating to the level of the fragment followed by clinical and radiographic monitoring yields a success rate exceeding 90%. Immediate apical surgery or intentional replantation is overly aggressive, invasive, and unnecessary in the absence of persistent periapical pathology, while extraction is unjustified because the tooth has an excellent long-term prognosis.

endodontics-65.question: During endodontic access and canal negotiation of a permanent mandibular central incisor (tooth #24), a clinician attempts to locate a suspected second (lingual) canal but causes an iatrogenic strip perforation. Which anatomical feature of mandibular incisors predisposes to this procedural error?
options: Pronounced mesiodistal root compression with developmental depressions on the mesial and distal root surfaces
Pronounced faciolingual root compression with excessively wide mesiodistal dimensions
Consistent C-shaped canal configurations with a single fused canal system
Widely divergent apical root bifurcations with distinct facial and lingual root trunks
endodontics-65.explanation: Option A is correct because mandibular incisor roots are broad faciolingually but severely compressed (flattened) mesiodistally with prominent developmental concavities on both the mesial and distal surfaces, resulting in thin proximal dentin that is highly vulnerable to strip perforation during canal scouting and shaping. Faciolingual compression is anatomically false because mandibular incisors are wide faciolingually, C-shaped anatomy is typical of mandibular second molars rather than incisors, and mandibular incisors are single-rooted teeth with internal branching rather than divergent multi-rooted anatomy.

endodontics-96.question: A clinician is performing an endodontic access cavity preparation on a permanent mandibular first molar (tooth #19) that contains two mesial canals and two distal canals. Which of the following coronal access outline forms correctly mirrors the internal pulp chamber morphology?
options: Rectangular outline with parallel mesial and distal borders extending equally from buccal to lingual
Trapezoidal outline with the broader base oriented toward the mesial
