Class II, Modification 1
Class IV, Modification 2
prosthodontics-implants-175.explanation: Option A is correct because both edentulous areas (missing tooth #4 bounded by #3 and #5; missing teeth #12 and #13 bounded by #11 and #14) are tooth-supported bounded spaces with posterior abutments remaining, designating a Kennedy Class III, with the additional space serving as Modification 1. Option B is incorrect because Class I designates bilateral distal extension spaces with no remaining posterior abutments. Options C and D are incorrect because Class II requires a unilateral distal extension, and Class IV represents a single anterior space crossing the midline which, by Applegate's rules, can have no modification spaces.

prosthodontics-implants-180.question: During occlusal equilibration in centric relation for a dentate patient, a premature contact is identified between the maxillary lingual cusp tip and the opposing mandibular central fossa. In eccentric excursive movements, this cusp tip exhibits harmonious disclusion without any interferences. According to the principles of occlusal adjustment, which procedure is most appropriate?
options: Reduce the height of the maxillary lingual cusp tip
Reduce the inner inclines of the maxillary lingual cusp
Deepen the opposing mandibular central fossa
Reduce the opposing mandibular buccal cusp tip
prosthodontics-implants-180.explanation: Option C is correct because the maxillary lingual cusp is a primary centric holding (stamp) cusp maintaining the vertical dimension of occlusion; when a premature contact occurs exclusively in centric relation without excursive interference, the opposing fossa must be deepened to preserve cusp height. Option A is incorrect because reducing the stamp cusp tip would cause loss of vertical dimension and eliminate centric contact once the tooth moves into excursive positions. Options B and D are incorrect because adjusting inclines or unaffected opposing cusps introduces lateral instability and fails to eliminate the vertical centric prematurity.

prosthodontics-implants-137.question: A 68-year-old patient reports unilateral clicking and tenderness in the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) during mastication two weeks after receiving new complete dentures. Evaluation reveals a lateral slide of the mandible upon initial tooth contact as the patient closes into maximum intercuspation. Which occlusal discrepancy is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
options: Deflective premature occlusal contact in centric relation
Excessive vertical dimension of occlusion
Insufficient horizontal overlap of the posterior teeth
Faulty placement of the posterior palatal seal
prosthodontics-implants-137.explanation: Option A is correct because a deflective premature contact in centric relation forces the mandible to deviate or slide into maximum intercuspation, causing abnormal condylar displacement within the glenoid fossa and resulting in TMJ clicking and muscular discomfort. Option B is incorrect because excessive vertical dimension of occlusion typically presents with generalized masticatory muscle fatigue, generalized ridge soreness, and teeth clicking during speech rather than a deflective lateral slide. Options C and D are incorrect because insufficient posterior horizontal overlap causes cheek biting, and a faulty posterior palatal seal leads to poor retention or gagging.

prosthodontics-implants-145.question: A 68-year-old patient presents with a mandibular complete denture that fractured down the midline during mastication. The denture was fabricated five years ago and has never been relined. Which of the following is the most common underlying cause of this midline fracture?
options: Inadequate acrylic thickness along the anterior labial flange
Residual alveolar ridge resorption creating a midline fulcrum and flexural fatigue
Excessive polymerization shrinkage during laboratory heat-curing
Accidental high-impact trauma from dropping the prosthesis
prosthodontics-implants-145.explanation: Option B is correct because progressive residual alveolar ridge resorption leads to loss of bilateral ridge support, converting the midline of the denture into an unyielding fulcrum that experiences cyclic bending and flexural fatigue failure during normal chewing. Option A is incorrect because while thin acrylic weakens a base, gradual flexural fatigue over years of ridge atrophy is the primary clinical etiology. Options C and D are incorrect because polymerization shrinkage causes initial fit inaccuracy rather than delayed fracture after years of use, and impact trauma is an acute extrinsic event rather than a functional masticatory fracture.

prosthodontics-implants-150.question: A 55-year-old edentulous patient requests a non-removable prosthesis to rehabilitate the maxillary arch. Significant residual ridge resorption has occurred, requiring prosthetic replacement of both dental units and deficient alveolar volume to restore facial lip support. Which implant-supported prosthesis design is most appropriate?
options: Screw-retained fixed complete-arch metal-acrylic prosthesis (hybrid prosthesis)
Cement-retained full-arch metal-ceramic fixed partial denture without pink porcelain
Implant-supported resilient stud-retained (Locator) removable overdenture
Implant-supported cast bar-retained removable overdenture
prosthodontics-implants-150.explanation: Option A is correct because a screw-retained fixed complete-arch metal-acrylic (hybrid) prosthesis provides a rigid, non-removable solution that easily replaces large amounts of resorbed alveolar tissue with an acrylic flange, while offering clinical retrievability and eliminating the risk of subgingival cement entrapment. Option B is incorrect because a conventional cement-retained metal-ceramic fixed bridge requires minimal bone loss; severe resorption would necessitate unhygienic, elongated pontics and risk cement-induced peri-implantitis. Options C and D are incorrect because Locator- and bar-retained overdentures are removable prostheses, directly failing the patient's demand for a non-removable restoration.

prosthodontics-implants-220.question: A 55-year-old male requires a mandibular Kennedy Class I removable partial denture. The terminal abutment teeth are #21 and #28, with bilateral distal extension bases replacing missing teeth #18-#20 and #29-#31. Which of the following rest locations functions as the most effective indirect retainer to resist dislodgement of the denture bases away from the residual ridge?
options: Distal rest on tooth #21
Mesial rest on tooth #28
Cingulum rest on tooth #22
Incisal rest on tooth #25
prosthodontics-implants-220.explanation: Option C is correct because an indirect retainer must be located perpendicular and as far anterior to the primary fulcrum line (which connects rests on terminal abutments #21 and #28) as possible, and the canine (#22) has favorable root surface area and crown anatomy for a supportive cingulum rest. Options A and B are incorrect because rests located on terminal abutments #21 and #28 form the axis of rotation itself and function as direct retainer components rather than indirect retainers. Option D is incorrect because the mandibular central incisor (#25) has a small, tapered root, thin enamel, and poor resistance to lateral forces compared to the canine.

prosthodontics-implants-221.question: A 38-year-old patient requires a full-coverage crown on tooth #14. The tooth is vital, and a monolithic lithium disilicate crown is planned. What is the recommended minimum axial wall reduction required to ensure adequate material strength and esthetic shade reproduction?
prosthodontics-implants-221.explanation: Option B is correct because lithium disilicate crowns require a minimum axial wall reduction of 1.0 to 1.2 mm with a rounded shoulder or deep chamfer finish line to provide adequate structural bulk for fracture resistance and accurate optical color expression. Option A is incorrect because an axial reduction of 0.4 to 0.7 mm provides insufficient thickness for glass-ceramics and is appropriate only for cast gold or monolithic zirconia. Options C and D are incorrect because axial reductions of 2.0 mm or greater are overly aggressive, unnecessarily sacrificing sound tooth structure, compromising retention form, and risking pulpal exposure.

prosthodontics-implants-230.question: A dentist is preparing teeth #13 and #15 to serve as abutments for a 3-unit fixed partial denture replacing missing tooth #14. Abutment tooth #15 is vital with average clinical crown height. Which tooth preparation principle is most critical to ensure adequate retention and resistance form for the fixed restoration?
options: Preparing axial walls with a total occlusal convergence of 6 to 10 degrees
Placing all finish lines supragingivally regardless of margin location
Reducing occlusal cusps by at least 3.0 mm across all planes
Establishing a knife-edge margin circumferentially on all axial surfaces
prosthodontics-implants-230.explanation: Option A is correct because achieving nearly parallel axial walls with an ideal total occlusal convergence of 6 to 10 degrees is the primary determinant of retention and resistance form in fixed prosthodontics, preventing dislodgement under functional shear and tensile forces. Option B is incorrect because although supragingival margins promote periodontal health, finish line position does not dictate retention or resistance form. Options C and D are incorrect because a 3.0 mm occlusal reduction is excessive and endangers the dental pulp, while knife-edge margins provide indistinct finish lines and inadequate bulk for porcelain or restorative material durability.

prosthodontics-implants-234.question: A 48-year-old patient requires a crown on an endodontically treated maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). The tooth has 2 mm of circumferential sound tooth structure coronal to the preparation finish line (adequate ferrule). Esthetics is paramount. Which post-and-core and crown material combination is most appropriate to optimize esthetics and distribute functional stress?
options: Prefabricated stainless steel post, composite resin core, and lithium disilicate crown
Fiber-reinforced resin post, composite resin core, and lithium disilicate crown
Custom cast gold post-and-core and porcelain-fused-to-metal crown
Prefabricated titanium post, amalgam core, and monolithic zirconia crown
prosthodontics-implants-234.explanation: Option B is correct because a translucent fiber-reinforced resin post bonded with a composite resin core prevents dark metallic shadowing under a translucent lithium disilicate crown, while possessing a modulus of elasticity similar to dentin that reduces the risk of root fracture. Option A is incorrect because a stainless steel post creates an unsightly gray shadow through the all-ceramic crown and thin root dentin. Options C and D are incorrect because cast metal and titanium posts have a significantly higher elastic modulus that concentrates stresses at the root apex, and their opaque metallic substructures compromise anterior esthetics.

prosthodontics-implants-200.question: A 70-year-old edentulous patient presents with a severely resorbed anterior maxillary alveolar ridge characterized by mobile, flabby (hyperplastic) tissue. Which impression technique is most appropriate for recording this flabby tissue during the master impression to prevent denture instability?
options: Mucocompressive technique using an unrelieved custom tray and heavy-body polyether
Closed-mouth functional impression using an unbordered stock tray with irreversible hydrocolloid
Minimal-pressure (mucostatic) technique using a relieved custom tray and light-body elastomeric material
High-pressure functional reline technique using modeling compound over the mobile tissue
prosthodontics-implants-200.explanation: Option C is correct because mobile, flabby hyperplastic tissue must be recorded in its undistorted, resting anatomical contour using a minimal-pressure (mucostatic) technique—such as a custom tray with extensive relief or a window technique with light-body material—to avoid tissue displacement that would cause denture dislodgement upon elastic rebound. Options A and D are incorrect because high-pressure or mucocompressive techniques displace the mobile tissue during the impression, causing constant instability and soreness when the denture is seated at rest. Option B is incorrect because an unbordered stock tray with irreversible hydrocolloid cannot record border extensions accurately and distorts mobile tissues.

prosthodontics-implants-201.question: For a mandibular Kennedy Class I removable partial denture where the terminal abutment tooth (#20) presents with a short clinical crown and a severe mesial tilt, which direct retainer design is most advantageous to minimize destructive tipping forces on the abutment?
options: I-bar clasp as part of an RPI (rest, proximal plate, I-bar) system
Conventional circumferential (Akers) clasp engaging a mesiobuccal undercut with a distal rest
Reverse circumferential (reverse circlet) clasp engaging a distobuccal undercut with a mesial rest
Ring clasp engaging a distolingual undercut with mesial and distal rests
prosthodontics-implants-201.explanation: Option C is correct because severe mesial tilt and a short clinical crown contraindicate an infrabulge I-bar clasp due to lack of vertical vestibular clearance and unfavorable soft tissue contours; a reverse circumferential clasp with a mesial rest provides suprabulge retention while releasing stress under functional load to protect the abutment. Option A is incorrect because an I-bar requires at least 3 to 4 mm of vestibular depth and a mid-facial undercut without severe tissue undercuts. Option B is incorrect because a conventional Akers clasp with a distal rest acts as a destructive Class I lever arm that torques the abutment distally under occlusal loading. Option D is incorrect because a ring clasp is indicated for tipped solitary mandibular molars, not premolars in distal extension cases.

prosthodontics-implants-391.question: According to CDC infection control guidelines for dental healthcare settings, which of the following is the MOST appropriate sterilization method for heat-sensitive critical instruments?
options: Steam autoclave sterilization
Unsaturated chemical vapor sterilization
Dry heat oven sterilization
Ethylene oxide gas sterilization
prosthodontics-implants-391.explanation: Option D is correct because according to CDC infection control guidelines, critical items that penetrate vascular tissue or bone must be sterilized, and heat-sensitive items require low-temperature sterilization methods such as ethylene oxide gas or hydrogen peroxide gas plasma. Options A, B, and C are incorrect because steam autoclaving (121°C), chemical vapor (132°C), and dry heat (160°C–170°C) all rely on elevated temperatures that will damage or melt heat-sensitive materials.

prosthodontics-implants-405.question: A 9-year-old female presents with a chief complaint from her parents about her front tooth biting behind the lower teeth. Clinical examination reveals an isolated anterior dental crossbite involving the permanent maxillary left central incisor (tooth #9) with adequate arch space and no skeletal discrepancy. What is the MOST appropriate initial orthodontic intervention?
options: Observation without active treatment until all permanent teeth have erupted
Comprehensive full fixed orthodontic appliance therapy across both dental arches
Fabrication of a removable appliance with a finger spring to proclinate tooth #9
Referral for surgical Le Fort I osteotomy to advance the maxilla
prosthodontics-implants-405.explanation: Option C is correct because an isolated dental anterior crossbite involving tooth #9 in the mixed dentition is best addressed interceptively with a removable Hawley-type appliance incorporating a finger spring (or a simple 2x4 fixed appliance) to proclinate the incisor and prevent labial gingival stripping or incisal attrition of the mandibular incisor. Option A is incorrect because anterior crossbites should be corrected interceptively as soon as detected rather than monitored. Options B and D are incorrect because comprehensive full fixed orthodontics and orthognathic surgery are excessively invasive for a localized dental malocclusion without skeletal discrepancy.

prosthodontics-implants-379.question: A 12-year-old male presents to the dental clinic following a bicycle accident with a fractured permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). His medical history is non-contributory. Clinical examination reveals a horizontal fracture involving enamel and dentin without pulpal exposure. The tooth tests vital to cold, is non-mobile, and is not tender to percussion. Radiographs confirm an uncomplicated crown fracture with no root fracture or periapical pathology. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide
Composite resin restoration and regular pulpal vitality monitoring
Full-coverage porcelain-fused-to-metal crown preparation
Complete pulpectomy followed by conventional root canal therapy
prosthodontics-implants-379.explanation: Option B is correct because an uncomplicated crown fracture involving enamel and dentin without pulp exposure on a vital permanent tooth (tooth #8) requires conservative restoration with composite resin (or fragment reattachment) and periodic clinical and radiographic vitality monitoring. Option A is incorrect because direct pulp capping is indicated only when there is mechanical or traumatic exposure of the pulp. Options C and D are incorrect because full-coverage crowns and pulpectomies are overly aggressive and contraindicated for an uncomplicated crown fracture with a healthy, vital pulp.

prosthodontics-implants-386.question: A 5-year-old female presents for a routine pediatric dental examination. Her medical history is non-contributory, and she is clinically caries-free but deemed to be at moderate risk for dental caries. She resides in an area where the community water fluoridation status is unknown. According to American Dental Association (ADA) and American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) guidelines, which of the following is the MOST appropriate caries prevention recommendation?
options: Prescribe daily systemic dietary fluoride supplements immediately
Apply 5% sodium fluoride varnish every 6 months
Recommend daily use of an over-the-counter fluoride mouth rinse
Instruct parents to brush twice daily with a non-fluoridated dentifrice
prosthodontics-implants-386.explanation: Option B is correct because ADA and AAPD guidelines recommend professionally applied 5% sodium fluoride (NaF) varnish every 3 to 6 months as an evidence-based topical preventive regimen for children at risk for dental caries. Option A is incorrect because systemic fluoride supplements must never be prescribed without first analyzing the community drinking water fluoride concentration to avoid dental fluorosis. Options C and D are incorrect because fluoride mouth rinses are contraindicated in children younger than 6 years due to risk of ingestion, and brushing with fluoridated toothpaste (pea-sized amount for ages 3–6) is strongly recommended.

prosthodontics-implants-389.question: A 50-year-old female presents with persistent, dull aching pain in the maxillary left posterior quadrant several weeks after completed endodontic treatment on tooth #14. The medical history is unremarkable. Clinical examination reveals the tooth is asymptomatic to percussion and palpation with normal gingival margins; however, periodontal probing reveals an isolated, narrow 8 mm probing depth along the mesiobuccal root with bleeding on probing. Adjacent teeth show normal probing depths of 2 to 3 mm. Periapical radiographs show a well-obturated canal and a subtle radiolucent halo along the lateral root surface. What is the MOST likely cause of her symptoms?
options: Persistent apical periodontitis
Vertical root fracture
Generalized stage III periodontitis
Acute maxillary sinusitis
prosthodontics-implants-389.explanation: Option B is correct because an isolated, narrow, deep periodontal pocket on an endodontically treated tooth (tooth #14), accompanied by dull discomfort and a lateral 'halo' radiolucency, is pathognomonic for a vertical root fracture. Option A is incorrect because persistent apical periodontitis typically presents with marked tenderness to percussion and an apical rather than an isolated lateral probing defect. Options C and D are incorrect because generalized periodontitis exhibits widespread bone loss and multiple pockets across the dentition, while acute maxillary sinusitis presents with generalized quadrant pain and nasal congestion without an isolated deep probing defect.

prosthodontics-implants-390.question: A 30-year-old pregnant female in her second trimester presents with a chief complaint of a rapidly growing, soft, red, pedunculated gingival mass on the facial aspect of the maxillary anterior gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily during toothbrushing, but does not interfere with mastication or speech. Her medical history indicates an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for this lesion?
options: Prescribe a 7-day course of systemic amoxicillin to resolve the lesion
Perform an immediate excisional biopsy down to periosteum
Provide conservative periodontal debridement and defer surgical excision until postpartum
Apply high-potency topical corticosteroids twice daily to reduce vascularity
prosthodontics-implants-390.explanation: Option C is correct because according to Neville, pregnancy pyogenic granulomas (granuloma gravidarum) without severe functional impairment or uncontrollable hemorrhage should be managed with meticulous oral hygiene and scaling, deferring surgical excision until postpartum due to a high recurrence rate during pregnancy and frequent spontaneous postpartum regression. Option B is incorrect because surgical excision during pregnancy carries a high recurrence rate under persistent hormonal stimulation. Options A and D are incorrect because pyogenic granulomas are benign reactive vascular hyperplasias that do not respond to systemic antibiotics, and potent topical corticosteroids are ineffective and contraindicated during pregnancy.

prosthodontics-implants-411.question: A 35-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of a 'gummy smile.' Clinical examination reveals 4 mm of excessive gingival display upon smiling, short clinical crowns on the maxillary anterior teeth (teeth #6 through #11), normal probing depths, and an adequate band of attached gingiva. Radiographic and sounding evaluations confirm that the alveolar crest is located 3 mm apical to the cementoenamel junction (CEJ), and the excessive gingival display is due entirely to gingival hyperplasia. What is the MOST appropriate initial surgical management?
options: Esthetic crown lengthening with osseous recontouring
Gingivectomy without osseous recontouring
Orthodontic extrusion of the maxillary anterior teeth
Maxillary orthognathic surgery via Le Fort I impaction
prosthodontics-implants-411.explanation: Option B is correct because when excessive gingival display is caused solely by gingival hyperplasia with short clinical crowns (teeth #6 through #11) and the alveolar crest is located normally at least 3 mm apical to the CEJ, gingivectomy without osseous resection successfully exposes the anatomic crown without violating the supracrestal tissue attachment (biologic width). Option A is incorrect because osseous recontouring is unnecessary and contraindicated when adequate biologic width space already exists between the CEJ and crestal bone. Options C and D are incorrect because orthodontic extrusion moves the gingival margin further coronally, worsening gingival display, and Le Fort I osteotomy is reserved for vertical maxillary excess rather than soft tissue hyperplasia.

prosthodontics-implants-414.question: A 45-year-old female presents with bleeding gums and persistent bad breath for several months. Her medical history is significant for well-controlled Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Clinical examination reveals generalized gingival erythema and bleeding on probing across 45% of sites, probing depths ranging from 4 to 6 mm, and Class II furcation involvement on tooth #19. Radiographs demonstrate generalized horizontal bone loss of 30% to 40% (extending into the middle third of the root). According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification system, what is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis?
options: Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade B
Generalized periodontitis, Stage I, Grade A
Generalized periodontitis, Stage II, Grade B
Localized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C
prosthodontics-implants-414.explanation: Option A is correct because according to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, generalized involvement (>30% of teeth affected), radiographic bone loss of 30% to 40% (extending into the middle third of the root), probing depths ≥6 mm, and furcation involvement classify this case as Stage III; well-controlled diabetes mellitus and a bone loss/age ratio between 0.25 and 1.0 designate Grade B. Options B and C are incorrect because Stage I and Stage II periodontitis are limited to coronal third bone loss (<33%), probing depths ≤5 mm, and no furcation involvement. Option D is incorrect because the disease involves over 30% of teeth (generalized, not localized), and well-controlled diabetes without rapid progression aligns with Grade B rather than Grade C.

prosthodontics-implants-436.question: A 9-year-old male presents to the clinic 1 hour after a fall with a crown fracture on his permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). Clinical examination reveals enamel and dentin loss with a vital, pinpoint (less than 1 mm) pulpal exposure. Radiographs confirm an immature root with an open apex and no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management to promote apexogenesis?
options: Complete pulpectomy followed by immediate gutta-percha obturation
Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide or MTA and composite resin restoration
Apexification protocol with long-term calcium hydroxide paste changes
Surgical extraction of the tooth followed by space maintenance
prosthodontics-implants-436.explanation: Option B is correct because in an immature, vital permanent tooth (tooth #8) with an open apex and a recent pinpoint traumatic pulp exposure, conservative vital pulp therapy such as direct pulp capping (or partial pulpotomy) with calcium hydroxide or MTA preserves radicular pulp vitality, allowing continued physiological root development and apical closure (apexogenesis). Option A is incorrect because complete pulpectomy halts root formation and gutta-percha cannot be condensed against an open apex. Options C and D are incorrect because apexification is indicated only for non-vital teeth with open apices, and extraction is overly aggressive for a restorable, vital tooth.

prosthodontics-implants-439.question: A 2-year-old female presents for her first dental examination. Her parents report that she routinely falls asleep with a nursing bottle filled with cow's milk. Clinical examination reveals extensive cervical demineralization and cavitation across the primary maxillary incisors (teeth #D, #E, #F, and #G). According to American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) guidelines for early childhood caries (ECC), which of the following is the MOST crucial dietary and behavioral counseling recommendation?
options: Instruct parents to use non-fluoridated toothpaste to prevent fluorosis
Advise against putting the child to bed with a bottle containing milk, formula, or juice
Recommend substituting bedtime milk with diluted 100% natural fruit juice
Advise deferring toothbrushing until all primary molars have fully erupted
prosthodontics-implants-439.explanation: Option B is correct because AAPD guidelines emphasize that nocturnal bottle feeding with liquids containing fermentable carbohydrates (such as milk, formula, or juice) pooling against maxillary anterior teeth is the primary behavioral driver of early childhood caries; eliminating bedtime bottles or offering only plain water is essential. Option A is incorrect because the AAPD and ADA recommend brushing twice daily with a smear (rice-sized amount) of fluoridated toothpaste for children under age 3. Options C and D are incorrect because fruit juice contains simple sugars that exacerbate caries, and toothbrushing should commence immediately upon the eruption of the child's first primary tooth.

prosthodontics-implants-440.question: A 10-year-old male presents to the clinic 30 minutes following an accidental fall resulting in the complete avulsion of his permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). The tooth was retrieved from the ground and transported in a cup of cold milk. Clinical examination shows an intact alveolar socket with no alveolar bone fracture. What is the MOST critical immediate step in managing this avulsed tooth?
options: Scrape the root surface with a curette and sterilize it in chlorhexidine
Administer oral antibiotics and defer replantation until an oral surgeon evaluates the patient
Gently rinse the root surface with saline and immediately replant the tooth into the socket
Perform extraoral endodontic treatment and gutta-percha obturation prior to replantation
prosthodontics-implants-440.explanation: Option C is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) and AAE guidelines, an avulsed permanent tooth with an extraoral dry time under 60 minutes transported in milk should have its root gently rinsed with saline to eliminate debris and be replanted immediately to maximize periodontal ligament (PDL) cell viability. Option A is incorrect because scraping or chemically sterilizing the root destroys viable PDL cells and induces progressive external root resorption or ankylosis. Options B and D are incorrect because delaying replantation or performing extraoral endodontics increases extraoral dry time, worsening the long-term prognosis; root canal therapy should instead be initiated 7 to 14 days after replantation.

prosthodontics-implants-450.question: A 12-year-old female presents to the dental clinic after a bicycle accident with a complicated crown fracture of her permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). Clinical examination reveals a 1 mm pinpoint traumatic pulp exposure that occurred 3 hours prior. The tooth responds positively to cold testing, is non-mobile, and radiographs confirm a closed apex without root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide followed by composite resin restoration
Partial (Cvek) pulpotomy with mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) followed by a coronal seal
Complete pulpectomy followed by immediate gutta-percha obturation
Surgical extraction of the tooth followed by provisional partial denture fabrication
prosthodontics-implants-450.explanation: Option B is correct because according to AAE and IADT guidelines, a partial (Cvek) pulpotomy—involving the excision of 1 to 2 mm of superficial, inflamed, and potentially contaminated pulp tissue followed by MTA placement and a bacteria-tight seal—demonstrates significantly higher success rates than direct pulp capping for traumatic exposures. Option A is incorrect because direct pulp capping leaves superficial inflamed and contused pulp tissue under the cap, resulting in higher failure rates. Options C and D are incorrect because complete pulpectomy and extraction are overly aggressive for a restorable permanent incisor (tooth #8) with a vital, salvageable pulp.

prosthodontics-implants-508.question: A 30-year-old female patient, who is 6 months pregnant, presents with localized gingival swelling, redness, and bleeding between teeth #12 and #13 (maxillary left premolars). The lesion is soft, pedunculated, and bleeds easily on palpation. She reports it has grown rapidly over the past month. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma
Pyogenic granuloma (pregnancy tumor)
Peripheral ossifying fibroma
Irritation fibroma
prosthodontics-implants-508.explanation: Option B is correct because a rapidly growing, soft, pedunculated, highly vascular gingival mass that bleeds easily in a pregnant patient is characteristic of a pyogenic granuloma (pregnancy tumor), exacerbated by heightened estrogen and progesterone levels. Options A, C, and D are incorrect because squamous cell carcinoma presents as an indurated, ulcerated lesion with rolled borders rather than an acute vascular proliferation, peripheral ossifying fibroma is a firm, pale, cellular growth containing mineralized bone or cementum-like material, and irritation fibroma is a dense, fibrous mass with low vascularity that does not bleed profusely.

prosthodontics-implants-513.question: A 14-year-old male patient presents for an orthodontic consultation. Clinical examination reveals that the mesiobuccal cusp of his maxillary first molar occludes distal to the buccal groove of his mandibular first molar. He also exhibits an anterior crossbite involving tooth #9 (maxillary left central incisor). What is the Angle classification of his molar relationship?
options: Class I malocclusion
Class II malocclusion
Class III malocclusion
Class II division 1 malocclusion
prosthodontics-implants-513.explanation: Option C is correct because Angle Class III malocclusion is defined by the mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first permanent molar occluding distal to the buccal groove of the mandibular first permanent molar, which frequently presents with an anterior crossbite. Options A, B, and D are incorrect because Class I features the mesiobuccal cusp occluding directly within the buccal groove, while Class II and Class II division 1 feature the mesiobuccal cusp occluding mesial to the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar.

prosthodontics-implants-515.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents to your dental office after falling on concrete, striking his anterior teeth. Clinically, tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor) exhibits a crown fracture involving enamel and dentin without pulpal exposure. The tooth is firm, and percussion is negative. Radiographically, the root appears intact with a wide-open apex. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for tooth #8?
options: Restore the tooth with glass ionomer cement or composite resin
Perform a complete pulpectomy and obturate with calcium hydroxide
Perform a partial pulpotomy with mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA)
Extract the tooth due to the traumatic injury
prosthodontics-implants-515.explanation: Option A is correct because an uncomplicated crown fracture involves enamel and dentin without pulpal exposure; immediate sealing of the exposed dentin with glass ionomer or composite resin protects the pulp-dentin complex from bacteria and thermal insults, preserving vitality and enabling continued apexogenesis. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because complete pulpectomy, pulpotomy, and extraction are overly invasive and contraindicated when the dental pulp remains unexposed, vital, and asymptomatic.

prosthodontics-implants-519.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of spontaneous, severe, lingering pain in the maxillary left posterior region, exacerbated by hot stimuli and relieved by cold. Medical history is non-contributory. Clinical examination reveals a deep carious lesion on tooth #14 (maxillary left first molar). Cold and electric pulp testing elicit severe, prolonged pain. Percussion and palpation are negative. Radiographs show deep caries approaching the pulp but no periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate pulpal diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis
prosthodontics-implants-519.explanation: Option A is correct because spontaneous, severe, lingering thermal pain that is exacerbated by heat and temporarily alleviated by cold is the classic presentation of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis according to AAE diagnostic standards. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because reversible pulpitis is characterized by quick, non-lingering pain to cold stimuli, pulp necrosis is completely non-responsive to thermal and electric pulp testing, and asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis lacks clinical pain despite deep caries reaching the pulp.

prosthodontics-implants-521.question: A 48-year-old female patient presents with sensitivity to cold and sweet on tooth #5 (maxillary right first premolar). Clinical examination reveals a deep, non-carious cervical lesion (NCCL) on the facial aspect of the tooth. She has a history of aggressive toothbrushing. What is the MOST appropriate restorative material for this NCCL?
options: Dental amalgam
Direct cohesive gold
Glass ionomer cement
Flowable composite resin without a bonding agent
prosthodontics-implants-521.explanation: Option C is correct because glass ionomer cement chemically adheres to both enamel and dentin without mechanical undercuts, releases fluoride, and has a low modulus of elasticity that flexes with the tooth during cervical stress concentration and abfraction. Options A, B, and D are incorrect because amalgam and cohesive gold require destructive mechanical undercuts that unnecessarily remove healthy cervical tooth structure, while flowable composite placed without an adhesive bonding agent has zero retention and fails immediately.

prosthodontics-implants-523.question: A 72-year-old male patient, a long-term complete denture wearer, presents with a chief complaint of recurrent denture looseness, especially during mastication. His existing dentures were fabricated 10 years ago. Clinically, there is significant alveolar ridge resorption in both arches and severe occlusal wear. He has no mucosal pain or oral lesions. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Fabricate new complete dentures
Perform a laboratory hard reline of the existing dentures
Recommend daily use of denture adhesive
Place a temporary soft tissue conditioner
prosthodontics-implants-523.explanation: Option A is correct because complete dentures that are 10 years old in a patient with severe alveolar resorption present with compromised occlusion, excessive tooth wear, and a collapsed vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO), which cannot be corrected by relining and necessitate the fabrication of new complete dentures. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because relining only refits the intaglio surface to basal bone without reestablishing proper VDO or occlusal relationships, denture adhesive is a temporary palliative measure that does not address significant instability, and tissue conditioners are indicated for traumatized or inflamed mucosa rather than uninflamed, resorbed arches.

prosthodontics-implants-530.question: A 38-year-old male patient presents with generalized moderate periodontitis and an acute periodontal abscess localized to tooth #15 (maxillary left second molar). The abscess presents as a painful, fluctuant swelling on the buccal gingiva, with purulent discharge upon probing. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for this acute condition?
options: Prescribe systemic antibiotic therapy alone
Prescribe a 0.12% chlorhexidine mouthrinse and schedule a 2-week recall
Perform emergency root canal therapy on tooth #15
Establish drainage through pocket debridement or incision and debride the root surface
prosthodontics-implants-530.explanation: Option D is correct because standard clinical guidelines mandate that the primary emergency management of an acute periodontal abscess is establishing drainage (via pocket debridement or surgical incision) accompanied by local mechanical debridement of the affected root surface. Options A, B, and C are incorrect because systemic antibiotics are reserved for patients with systemic involvement (fever, lymphadenopathy, or cellulitis) and are never used as monotherapy, chlorhexidine rinses do not penetrate deep subgingival tissues, and endodontic therapy is unnecessary because the pulp remains vital in a primary periodontal abscess.

prosthodontics-implants-533.question: A 45-year-old male patient presents with a fractured cusp on tooth #3 (maxillary right first molar) associated with an existing large amalgam restoration. He reports localized sharp pain when biting pressure is applied to the fractured tooth. Clinically, the fracture extends subgingivally on the buccal aspect. Radiographs confirm the fracture line extends into dentin without pulpal involvement or periapical pathology. What is the MOST appropriate definitive restorative treatment?
options: Direct composite resin restoration
Amalgam repair of the fractured cusp
Full-coverage crown restoration
Endodontic therapy followed by a post and core
prosthodontics-implants-533.explanation: Option C is correct because a fractured cusp extending subgingivally on an extensively restored posterior tooth requires a full-coverage crown to provide a circumferential ferrule, brace remaining cusps against occlusal forces, and prevent catastrophic tooth fracture. Options A and B are incorrect because direct composite or amalgam repairs lack adequate resistance and retention form under heavy posterior occlusal forces, while Option D is incorrect because elective endodontic therapy and post placement are contraindicated in a vital tooth without pulpal or periapical disease.

prosthodontics-implants-536.question: A 68-year-old male patient, with a history of angina managed with sublingual nitroglycerin, is undergoing a root canal procedure. During the procedure, he suddenly complains of substernal chest pain and tightness radiating to his left arm. He appears pale and anxious. His blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg and pulse is 88 bpm. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) and monitor vital signs
Administer supplemental oxygen and immediately activate emergency medical services (EMS)
Place the patient in a supine position with the legs elevated
Administer an oral opioid analgesic and reschedule the appointment
prosthodontics-implants-536.explanation: Option A is correct because Malamed's medical emergency protocols dictate that an anginal attack in a patient with diagnosed stable angina should be immediately managed by stopping the procedure, seating the patient comfortably, administering sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg every 5 minutes up to 3 doses), and monitoring vital signs. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because activating EMS prior to administering prescribed nitroglycerin is premature for known stable angina (EMS is activated if pain persists after 3 doses or 10-15 minutes), placing the patient supine increases venous return and cardiac workload, and oral analgesics are ineffective and dangerously delay coronary vasodilation.

prosthodontics-implants-537.question: A 7-year-old female patient presents to the dental office after falling from a swing. Clinical examination reveals a complicated crown fracture of tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor) with visible pulp exposure. The tooth is vital, slightly mobile, and not displaced. The root apex is wide open on radiographic examination. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for tooth #8?
options: Immediate complete pulpectomy and obturation with gutta-percha
Direct composite resin placement without pulpal capping
Extraction of tooth #8 and placement of a removable space maintainer
Vital pulp therapy (partial pulpotomy or direct pulp cap) using mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA)
prosthodontics-implants-537.explanation: Option D is correct because vital pulp therapy (such as a Cvek partial pulpotomy or direct pulp cap) using MTA or bioceramics is the standard of care for an immature permanent tooth with an open apex to preserve pulp vitality and promote apexogenesis (root completion). Options A, B, and C are incorrect because complete pulpectomy halts root dentin formation and leaves thin, fracture-prone walls, direct resin placement without pulp capping induces chemical irritation and pulp necrosis, and extraction is unnecessarily radical for a restorable permanent incisor.

prosthodontics-implants-540.question: A 55-year-old male patient presents with severe, throbbing pain in the maxillary left posterior region that is spontaneous and exacerbated by lying down. He reports the pain wakes him at night. Clinical examination reveals tooth #14 (maxillary left first molar) has a large, deep restoration, is tender to percussion, and responds severely and lingeringly to cold testing. Radiographs show a deep restoration approximating the pulp and a widened periodontal ligament space around the mesiobuccal root. What is the MOST likely diagnosis for tooth #14?
options: Reversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues
Pulp necrosis with asymptomatic apical periodontitis
Cracked tooth syndrome without pulpal involvement
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis
prosthodontics-implants-540.explanation: Option D is correct because spontaneous, nocturnal, throbbing pain with exaggerated, lingering cold sensitivity defines symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, while localized tenderness to percussion and a widened periodontal ligament establish concurrent symptomatic apical periodontitis according to AAE diagnostic criteria. Options A, B, and C are incorrect because reversible pulpitis produces only transient, non-lingering cold sensitivity without spontaneous nocturnal pain, pulp necrosis results in a non-responsive pulp to cold testing, and cracked tooth syndrome without pulpal involvement produces sharp pain upon masticatory release rather than lingering thermal pain.

prosthodontics-implants-586.question: An 8-year-old male patient presents after the avulsion of tooth #9 (maxillary left central incisor) approximately 45 minutes ago. The tooth was stored in cold milk. Clinical examination shows a clean avulsed tooth. Radiographic examination reveals an open apex on tooth #9 and no alveolar fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management step after re-implantation?
options: Initiate root canal therapy immediately
Place a rigid splint for 4 weeks
Prescribe systemic antibiotics
Perform a surgical pulpotomy
prosthodontics-implants-586.explanation: Option C is correct because AAE and IADT trauma guidelines mandate prescribing systemic antibiotics (such as amoxicillin) following reimplantation of an avulsed tooth to prevent microbial colonization, promote periodontal healing, and decrease the risk of inflammatory root resorption. Options A, B, and D are incorrect because immediate root canal therapy is contraindicated in teeth with open apices where spontaneous pulpal revascularization may occur, splinting must be flexible and maintained for only 2 weeks (rigid splinting for 4 weeks induces ankylosis), and pulpotomy has no role in the immediate post-reimplantation protocol.

prosthodontics-implants-426.question: A 22-year-old male patient presents to your dental office with a severe laceration of his lower lip and avulsion of his mandibular left central incisor (tooth #24) following a sports injury. The patient is alert and oriented. Clinical examination reveals a 3-cm full-thickness laceration extending through the vermilion border of the lower lip with active hemorrhage, and tooth #24 is missing from its socket. What is the MOST immediate clinical priority for this patient?
options: Control active bleeding from the lip laceration
Immediately locate and replant the avulsed tooth
Suture the laceration to reapproximate the vermilion border
Obtain a panoramic radiograph to evaluate for mandibular fracture
prosthodontics-implants-426.explanation: Option A is correct because basic trauma management protocols prioritize airway, breathing, and circulation (hemostasis) before addressing secondary dental injuries. Although replantation of an avulsed permanent tooth is time-sensitive according to IADT guidelines, active hemorrhaging from a full-thickness laceration presents an immediate hemodynamic concern that must be stabilized first. Primary surgical suturing (Option C) and diagnostic radiographic imaging (Option D) are performed only after active bleeding is controlled and the patient is stabilized.

prosthodontics-implants-457.question: A 35-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of lingering pain (lasting more than 30 seconds) after consuming cold beverages on his maxillary left first molar (tooth #14). He denies any spontaneous pain. Clinical examination reveals a deep carious lesion involving the dentin on the occlusal surface of tooth #14, but the tooth is not tender to percussion and there is no mobility or swelling. What is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis?
options: Reversible pulpitis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Normal pulp
prosthodontics-implants-457.explanation: Option B is correct because according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic terminology, lingering pain lasting more than 30 seconds following thermal stimulation indicates that the vital pulp has sustained irreversible inflammatory damage incapable of healing. Reversible pulpitis (Option A) is characterized by a sharp, transient response to thermal stimuli that subsides immediately within seconds upon stimulus removal. Pulp necrosis (Option C) presents with a non-responsive reaction to thermal and electric pulp testing, while a normal pulp (Option D) produces a mild, non-lingering sensory response.

prosthodontics-implants-458.question: An 8-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic after falling off his skateboard, exhibiting an intrusive luxation of his permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth #8). The tooth is significantly displaced into the alveolar bone and clinically appears shorter than the adjacent incisors. Radiographs confirm that tooth #8 has an open apex and incomplete root development without root or alveolar fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Allow for spontaneous re-eruption and monitor pulp vitality
Surgically reposition the tooth and stabilize it with a flexible splint
Extract the tooth to prevent damage to the adjacent developing teeth
Initiate immediate pulpectomy and reposition the tooth
prosthodontics-implants-458.explanation: Option A is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, intruded permanent teeth with open apices (immature roots) exhibit significant eruptive potential and should be allowed to spontaneously re-erupt. Surgical repositioning (Option B) or orthodontic extrusion is reserved for mature closed apices or when spontaneous re-eruption fails within 4 weeks. Extraction (Option C) is contraindicated because spontaneous re-eruption preserves alveolar bone and tooth vitality, while immediate endodontic intervention (Option D) is contraindicated since revascularization is common in immature permanent teeth.

prosthodontics-implants-483.question: A 42-year-old male patient presents to the dental office with swelling on the buccal aspect of his upper right jaw. He experienced mild pain on his maxillary right second molar (tooth #2) a few days prior, which has since subsided. Clinical examination reveals a firm, non-fluctuant swelling in the buccal vestibule adjacent to tooth #2. Tooth #2 is non-responsive to vitality testing and is tender to percussion. Radiographs show a well-defined periapical radiolucency associated with the root apices of tooth #2. What is the MOST appropriate initial treatment for tooth #2?
options: Prescribe systemic antibiotics and NSAIDs without operative intervention
Perform an immediate incision and drainage of the buccal swelling
Initiate endodontic therapy with complete pulpal debridement
Extract the tooth and place an immediate implant
prosthodontics-implants-483.explanation: Option C is correct because the tooth exhibits pulpal necrosis and symptomatic apical periodontitis, which requires elimination of the intracanal microbial source through nonsurgical endodontic debridement. Systemic antibiotics (Option A) are not indicated in immunocompetent patients without systemic signs of infection or spreading cellulitis. Incision and drainage (Option B) is ineffective and contraindicated for indurated, non-fluctuant swelling where no localized purulence exists, and extraction (Option D) is an aggressive, unnecessary procedure for a restorable tooth.

prosthodontics-implants-470.question: A 32-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic with sensitivity to cold and air on his maxillary right first molar (tooth #3). He had a deep amalgam restoration placed on tooth #3 two weeks ago. He reports no spontaneous pain and no discomfort during mastication. Clinical examination reveals an intact, well-contoured amalgam restoration on tooth #3. Pulp vitality tests elicit sharp, transient pain that subsides immediately upon removal of the cold stimulus. Percussion and palpation tests are negative, and periapical radiographs demonstrate close proximity of the restoration to the pulp without periapical pathology. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Apply a desensitizing agent and monitor the tooth
Initiate nonsurgical root canal treatment
Replace the amalgam restoration with a composite restoration
Extract the tooth and plan for an implant-supported crown
prosthodontics-implants-470.explanation: Option A is correct because the clinical findings (transient pain resolving immediately upon stimulus removal) are diagnostic of reversible pulpitis secondary to recent restorative trauma, which is managed conservatively with topical desensitization, occlusion verification, and observation. Nonsurgical root canal treatment (Option B) is contraindicated because the pulp retains its healing capacity and does not demonstrate irreversible inflammation. Replacing the amalgam restoration (Option C) would induce further thermal and chemical trauma to an already irritated pulp, while extraction (Option D) is an inappropriate overtreatment for a reversible condition.

prosthodontics-implants-473.question: A 7-year-old female patient presents to the dental clinic with a toothache in the lower left posterior quadrant. Her parents report that she has experienced persistent discomfort for two days with no history of trauma. Clinical examination reveals tooth L (mandibular left primary first molar) with a large, deep carious lesion extending into the pulp, tenderness to percussion, and slight buccal vestibule swelling. A periapical radiograph reveals furcation and periapical radiolucency associated with tooth L. What is the MOST appropriate definitive management for tooth L?
options: Extraction of the tooth
Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide
Vital pulpotomy with formocresol
Indirect pulp capping with glass ionomer
prosthodontics-implants-473.explanation: Option A is correct because the presence of pulpal necrosis with furcation radiolucency and vestibular swelling in a primary molar contraindicates vital pulp therapies and necessitates tooth extraction (followed by space maintenance assessment) or complete pulpectomy. Direct pulp capping (Option B) is contraindicated in primary teeth due to high rates of internal root resorption and abscess formation. Vital pulpotomy (Option C) and indirect pulp capping (Option D) are strictly indicated only for teeth with reversible pulpitis that maintain vital, uninfected radicular pulp tissue.

prosthodontics-implants-476.question: A 62-year-old male patient presents to the dental office with a loose maxillary central incisor after falling from a ladder 3 days ago. Clinical examination reveals that tooth #8 (permanent maxillary right central incisor) exhibits Class II mobility, is displaced palatally, and is tender to percussion. Vitality testing is negative. Radiographs show a widened periodontal ligament space and displacement of the tooth, but no root fracture or alveolar bone fracture. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for tooth #8?
options: Immediate extraction of tooth #8
Reposition the tooth manually and stabilize with a flexible splint
Initiate root canal treatment immediately prior to repositioning
Prescribe systemic antibiotics and monitor without repositioning
prosthodontics-implants-476.explanation: Option B is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, the initial emergency management for a laterally luxated permanent tooth is gentle manual or digital repositioning into its original socket followed by stabilization with a flexible, passive splint for 4 weeks. Immediate extraction (Option A) is contraindicated as the periodontal ligament can heal with favorable long-term retention. Immediate endodontic therapy (Option C) should not precede repositioning and stabilization, and systemic antibiotics (Option D) are not indicated for uncomplicated dental luxations.

prosthodontics-implants-478.question: According to the American Dental Association (ADA) Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct, which ethical principle mandates that dentists have an obligation to maintain and update their professional knowledge and skills throughout their careers?
options: Patient autonomy
Nonmaleficence
Beneficence
Veracity
prosthodontics-implants-478.explanation: Option B is correct because Section 2.A (Education) of the ADA Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct places the duty of keeping knowledge and clinical skills current through continuing education under the principle of Nonmaleficence ('do no harm'). Patient autonomy (Option A) requires dentists to respect the patient's right to self-determination and confidentiality. Beneficence (Option C) mandates promoting the patient's welfare through competent and timely care, while veracity (Option D) requires truthfulness and integrity in all professional communications.

prosthodontics-implants-479.question: An 18-year-old male patient presents to your dental office with a fractured front tooth after falling while playing basketball one hour ago. He reports mild sensitivity to cold on the affected tooth but no spontaneous pain. Clinical examination reveals an uncomplicated crown fracture of tooth #9 (permanent maxillary left central incisor) involving enamel and dentin without pulp exposure. The fractured tooth fragment was stored in water and brought to the clinic intact. The tooth is not mobile and is non-tender to percussion. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Reattach the fractured tooth fragment using adhesive composite resin
Place a temporary zinc oxide-eugenol restoration and refer for endodontics
Initiate root canal treatment and place a full-coverage crown
Extract the tooth and plan for an immediate dental implant
prosthodontics-implants-479.explanation: Option A is correct because adhesive reattachment of the intact coronal tooth fragment using resin bonding agents is the gold-standard immediate management for an uncomplicated enamel-dentin crown fracture (Ellis Class II) when the segment is preserved. Endodontic referral or root canal therapy (Options B and C) is contraindicated because the pulp is unexposed, asymptomatic, and vital with normal periapical status. Extraction (Option D) is unnecessarily invasive and clinically contraindicated for a highly restorable, structurally sound incisor.

prosthodontics-implants-502.question: A 9-year-old female patient presents to the dental clinic after falling off her bicycle and sustaining facial trauma. Clinical examination reveals that tooth #8 (permanent maxillary right central incisor) is displaced lingually, locked firmly in the alveolar bone, and not mobile. There is no evidence of crown or root fracture. Radiographically, the periodontal ligament space is widened and the root apex is displaced labially. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate extraction of tooth #8
Reposition the tooth manually and stabilize with a flexible splint
Monitor for vitality changes and observe without repositioning
Initiate root canal treatment immediately prior to splinting
prosthodontics-implants-502.explanation: Option B is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, lateral luxation injuries with alveolar locking require immediate disengagement, gentle manual repositioning back into the anatomical socket, and stabilization with a flexible splint for 4 weeks. Immediate extraction (Option A) is contraindicated because permanent incisors have favorable healing outcomes when promptly repositioned. Passive observation (Option C) leads to osseous healing and ankylosis in an esthetically and functionally compromised position, while immediate root canal treatment (Option D) is not indicated before establishing periodontal stability and evaluating pulpal vitality.

prosthodontics-implants-505.question: A 40-year-old female patient presents with significant pain and swelling associated with a partially erupted tooth #17 (mandibular left third molar). Clinical examination reveals inflamed, erythematous gingival tissue partially covering the occlusal surface with purulent exudate upon pressure. Her body temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), and she has mild trismus. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate surgical extraction of tooth #17
Prescribe systemic antibiotics, perform local irrigation, and recommend warm saline rinses
Perform an immediate operculectomy under local anesthesia
Administer local infiltration and incise the inflamed operculum
prosthodontics-implants-505.explanation: Option B is correct because the patient demonstrates acute pericoronitis with systemic involvement (fever of 38.5°C and trismus), which necessitates local debridement and irrigation combined with systemic antibiotic therapy and warm saline rinses to control the infection. Immediate surgical extraction (Option A) and operculectomy (Option C) are contraindicated during the acute febrile phase due to the risk of disseminating infection into deep fascial spaces and poor local anesthetic efficacy in acidotic tissue. Incision of the operculum (Option D) is ineffective and unnecessary when purulent exudate can be mechanically evacuated via gentle subopercular irrigation.

prosthodontics-implants-506.question: A 65-year-old male patient presents with a fractured porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown on tooth #14 (maxillary left first molar). He reports that the buccal porcelain fractured off while eating hard food. Clinical examination reveals that the porcelain veneer has fractured off, exposing a substantial area of the underlying metal coping, but the crown margins are intact and the tooth is asymptomatic. What is the MOST appropriate definitive management?
options: Fabricate and cement a new full-coverage crown for tooth #14
Smooth the sharp edges of the remaining porcelain and monitor
Place a direct composite resin restoration to repair the fractured porcelain
Fabricate a cast metal onlay to place over the exposed coping
prosthodontics-implants-506.explanation: Option A is correct because the definitive management for a fractured porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown with extensive metal coping exposure in a high-stress molar region is replacement with a newly fabricated full-coverage restoration. Direct composite resin bonding to exposed metal (Option C) yields weak mechanical and chemical adhesion with poor longevity under heavy occlusal forces, serving only as an interim repair. Smoothing edges (Option B) leaves an unesthetic, abrasive metal surface that causes accelerated wear of opposing dentition, while placing an onlay over an existing coping (Option D) is biomechanically unacceptable.

prosthodontics-implants-595.question: On a maxillary periapical radiograph of the canine-premolar region, the radiopaque inverted Y-shaped structure (inverted Y of Ennis) is formed by the intersection of which two anatomical structures?
options: Anterior border of the maxillary sinus and lateral wall of the nasal cavity
Zygomatic process of the maxilla and inferior border of the maxillary sinus
Nasal septum and inferior nasal concha
Anterior nasal spine and lateral pterygoid plate
prosthodontics-implants-595.explanation: Option A is correct because the inverted Y of Ennis is a classic radiopaque landmark formed by the intersection of the anterior/inferior wall of the maxillary sinus and the lateral wall or floor of the nasal cavity. Option B describes anatomical structures that form the U-shaped or J-shaped radiopacity of the zygomatic process. Options C and D represent midfacial and posterior anatomical landmarks that do not contribute to the inverted Y configuration.

prosthodontics-implants-596.question: A 55-year-old female patient presents for a periodontal maintenance appointment. She has a history of generalized periodontitis, previously stabilized with scaling and root planing. Clinical examination reveals localized gingival inflammation and bleeding on probing around tooth #3, with a probing depth of 5 mm and radiographic evidence of localized horizontal bone loss. What is the MOST appropriate next step in the management of tooth #3?
options: Prescribe systemic amoxicillin and re-evaluate in 3 months.
Recommend immediate open flap debridement surgery.
Perform localized scaling and root planing and re-evaluate in 4 to 6 weeks.
Advise daily chlorhexidine rinse monotherapy without mechanical debridement.
prosthodontics-implants-596.explanation: Option C is correct because localized recurrent inflammation with bleeding on probing and a 5 mm probing depth during maintenance requires localized subgingival debridement (scaling and root planing) followed by re-evaluation in 4 to 6 weeks. Option A is incorrect because systemic antibiotics are not indicated for localized, manageable chronic periodontal defects and contribute to antimicrobial resistance. Options B and D are incorrect because surgical intervention is premature prior to re-evaluating non-surgical mechanical debridement, and chlorhexidine cannot penetrate subgingival pockets without prior root instrumentation.

prosthodontics-implants-597.question: An 8-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic 25 minutes after traumatic avulsion of tooth #8. The tooth was recovered immediately and stored in cold milk by the parents. Clinical examination confirms an intact alveolar socket, and tooth #8 exhibits an open apex with no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Gently rinse the root with saline, irrigate the socket, and replant the tooth immediately.
Scrub the root surface with a chlorhexidine brush prior to replantation.
Perform immediate extraoral pulpectomy and obturation prior to replantation.
Store the tooth in sterile saline and refer to an oral surgeon for delayed replantation.
prosthodontics-implants-597.explanation: Option A is correct because an avulsed permanent central incisor with an extraoral dry time under 60 minutes stored in physiologic medium (milk) should be gently rinsed with saline to preserve viable periodontal ligament cells, gently replanted, and stabilized. Option B is incorrect because scrubbing the root mechanically destroys viable PDL cells and induces replacement root resorption (ankylosis). Options C and D are incorrect because immature teeth with open apices have revascularization potential and should not undergo immediate extirpation, while delayed replantation predictably leads to PDL necrosis.

prosthodontics-implants-600.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with a dull, constant ache in the maxillary left posterior region that has persisted for two weeks. She reports that the discomfort worsens when she bends forward and notes concurrent nasal congestion with postnasal drip. Clinical examination reveals intact dentition with no caries or defective restorations, normal pulp sensibility responses to cold on all maxillary left teeth, and negative percussion and palpation findings. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
Acute maxillary sinusitis
Trigeminal neuralgia
prosthodontics-implants-600.explanation: Option C is correct because facial pressure exacerbated by postural changes (bending forward) accompanied by nasal congestion and postnasal drip in the presence of normal pulp sensibility and negative percussion findings is diagnostic of rhinogenic acute maxillary sinusitis. Options A and B are incorrect because pulpal and apical inflammatory diseases would produce abnormal thermal responses or localized percussion sensitivity, respectively. Option D is incorrect because trigeminal neuralgia manifests as sudden, unilateral, electric shock-like paroxysms triggered by light touch rather than a persistent dull postural ache.

prosthodontics-implants-544.question: A 60-year-old female patient presents with a white, corrugated lesion on her buccal mucosa that has been present for several months. She reports placing smokeless tobacco in that specific vestibule daily for over 20 years. Clinical examination reveals a diffuse, non-scrapable, leathery white patch measuring 2 x 3 cm without induration, ulceration, or erythema. What is the MOST appropriate initial management step?
options: Prescribe topical nystatin oral suspension for 14 days.
Advise cessation of smokeless tobacco use and re-evaluate in 2 to 3 weeks.
Perform an immediate excisional biopsy of the entire lesion.
Perform an immediate incisional biopsy of the thickest area.
prosthodontics-implants-544.explanation: Option B is correct because smokeless tobacco keratosis is a benign reactive hyperkeratosis that characteristically undergoes complete clinical resolution within 2 to 3 weeks following habit cessation, making cessation with scheduled re-evaluation the mandatory initial standard of care. Options C and D are incorrect because immediate invasive biopsy is premature unless the lesion persists, ulcerates, or shows induration after a 2- to 3-week trial of cessation. Option A is incorrect because this non-scrapable hyperkeratotic lesion is chemically induced rather than a fungal infection (candidiasis).

prosthodontics-implants-551.question: A 6-year-old female patient presents for restorative treatment. Clinical examination reveals an asymptomatic deep occlusal carious lesion on tooth K (mandibular left primary second molar). Radiographic examination shows the carious lesion extends into deep dentin approximating the pulp chamber without periapical or furcation radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate management for this tooth?
options: Indirect pulp therapy followed by placement of a stainless steel crown.
Direct pulp capping followed by an amalgam restoration.
Complete pulpectomy with gutta-percha obturation.
Topical application of fluoride varnish and periodic observation.
prosthodontics-implants-551.explanation: Option A is correct because indirect pulp therapy (IPT) followed by a full-coverage stainless steel crown has the highest long-term success rate for preserving pulpal vitality in asymptomatic primary molars with deep dentinal caries approximating the pulp. Option B is incorrect because direct pulp capping in primary teeth has an unacceptably high failure rate associated with internal root resorption. Options C and D are incorrect because pulpectomy with non-resorbable gutta-percha interferes with normal root resorption and eruption of the succedaneous premolar, while topical fluoride varnish cannot arrest cavitated lesions extending deep into dentin.

prosthodontics-implants-575.question: A 32-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of a persistent dull ache in the maxillary right posterior region that began shortly after receiving a deep amalgam restoration on tooth #3 one week ago. She reports pain when chewing on that tooth, but denies spontaneous pain or lingering sensitivity to cold or hot liquids. Clinical examination reveals tooth #3 is acutely tender to vertical percussion and exhibits a hyperocclusal contact in centric occlusion. Radiographs reveal no periapical pathology. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Initiate nonsurgical root canal therapy on tooth #3.
Extract tooth #3 and place an immediate implant.
Perform an occlusal adjustment on tooth #3.
Prescribe systemic amoxicillin and observe for 2 weeks.
prosthodontics-implants-575.explanation: Option C is correct because isolated tenderness to percussion and chewing following a recent restoration in the absence of lingering thermal sensitivity indicates acute apical periodontitis secondary to hyperocclusion, which is resolved promptly by occlusal adjustment. Option A is incorrect because the dental pulp remains healthy and vital without irreversible inflammatory symptoms. Options B and D are incorrect because extraction of a restorable tooth is unwarranted and systemic antibiotics have no role in managing mechanical, non-infectious occlusal trauma.

prosthodontics-implants-577.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents following a fall from a bicycle with trauma to the anterior mandible. Clinical examination reveals a displaced, highly mobile crown-root fracture extending subgingivally on tooth O (mandibular left primary central incisor). Radiographic examination confirms the fracture extends well below the alveolar crest, and the succedaneous tooth #24 appears intact and undamaged. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Extract tooth O.
Apply a flexible splint to adjacent teeth for 4 weeks.
Perform pulpectomy and coronal buildup on tooth O.
Rebond the fractured coronal segment using composite resin.
prosthodontics-implants-577.explanation: Option A is correct because an unrestorable, mobile crown-root fracture in a primary incisor carries a severe risk of pulp necrosis, localized abscess formation, and secondary damage or hypoplasia (Turner tooth) to the underlying succedaneous permanent incisor (tooth #24), mandating prompt extraction. Option B is incorrect because splinting cannot stabilize an extensive subgingival root fracture and compromises periodontal healing. Options C and D are incorrect because endodontic and restorative procedures are contraindicated when the fracture line extends subgingivally on a primary tooth.

prosthodontics-implants-556.question: Which of the following ligaments becomes taut during protrusion to provide the primary anatomical limitation to excessive anterior movement of the mandible?
options: Temporomandibular (lateral) ligament
Sphenomandibular ligament
Stylomandibular ligament
Capsular ligament
prosthodontics-implants-556.explanation: Option C is correct because the stylomandibular ligament extends from the styloid process to the posterior border of the ramus and angle of the mandible, becoming taut during mandibular protrusion to limit excessive anterior translation. Option A is incorrect because the temporomandibular (lateral) ligament limits posterior condylar displacement and rotational opening. Options B and D are incorrect because the sphenomandibular ligament acts as a passive axis of rotation without restricting protrusion, and the capsular ligament serves primarily to resist medial, lateral, and inferior distracting forces while enclosing the synovial space.

prosthodontics-implants-557.question: A 65-year-old female patient taking daily low-dose aspirin (81 mg) presents 4 hours after an uncomplicated extraction of tooth #3 (maxillary right first molar) with persistent slow oozing from the extraction socket. Intraoral examination reveals an incomplete clot with continuous capillary oozing, but no pulsatile arterial bleeding or expanding hematoma. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Prescribe a 7-day course of systemic amoxicillin and discharge.
Apply firm biting pressure over the extraction socket using a moist tea bag.
Administer an intramuscular injection of phytonadione (vitamin K).
Immediately discontinue aspirin therapy and refer to the emergency department.
prosthodontics-implants-557.explanation: Option B is correct because sustained local mechanical pressure combined with the local hemostatic and vasoconstrictive action of tannic acid in a moist tea bag is the recognized first-line management for post-extraction capillary oozing in patients taking antiplatelet therapy. Option A is incorrect because antibiotics have no hemostatic effect and are not indicated for routine extractions. Options C and D are incorrect because vitamin K antagonizes coumarin-derivative anticoagulants (warfarin) but has no effect on aspirin-induced cyclooxygenase-1 inhibition, and discontinuing aspirin postoperatively fails to treat acute bleeding while increasing thrombotic risk.

prosthodontics-implants-558.question: A 9-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic 30 minutes after traumatic avulsion of tooth #9 (maxillary left central incisor) following a sports injury. The tooth was recovered immediately, rinsed briefly with saline, and gently repositioned into the socket by his school nurse. Radiographic examination confirms correct anatomical repositioning and an open apical foramen. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Perform immediate pulpectomy and obturate the canal with gutta-percha on tooth #9.
Place a rigid stainless steel splint for 6 to 8 weeks.
Stabilize tooth #9 with a flexible, non-rigid splint for 1 to 2 weeks.
Extract tooth #9 and fabricate an immediate removable partial denture.
prosthodontics-implants-558.explanation: Option C is correct because American Association of Endodontists (AAE) and IADT guidelines recommend that an avulsed permanent incisor replanted within 60 minutes should be stabilized using a flexible, non-rigid splint for 1 to 2 weeks (7–14 days) to facilitate physiological periodontal ligament healing. Option A is incorrect because an immature tooth with an open apex has revascularization potential and must be monitored clinically and radiographically rather than undergoing immediate extirpation. Options B and D are incorrect because rigid, prolonged splinting promotes dentoalveolar ankylosis and replacement root resorption, while extraction is contraindicated for a successfully replanted permanent tooth.

prosthodontics-implants-570.question: An 8-year-old male patient presents with a localized anterior crossbite involving tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor). Clinical examination reveals adequate arch perimeter, a Class I molar relationship, and no underlying skeletal discrepancy. What is the MOST appropriate initial orthodontic intervention?
options: Comprehensive full fixed orthodontic appliances bonded to all erupted teeth.
Removable Hawley appliance incorporating a finger spring (or Z-spring).
Surgical Le Fort I osteotomy to advance the anterior maxilla.
Periodic observation until the permanent canines and premolars have fully erupted.
prosthodontics-implants-570.explanation: Option B is correct because an isolated anterior dental crossbite with adequate arch space in the mixed dentition is most effectively intercepted using a removable Hawley-type appliance with an auxiliary finger spring or Z-spring to tip the incisor labially. Option A is incorrect because comprehensive full fixed appliances represent unnecessary overtreatment for a single-tooth dental malposition in early mixed dentition.
